[#3810] Add async session-revocation sweep job with credential-watermark guard

Declare session.revoke.sweep queue with dlx/dlq.session.revoke pair.
Publisher.enqueue_session_revocation_sweep publishes {custid,
except_session_id, requested_at}; when jobs are disabled it runs the
sweep inline (small keyspaces sweep fast; the watermark, not the sweep,
is the security boundary). New Sneakers worker delegates to
RevokeAllForCustomerExceptCurrent with scan_untracked: true and rejects
to DLQ on error (op is idempotent, replay safe); scan_capped logs at
ERROR so a truncated sweep is never silent.

The op gains honor_credential_watermark: (default off, byte-compatible):
when set, blobs authenticated at/after Customer#last_password_update are
spared in both tracked and untracked purges, so the async sweep running
seconds after a credential change cannot kill the rotated current
session or a fresh post-reset login.

[#3810] Enqueue post-commit session sweep and rotate sid on password change

Both password hooks now register a db.after_commit block (first Sequel
after_commit use in the repo) that enqueues the full untracked sweep —
outside the Rodauth transaction, skipped on rollback, rescued internally
so a broker failure can never 500 a committed credential change. The
enqueue registers before the inline revoke so it doubles as the durable
retry the ACCEPTED RESIDUAL RISK comments promised.

after_reset_password now stamps the credential watermark (previously
only the change hook did). after_change_password re-stamps
session[authenticated_at] so the preserved session postdates the
watermark, then rotates the session id via rack.session.options renew
and tidies the old sid's sidecar and active_sessions entry — closing
the session-fixation gap on credential change.

[#3810] Reject sessions predating last credential change at auth time

Shared nil-safe predicate: authenticated_at < last_password_update
(strict, epoch ints). BaseSessionAuthStrategy fails stale sessions with
SESSION_STALE_CREDENTIALS across every app registering sessionauth; the
noauth path degrades to anonymous instead of 401. Missing
authenticated_at with a watermark set rejects (fail-secure stale legacy
blob); absent or zero watermark never rejects, so deploying this cannot
mass-logout users who never changed a password.

This makes revocation authoritative by construction: a session blob the
sidecar index missed can no longer outlive a credential change, closing
the residual gap in #3810 — enumerated deletion (hooks + sweep job) is
now hygiene, not the security boundary.

[#3810] Harden credential-watermark stamping with email fallback and loud failure

UpdatePasswordMetadata resolved the customer by external_id only, so a
NULL-external_id account (schema-legal) never got its watermark stamped
and the async sweep then ran unguarded — killing the freshly rotated
session. Resolve external_id-first with email fallback, matching the
hooks' custid derivation and the revoke op's load_customer.

Both hooks now surface a failed stamp explicitly instead of letting
safe_execute swallow it to a warn: :credential_watermark_stamp_FAILED at
error level (+ Sentry, tagged M-2) since the watermark is the
authoritative revocation boundary. A stamp failure still never fails the
password change. Comments note the Redis stamp is not rollback-aware
(fail-secure) and that rotated-session sweep protection is conditional
on the stamp landing.

[#3810] Surface inline-sweep outcomes and release idempotency claim on failure

The jobs-disabled inline branch of enqueue_session_revocation_sweep
discarded the op Result, silently dropping scan_capped — the exact
condition the worker escalates to ERROR. Capture it: ERROR on
scan_capped, info with counts otherwise, and WARN (not info) when
config says jobs enabled but the pool never initialized (configured
async, runtime degraded). Docblock corrected: publish errors propagate
only from a live pool; a never-initialized pool degrades to inline.

The worker's idempotency claim (1h TTL) was never released on failure,
making a DLQ replay within the hour a silent ack-no-op. New
BaseWorker#release_processing_claim, called before reject! — safe
precisely because the op is idempotent — so operator replay actually
re-runs. Also register session.revoke.sweep in the queue ping map.

[#3810] Cover noauth watermark degrade; mark identity flags non-authoritative

The Helpers#load_user_from_session watermark path (stale session on an
anonymous-capable route must degrade to nil user, not resolve the
customer) had no test — a refactor could drop the check silently. Pin
both directions: stale degrades to anonymous, at-watermark resolves.

IdentityResolution's resolved-identity env flags deliberately skip the
credential watermark: no consumer gates on them; the authoritative check

[#3837] Normalize request scheme behind TLS-terminating proxies via AssumeHttps

Behind a proxy that terminates TLS and forwards plain HTTP without
X-Forwarded-Proto (e.g. Cloudflare Tunnel), the origin sees every request
as non-SSL. The production-forced Secure session cookie is then silently
never written -> fresh empty session each request -> CSRF token mismatch
surfaced as a misleading 403. Root cause of #3831.

Add Onetime::Middleware::AssumeHttps, mounted FIRST so the normalized
scheme is visible to every downstream middleware and the mounted auth app.
Upgrade-only: it marks http->https only when site.network.assume_https
(ASSUME_HTTPS=true) is set AND the request is not already SSL. It never
downgrades, never strips/rewrites forwarded headers, and is a strict no-op
when off -- native Rack X-Forwarded-Proto handling for nginx/Caddy/ALB is
untouched. Opt-in and off by default; does not weaken the M-7 secure
default. Config flag and the mixed-content footgun are documented in
config.defaults.yaml and .env.reference.

[#3837] Unify API v1 secure? on Rack request.ssl? instead of header sniffing

secure? hand-rolled its own scheme check (HTTP_X_FORWARDED_PROTO /
HTTP_X_SCHEME), a third scheme-detection path that diverged from Rack's
Request#scheme and from the session cookie's Secure gate. Route it through
request.ssl? so the whole app agrees on one scheme signal -- the same
signal AssumeHttps normalizes and the session-cookie diagnostics report on.

[#3837] Warn loudly when a Secure session cookie is silently dropped

Rack's PersistedSecure#security_matches? returns false when a :secure
cookie meets a request it sees as non-SSL, and commit_session then bails
before writing Set-Cookie -- silently. That silent drop is the failure in
#3837/#3831.

Override security_matches? for observability only: it returns the parent's
verdict unchanged and never touches @assume_ssl semantics. When the drop
happens it emits a throttled (once per 5 min/process) warning that carries
its own proof -- a scheme_evidence snapshot of the signals Rack's
Request#scheme consults (rack.url_scheme value; presence/absence of
X-Forwarded-Proto, Forwarded, X-Forwarded-Ssl, HTTPS). Presence/absence
rather than raw values: we reach this path only when req.ssl? is already
false, so any header present did not carry https, and booleans keep the
forwarded client IP (RFC 7239 for=) out of the logs. The next field report
then contains the observation directly instead of us reconstructing it.

session_scheme_try.rb (12 cases) pins the AssumeHttps upgrade, the dropped-
cookie warning + evidence snapshot, the X-Forwarded-Proto-alone regression,
and the upgrade-only no-op/no-downgrade invariants.

[#3837] Distinguish session-continuity break from token mismatch on CSRF 403

A dropped session cookie and a genuinely bad CSRF token both surface as an
identical 403, so the #3831 root cause read as an "attack prevented" false
positive. Capture whether the session already held a CSRF token BEFORE
delegating down the stack (rack-protection's AuthenticityToken mutates the
session via set_token during validation, so it must be sampled first), then
on a 403 for an unsafe method log one of two distinct lines: token-mismatch
(session had a token) vs session-continuity break (no token at request
start -- the #3837 signature). Logs method and path only, never token
values. Safe methods and non-403 responses are not logged.

[#3858] Address review: blob-wins merge, authoritative commit TTL ceiling, tests

Follow-up to the SessionSidecar checkpoint, folding in the test/review pass
and reviewer feedback on PR #3861.

merge (read-side): a blob-resident copy now WINS over the sidecar on conflict.
A blob still carrying an externalized field means its last write happened
without a successful sidecar commit (pre-deploy writer, or the commit-failure
fallback), so the blob copy is at least as fresh. The old sidecar-wins rule
laundered a stale value back to freshness on every commit: an awaiting_mfa=true
whose clearing SET-false was lost to a transient pipeline failure would override
the blob's healing false each request, be re-committed with a fresh 900s TTL,
and lock the authenticated session out of every gated route indefinitely.
Blob-wins bounds that degradation to the documented single cycle -- the next
healthy commit re-externalizes the blob copy and heals the sidecar. Outranked
fields still count as merged so commit owns their lifecycle (heal-by-SET while
present, DEL on app-side delete).

commit (write-side) TTL ceiling: the middleware's expire_after passed via
ceiling: is now AUTHORITATIVE. write_session refreshes the blob to exactly that
TTL in the same request, right after commit, so it -- not the blob's
about-to-be-overwritten remaining TTL -- is the clamp ceiling. Reading the stale
remaining TTL stranded a fresh sidecar on a rolling session's last seconds (a
new awaiting_mfa landing on a blob with 10s left got EX 10, then the blob was
extended a full day). The standalone write() path, which does not refresh the
blob, still clamps to the live remaining TTL. clamp_ttl is now total: a
non-positive ceiling falls back to the module default instead of raising.

authoritative-ceiling and standalone-write ceiling cases (sidecar_try);

[#3857] Make Rodauth reset-password-request path enumeration-safe

In full auth mode the Rodauth app is mounted at /auth and, because
Rack::URLMap dispatches to the longest matching prefix, it handles every
/auth/* route -- including POST /auth/reset-password-request. That route
(not the enumeration-safe custom endpoint in apps/web/core, which is
shadowed) is what unauthenticated callers actually reach.

Stock Rodauth 2.44.0 distinguishes "account exists" from "no account" on
that request path in three ways, each an account-existence oracle
(CWE-204): no_matching_login for an unknown login, unverified_account for
an existing-but-unopen account, and a "recently sent" error for an
existing account emailed moments earlier. A registered, verified account
gets 200 { success: "An email has been sent..." } while a non-existent
login gets an error tuple with a field-error, letting a caller enumerate
accounts.

Disabling the request route is not viable: in full mode the reset consume
path (/auth/reset-password) is Rodauth's and expects a Rodauth-generated
token, and the reset email links to it, so the request path must remain
Rodauth's to mint that token. Instead, override the three oracle branches
(config/overrides/reset_password_enumeration.rb) so every POST returns the
same generic "email sent" response. Side effects (key + email) still
happen only for a valid, open, non-throttled account, and Rodauth's resend
throttle is preserved -- a recently-emailed account returns the same
success without resending, so closing the oracle opens no email-bomb path.

The no_matching_login override is scoped to the reset-password-request
route via current_route so the shared account_from_login is unchanged on
the login route and everywhere else.

Adds an integration regression test asserting an existing (verified)
login, an unverified account, and a throttled account each yield a
response identical to a non-existent login.

[#3858] Move sidecar keys to a disjoint sidecar: namespace

session:<sid>:<field> intersected the shared *session* scan, forcing a
client-side reject (SIDECAR_KEY_PATTERN) into Store.scan_keys and the
account-close/email-change sweeps — and because the reject ran after the
MAX_SCAN cap, truncation reporting needed the raw-vs-survivor split that
scan_keys_capped existed to carry. Renaming the prefix to
sidecar:<sid>:<field> makes the namespaces disjoint by construction, so
this deletes the pattern, the rejects, and scan_keys_capped outright, and
restores `keys.size >= MAX_SCAN` as an exact truncation signal.

The constraint now lives in SessionSidecar.key_for (the prefix must never
contain the substring "session") and is pinned by a File.fnmatch
regression test against the real derived key name.

Cost: operators glob two namespaces (sidecar:<sid>:* alongside
session:<sid>) instead of one. In exchange no scan consumer needs to know
sidecar keys exist. Net -33 lines.

Fix CloseAccount session sweep skipping all encrypted sessions

delete_redis_sessions decoded session values as base64(json)--hmac, but
the middleware writes AES-256-GCM encrypted blobs
(base64(iv+tag+ciphertext)--hmac). The base64 part decoded to binary
ciphertext, JSON.parse raised, and the per-key rescue skipped the blob —
so closing an account silently left every authenticated session alive.

Decode through Store.load_data with a SessionCodec built from the same
secret-resolution chain the middleware uses (ENV SESSION_SECRET, then
site secret); load_data falls back to legacy plaintext JSON, preserving
the old behavior for pre-encryption blobs. The per-key rescue widens to
StandardError so one undecodable key can never abort the whole sweep.

Tryouts plant a codec-encrypted blob for the closing account plus one
for another account and assert the real Redis effects: match deleted,
non-match survives, count returned.

Extracted from #3861 so the fix can merge on its own timeline.

[#3859] Make SSO connect-intent nonce single-use via short-TTL sidecar key

The account-bound connect-intent nonce (#3840 Phase 2) was cleared at
exactly one site: the delete-on-read in account_from_omniauth. A connect
abandoned at the IdP (cancel, IdP error, closed tab) never reaches that
callback, leaving the intent live in the session blob for the NEXT SSO
callback -- even a plain connect=0 sign-in -- to consume and bind on:
the shared-browser bind the nonce exists to prevent.

Store the nonce as the sidecar key sidecar:<sid>:sso_connect_intent
(SessionSidecar, #3858) instead of a session-blob field:

- Registered as an explicit-use field: 300s TTL (one IdP round-trip),
  encrypted (account id, capability-adjacent; codec binds sid+field so
  a Redis-writing attacker cannot replay one session's intent under
  another), never merged or externalized. Registry membership makes
  every purge surface (logout, revocation sweeps, email-change,
  close-account) cover it with no further changes.
- Request phase writes the sidecar key on connect=1; on any NON-connect
  initiation it deletes a dangling intent, so a plain sign-in kills a
  stale nonce before its own callback runs (every callback's flow mints
  its state in this phase first). TTL covers every other abandonment
  path unconditionally.
- Callback consumes via atomic GETDEL; a miss means absent-or-expired
  and stays default-deny. Blob copies written by pre-#3859 code are
  discarded unconsumed.

Regression specs: abandoned-then-expired intent must not bind (H-3
fall-through); abandoned intent followed by a plain sign-in within the
TTL must be cleared at the request phase and must not bind; a
successful connect consumes the nonce. Tryouts lock the registry
policy and the single-use consume round-trip.

Closes #3859

[#3840] Phase 4: mailbox-proof SSO linking for passwordless accounts

When an unauthenticated SSO sign-in resolves to an existing PASSWORDLESS
account, Phase 3's password interstitial cannot help (no password to
challenge) and the flow dead-ended at the H-3 refusal. This adds the
passwordless counterpart: the account proves ownership via control of its
on-file mailbox — the same proof magic-link (email_auth) uses.

The callback emails a single-use token to the on-file address and redirects
the browser to a TOKEN-LESS notice; the token never rides the callback
redirect, so a caller who merely completed an SSO round-trip asserting the
victim's email cannot self-consume it. Binding (provider, issuer, uid) happens
only when the user clicks the emailed link and confirms. Preserves the
invariant "email may LOCATE an account; only a demonstrated credential may
BIND" — mailbox control is the credential. Platform surface only (tenant
callbacks keep the H-3 refusal).

Backend:
- Onetime::SsoLinkVerification single-use token (Redis, 15-min TTL) snapshotting
  provider/issuer/uid/email/account_id/sid/password_watermark.
- account_from_omniauth passwordless branch: issue token, email on-file address
  (sync, fail-closed), token-less redirect (?auth_notice=link_verification_sent).
- Auth::Operations::ConfirmSsoLink: atomic single-use consume -> ownership
  re-check -> watermark (credential-change) invalidation -> MFA-safe deferred
  bind -> bind via shared BindSsoIdentity primitive.
- GET/POST /auth/sso-link-confirm: display-only GET (never consumes), POST

[#3877] Move the deferred SSO bind stash onto SessionSidecar (#3858)

The pending link-sso bind was a distributed session-blob hand-off: the
route wrote a hash under a string key, two hooks read it, and the whole
contract hung on the timing assumption that nothing clears the session
between login_session and the MFA-verify request. This replaces it with
a registered explicit-use SessionSidecar field — the sso_connect_intent
pattern:

  sidecar:<sid>:link_sso_pending_bind
  { ttl: 900, encrypted: true, merge_on_read: false, externalize: false }

What the sidecar buys over the blob stash:

- BOUNDED IN TIME: the 900s TTL matches awaiting_mfa's MFA completion
  window, so an abandoned half-done MFA login expires the pending bind
  with the window instead of leaving it live for the blob's full 24h.
- ATOMIC SINGLE-USE: complete consumes via GETDEL at the store, replacing
  the Ruby delete-then-act sequence; two concurrent completions can never
  both observe the stash.
- SID/FIELD-BOUND ENVELOPE: a stash value replayed under another sid
  decodes as absent — a property the blob-resident hash did not have.
- REGISTRY-DRIVEN CLEANUP: logout/delete_session purge covers the field
  with no new code.

The admission rule holds by construction: absence of the stash means no
bind, which is the flow's documented fail-closed state, and the bind is
already best-effort by contract (audit-and-skip) — so `.defer` swallows
storage failures rather than aborting a login whose password already
verified.

The sid is read inside the rodauth.login block (session.id&.public_id),
the only point that both sees the login's FINAL sid (login_session
re-keys it) and precedes after_login's self-heal reader; the sid is then
stable through the MFA hand-off. A legacy blob-resident stash from a
pre-sidecar writer is discarded unconsumed (rolling-deploy hygiene,
mirroring the sso_connect_intent migration).

Unit spec now exercises the real encrypted envelope via SessionCodec
against a minimal in-memory Redis stand-in; the sidecar tryout locks in
the registry policy and round-trip. The AUTH_MFA_ENABLED integration
lane covers the end-to-end path unchanged.

[#3858] Warn when a session is destroyed with in-flight sidecar state

Tripwire for the sid-stability assumption the short-TTL hand-off fields
(awaiting_mfa, sso_connect_intent, link_sso_pending_bind) ride on: their
consume sides cannot log a miss — absence is their overwhelmingly common
case — so a future auth refactor that re-keys sessions mid-flow would
strand them silently, detectable only by the integration suite.

The registry gains a destroy_warn policy flag, and the middleware's
delete_session probes those fields (SessionSidecar#inflight_fields, one
pipelined GET) before the purge, logging a warning naming any that still
hold a live TRUTHY value. Truthy, not present, is the line: every
authenticated login parks awaiting_mfa=false (refreshed each commit), so
key existence would fire on every logout and drown the signal.

Scoped to the request-path middleware: the admin/colonel revoke
operations destroy sessions deliberately, where killing in-flight state
is the point, not a signal. Probe failure degrades to no-warning and
never blocks the purge.

[#3858] Converge falsy awaiting_mfa to absent instead of parking it

Every reader of awaiting_mfa treats absence as false (the M-11 guard in
BaseSessionAuthStrategy checks == true), yet every completed MFA login
left a sidecar key storing false, refreshed with a fresh TTL on every
commit for the session's remaining life. The false itself is
load-bearing for exactly one failure case — if the MFA-completion
request's sidecar commit fails, write_session's rescue keeps it in the
blob, where blob-wins outranks the stale sidecar true whose DEL was
lost (a deletion could not win that conflict; without the tombstone the
stale true would re-merge and re-commit indefinitely, locking the
authenticated session out of every gated route). The perpetual re-SET
afterwards was incidental residue of that one-request role.

Make falsy-is-absent a registry policy instead: a new absent_when_falsy
axis (set only on awaiting_mfa) under which commit treats a present
falsy value exactly like an app-side deletion — DEL the sidecar key and
strip the field from the blob. The heal is preserved (on commit failure
the false still lands in the blob via the rescue; the next healthy
commit converges it to a DEL), and the steady state for authenticated
sessions becomes absent-everywhere: no parked key, no per-commit SET.

The MFA-success hook now writes the healing false under the STRING key
('awaiting_mfa', the one the registry, PrepareMfaSession, and the guard
all use) instead of the symbol, so convergence happens on the completion
request itself rather than one request later via the blob's JSON
round-trip; the comment there now documents the tombstone role in place
of the misleading "Clear awaiting_mfa flag".

inflight_fields keeps its truthy (not existence) line: a stored false
can still appear transiently — e.g. parked by a pre-absent_when_falsy
worker during a rolling deploy — and remains healthy residue, not an
in-flight hand-off.

Tryouts: heal cases now assert the DEL (key gone, blob stripped,
converged absent) instead of a re-SET false; new cases pin the registry
policy, falsy-commit-DELs for awaiting_mfa, and falsy-commit-still-SETs
for fields without the policy. MFA integration lane, interstitial and
connect-link suites, and the DeferredSsoBind unit spec all green.

fix(colonel): index-backed customer detail + contained row controls

Three operator-reported bugs in the admin User Management surface.

1. The customer detail page timed out. scan_user_secrets and
   scan_user_receipts each walked the whole secret:*/receipt:* keyspace,
   issuing one object load per key to filter by owner. The 10k guard
   counted MATCHES, not keys scanned, so it never tripped for a normal
   account and the loop always ran to cursor == '0'.

   Receipts now read customer:<id>:receipts, which is already written at
   every authenticated creation path (cust.add_receipt) and was
   backfilled by the v0.24.5 upgrade script -- the scan is deleted, not
   merely bounded. Secrets get a new symmetric customer:<id>:secrets
   index written at the SAME two chokepoints as the secrets_active
   counter (Receipt.spawn_pair and Secret#destroy!), so index and counter
   can only drift together. The index is trimmed to SECRET_INDEX_LIMIT on
   write, so it is bounded by construction.

   Pre-index accounts keep a fallback scan, but bounded by SCAN ROUNDS
   and a monotonic wall-clock deadline -- never by match count -- and any
   partial result sets details.{secrets,receipts}.truncated so the UI
   says the list is partial instead of implying it is complete. Object
   loads are pipelined via load_multi. Each section is read behind its
   own rescue, so a slow or failing activity lookup degrades that section
   alone and the rest of the record still renders.

2. RevealEmail's toggle and copy button bubbled into the row's @click,
   so revealing an address also opened the detail drawer. Fixed at the
   component so every console table inherits it; the address text still
   activates the row like any other cell. Audited all consumers -- none
   depended on the bubbling -- and the other clickable-row tables
   (sessions, domains) already contained their controls.

3. Added a per-row link from the customers table straight to the detail
   page. A real router-link (middle-click / new-tab must work) with
   @click.stop and an accessible name, matching the domains table's
   existing row-escalation precedent.

Also noted in-file: export_usage.rb still has the match-count-capped
variant of bug 1 (its cap counts date-range matches); list_secrets.rb has
the same shape but filters nothing, so its cap does bound the scan.

[#3840] security(sso): refuse issuerless providers on tenant surfaces (PR #3900 P1)

GitHub/Google carry no issuer, so every surface resolves them to the
shared '' sentinel and the step-1 exact (provider, '', uid) lookup —
which has no platform_path gate — matches identity rows created on the
platform or another tenant. rodauth-omniauth then logs the matched
account in before any tenant refusal in hooks/omniauth.rb runs, and the
additive org-join pulls it into the callback tenant's org.

Fail closed: refuse_issuerless_on_tenant? rejects issuerless callbacks
on tenant surfaces before lookup_identity, blocking both the
cross-surface match and JIT-creation of a colliding '' row. Platform
issuerless SSO and tenant OIDC/Entra (real, distinct issuers) are
unaffected. Reuses the sso_not_configured auth_error code.

Consequence: tenant GitHub/Google SSO is disabled — there is no
per-tenant issuer to isolate on, so these providers cannot satisfy the
surface-isolation invariant. Follow-up: drop github/google from tenant
SsoConfig PROVIDER_TYPES.

Confirms greptile P1 'Issuerless identities cross tenant boundaries'.

chore(review): disable greptile score, scope invariant exemptions, add non-blocking channel

Follow-ups from the empirical review-value analysis of the last 250 PRs
(git-level iteration data + 48-PR stratified review-thread sample):

1. Disable greptile confidence score, issues table, and summary sections.
   All 31 observed scores in the sample were 4/5 or 5/5; re-reviews left
   the score unchanged (#3843: 4/5 both rounds). A saturated metric cannot
   distinguish a median PR from a strong one, and re-scoring for
   consistency spends a review cycle moving a number nobody can act on.
   Qualitative findings remain enabled via commentTypes: ["logic"].

2. Drop customContext.rules from greptile.json. The {id, rule} shape is
   unverified against the documented schema, so the entries risked being
   silently ignored. The same invariants live in AGENTS.md, which greptile
   indexes and the instructions reference.

3. Scope the invariant exemptions to the current mechanisms. A blanket
   "do not flag" on OAuth state binding and sidecar TTL semantics would
   also silence the reviewer on the PR that breaks the mechanism itself
   (e.g. an omniauth-oauth2 downgrade below 1.9 or a second state slot).
   Security findings were 13% of real review findings in the sample;
   exemptions now explicitly go in-scope when the enforcing mechanism
   changes. Applied to AGENTS.md, greptile instructions, copilot
   instructions, and the claude-review prompt.

4. Reopen the deferred-improvements channel, bounded. 31 of 48 sampled
   PRs turned review observations into follow-up issues (#3634 ->
   #3649-#3651); SessionSidecar and BindSsoIdentity both originated as
   review observations. A strict defects-only bar closes that pipeline.
   Reviewers may now raise at most two explicitly non-blocking structural
   observations per review; author tickets or declines, neither blocks
   merge.

the customer un-verifiable through every admin surface.

live statuses so Closed rows are never touched; legacy rows fall back to
email restricted to unlinked (external_id IS NULL) live rows, never bare
email. A row that exists but is not live raises the new AccountClosed
error, which the CLI verify/unverify commands and the colonel
set-verification endpoint report cleanly.

The Rodauth after_verify_account hook path is unaffected: it passes
rodauth_already_synced: true and never reaches the SQL update.

Regression coverage runs the real migrations on SQLite (which supports
partial indexes) and pins both failure modes RED against the old code:
silent resurrection and the mid-statement constraint violation.

patching call sites. Scoped with :not(:disabled) so disabled buttons fall
through to the browser default instead of showing a misleading pointer.

utilities layer, which the cascade orders after base regardless of specificity.

Audit failures of destructive admin ops, not just successes

Every AdminAuditEvent.record call site sits inside the success path, after
the mutation. When an op raises (privilege guard, precondition, validation,
unexpected error) that line never executes, so the trail shows only what
worked. Passing result: :failure at those call sites would change nothing —
they do not run. This is structural, not an argument sweep.

Onetime::AuditedFailure supplies the structure as a declarative class macro.
It prepends a rescue around the op's entry method that records exactly one
result: :failure event and re-raises the original exception unchanged, so
callers, control flow, and HTTP status mapping are untouched.

One mechanism, two hierarchies: the macro takes the entry method name, so it
covers Operations (#call, also driven by the CLI) and the colonel Logic
classes that mutate inline (#process). Opt-in per class rather than a
base-class wrapper — most colonel Logic classes are reads, and reads must
never write an audit event (CONTRACT 4).

Authorization rejections are never recorded. The set is capped by COUNT with
no TTL, so an event an unauthorized caller can trigger is a log-eviction
primitive: 10k rejected requests would flush the real trail. Two controls
keep that closed — for Logic classes the wrapped method (#process) runs after
raise_concerns, where verify_one_of_roles! lives, and Forbidden/Unauthorized
are dropped by class as defense-in-depth. Everything else post-authorization
is recorded.

Nesting records once: the exception instance is tagged, so an outer audited
frame re-raising the same error does not write a second event.

Applied to the destructive/privileged ops first: customer purge/set_role/

write an event.

success on the applied path only — a preview mutates nothing and audits
nothing. Failure auditing therefore introduced an asymmetry: a preview that
blew up wrote a domain.remove / queue.dlq.purge failure event with no possible

failed mutation. Remove defaults dry_run to TRUE, so that was the common case.

failure's own identity), and both ops declare dry_run through it. Same rules as
any audit detail: public ids only, never secret content. A detail lambda that
raises or returns a non-Hash is dropped — extra context is never worth risking
the event itself.

  check-and-record (same shape as IncomingRateLimiter) with a tight
  per-client-IP tier (default 10/hour) and a higher per-submitted-login
  backstop (default 30/hour, case-normalized) that bounds IP-rotating
  callers probing one target. Both tiers key only on request-observable
  inputs, never on account existence, so the 429 introduces no new
  oracle. The per-email tier is deliberately the looser one so a tight
  email-only lockout cannot be weaponized as a targeted reset-flow DoS
  (the RL-3 pattern from LoginRateLimiter).

  limiter on POST only, using the trusted-proxy-resolved, privacy-masked
  client IP (env['otto.client_ip'], request.ip fallback) so forwarded
  headers cannot spoof the subject. A missing IP skips the IP tier
  rather than pooling unknown callers into a poisonable shared bucket.

  unhandled-exception error log; the router's error_handler translates

fix(deps): pin patched brace-expansion per major line (CVE-2026-14257)

The advisory (GHSA-mh99-v99m-4gvg) is written `<=5.0.7` / patched `>=5.0.8`,
which reads as "only v5 is safe". It isn't: the EXPANSION_MAX_LENGTH fix was
backported to every maintenance line — 1.1.17, 2.1.3, 3.0.5, 5.0.8.

Taking the range literally produced an unshippable fix. brace-expansion v5 is
ESM-first and its CJS build exports `{EXPANSION_MAX, EXPANSION_MAX_LENGTH,
expand}` where v1/v2 export a bare callable. minimatch@3 and @9 do
`const expand = require('brace-expansion')`, so a flat '5.0.8' override is a
TypeError at require() time. The tree carries three minimatch majors and none
can move: @3 comes from eslint 9 itself (@eslint/config-array, @eslint/eslintrc),
@9 from glob@10 and editorconfig, @10 from typescript-estree, glob@13, ts-morph.

Pin the patched floor per line instead:

  minimatch@3.1.5  -> brace-expansion 1.1.17
  minimatch@9.0.9  -> brace-expansion 2.1.3
  minimatch@10.2.4 -> brace-expansion 5.0.8

Also drop the "brace-expansion": "5.0.8" entry from package.json dependencies.
It existed only to force resolution — nothing in src/ imports the package — and
it dragged a dev-only transitive into the production graph.

Verified with the advisory's own PoC: expand('{a,b}'.repeat(1500)) returns a
bounded 2666 results in under 300ms on all three installed copies instead of
crashing the process with a fatal OOM. lint:quick and type-check both exit 0.

`pnpm audit` still reports this advisory against 1.1.17 and 2.1.3 — a false
positive from the `<=5.0.7` range, not an unpatched dependency. Left visible
rather than blanket-ignoring a high-severity GHSA; no CI job gates on audit.
Renovate is disabled for brace-expansion so the flat v5 pin stops coming back.

Gate domain sign-in SSO controls on tenant SSO, not platform SSO

The Single Sign-On controls on /org/:orgid/domains/:extid/signin read the
PLATFORM SSO flag (bootstrap features.sso = AUTH_SSO_ENABLED, resolved by
ConfigSerializer against the current request's display_domain — the canonical
workspace host). Per-domain SSO is TENANT SSO (CustomDomain::SsoConfig
credentials), whose authorities are ORGS_SSO_ENABLED + manage_sso. This page
was the sole surface on that axis; DomainsTable and OrganizationSettings
already gate on isOrgsSsoEnabled() && can(MANAGE_SSO).

Root of the confusion: signin_config.rb still documents
`field :sso_enabled  # Override for AUTH_SSO_ENABLED`, but sso_permitted_for?
repurposed it as the tenant-SSO activation gate feeding
SsoConfig.tenant_sso_available_for? and the omniauth_tenant hook. One field,
two meanings; the UI implemented the stale one. `ssoAvailable` arrived with
the ADR-024 {email_auth, webauthn, sso} triple — harmless for the other two
(genuinely install-wide), wrong for SSO.

- Drop `sso` from GlobalMethodAvailability; the form reads isOrgsSsoEnabled().
- Seed sso_enabled from the backend authority instead of the platform flag.
  createSeededFormState previously seeded it from features.sso, and since the
  page auto-saves a full-replacement PUT, the first edit to ANY field
  persisted {enabled: true, sso_enabled: false} on installs with platform SSO
  off — flipping sso_permitted_for? to false and darkening a domain's working
  tenant SSO. Both seed call sites run with no record, where
  sso_permitted_for? returns true unconditionally, so the inherited state is
  literally true. Same failure class as the PR #3817 signin_enabled bug.
- Report the STORED sso_enabled on the toggle. ORGS_SSO_ENABLED and manage_sso
  govern who may CONFIGURE tenant SSO; the runtime ladder
  (SsoConfig.tenant_sso_unavailable_reason) never consults them, so ANDing
  them into :enabled rendered OFF for domains whose SSO is live. The lock is
  expressed by :disabled alone.

[#3856] Close account-enumeration oracle in invite signup

The invite signup endpoint (POST /api/invite/:token/signup) returned a
distinct account_exists error_type when the invited email already had an
account, re-opening the enumeration oracle the AZ7 hardening removed
from the sibling show-invite endpoint. Any registered user could mint an
invitation for an arbitrary address (the create response includes the
token), probe the signup endpoint with a junk password, and cleanly read
account existence off the error_type — non-destructively, since the
existence checks ran before password validation.

Align the endpoint to the AZ7 generic posture:

- Validate the password BEFORE any account-existence check, so an
  invalid-password probe gets a byte-identical password_too_short error
  whether or not the account exists.
- Collapse every existing-account outcome (authdb pre-check, Redis
  pre-check, and the Rodauth create-race in the InternalRequestError
  rescue) into one chokepoint that raises a generic signup_unavailable
  error with a conditional message that never confirms account
  existence.
- Frontend keys its sign-in fallback off the new error_type instead of
  sniffing the message for "already exists"; the accountExists /
  account-exists plumbing is renamed signinRequired / signin-required
  since the client no longer learns that an account exists. Invitee UX
  is unchanged.

Documented residual (ratified inline): with a valid password, "exists"
(the generic error) remains distinguishable from "does not exist"
(signup succeeds). That is inherent to any signup endpoint, and probing
it is destructive and noisy — it creates the account and emails the
invitee. The per-IP InviteTokenRateLimiter bounds it.

Regression specs assert identical error payloads across both existence
stores and across exists/not-exists invalid-password probes, that
error_type account_exists is never used, and that the create-race path
returns the same generic error. Frontend specs cover error_type-driven
detection on both the 200-with-error and 422 paths, and that message
text mentioning existing accounts no longer flips the signin fallback.

Closes #3856

fix(auth): revoke sessions on password change/reset in simple mode

Password change (UpdatePassword) and self-service reset (ResetPassword)
never revoked other active sessions or stamped
Customer#last_password_update in simple mode — the application default —
because the M-2 defenses live only in the full-mode Rodauth hooks
(after_change_password / after_reset_password), which never fire there.
A stolen session survived the victim's own password change or reset for
the full session TTL (HIGH finding, 2026-07-30 audit, #3948).

Add Onetime::Logic::CredentialChangeSessionRevocation, a simple-mode
counterpart of the hook sequence with the same ordering and fail-secure
posture: stamp the credential watermark (the authoritative revocation
boundary for the auth-time <= check), enqueue the async full sweep
(#3810; inline fallback when jobs are disabled), then run the inline
tracked-only revoke (scan_untracked: false keeps the keyspace SCAN off
the request path). Each step rescues independently and loudly
(error-level auth log + Sentry) so a non-revoking change alerts instead
of blending into routine logging.

UpdatePassword keeps the session the user changed their password from
and re-stamps its authenticated_at strictly past the watermark (the
full-mode hooks' post-rotation maneuver); an unresolvable current sid
degrades to revoking ALL sessions. ResetPassword revokes ALL sessions —
the user followed an email link and holds no session worth keeping.

Covered by new tryouts: other-session blob + index revocation, kept
session preserved and re-stamped, watermark stamped on both paths, and
the fail-secure no-sid path.

fix(auth): repair broken simple-mode password reset flow

Writing tryouts for the session-revocation fix surfaced that the
simple-mode reset completion (POST /auth/reset-password) was broken
end-to-end on main by three independent pre-existing bugs — every
attempt 500'd before reaching the passphrase change:

1. ResetPasswordRequest created the reset secret with the legacy v1
   positional call (`Secret.create! email, [email]`), which mapped the
   EMAIL into the identifier and left owner_id nil. That made the
   emailed token (/forgot/:identifier) the user's own email address —
   guessable by anyone — and broke ResetPassword#process, whose
   `secret.load_owner` returned nil. Now uses the owner_id keyword,
   matching RequestEmailChange, so the identifier is the auto-generated
   unguessable objid and the owner resolves. The nil-token risk was not
   exploitable only because of bug 2.

2. Customer's feature-module `reset_secret?(secret)` predicate was
   shadowed by the zero-arity `reset_secret?` that Familia generates for
   the `string :reset_secret` field, so valid_reset_secret! raised
   ArgumentError on every call. Renamed to matches_reset_secret? (no
   other callers).

3. ResetPassword called non-bang `update_passphrase`, which only mutates
   in memory — even without the crashes, the new password was never
   persisted. Now uses update_passphrase!, matching UpdatePassword.

Also treat an orphaned secret (load_owner nil) as OT::MissingSecret
instead of 500ing on nil.

With the flow functional, the M-2 session revocation added in the
previous commit now applies to resets as intended; the new
reset_password tryouts cover the full round trip.

fix(security): rate-limit reset-password requests in simple mode

Issue #3872 added Onetime::Security::ResetRequestRateLimiter but wired it
only into the Rodauth before_reset_password_request_route hook, which the
registry loads exclusively when auth_config.full_enabled?. Simple mode is
the application default and serves POST /auth/reset-password-request from
the Core app (routes.txt -> Registration#request_reset_email ->
AccountAPI::Logic::Authentication::ResetPasswordRequest), so in a default
install the endpoint had no throughput cap at all: an unauthenticated
caller could mail-bomb arbitrary addresses and accumulate unbounded
samples against the response-timing residual that logic accepts.

ResetPasswordRequest now enforces the same limiter itself, as the first
statement of #raise_concerns — ahead of the valid_email? format check and
ahead of the Customer.find_by_email lookup in #process, mirroring the
full-mode hook's before-the-route-body ordering, so a throttled probe
never executes the timing-sensitive path.

Subjects match the hook: the per-IP tier keys on the strategy-metadata
client IP (AuthStrategies::Helpers#client_ip -> env['otto.client_ip'],
trusted-proxy-resolved and privacy-masked, as the other logic-layer
limiters read it), and the per-login backstop keys on the sanitized login
actually used for the lookup, so variants that resolve to one target share
one bucket. Both tiers key only on request-observable inputs, never on
account existence, so the 429 introduces no enumeration oracle.
Onetime::LimitExceeded is not an OT::FormError, so it bypasses the
controller's form-error rescue and reaches the Otto error handler that
renders the ADR-013 429 with retry_after.

Configuration is unchanged (site.authentication.reset_request_rate_limit /
RESET_REQUEST_RATE_LIMIT_*, enabled by default) and now documented as
applying in both auth modes.

Tests: new spec/integration/simple/reset_password_request_rate_limit_spec.rb
drives real HTTP through the mounted Core app (per-IP tier across distinct
logins, per-login backstop case-insensitively, 429 symmetry for existing vs
non-existent targets, no lookup or dispatch once locked out, no throttling
when disabled by config); unit coverage asserts the call site, its subjects
and its ordering. Removing the enforce call fails four of the integration
examples.

Closes finding #2 of docs/security/security-audit-2026-07-30.md.

fix(security): scrub invalid UTF-8 before sanitizing the reset-request login

Adversarial review found a hole in the cap added by this branch, reproduced
end to end: a form-urlencoded POST /auth/reset-password-request with an
invalid byte sequence in `login` returned an unauthenticated 500 and
consumed ZERO limiter budget.

Rack::Parser parses the urlencoded body eagerly and caches it in
rack.request.form_hash, so the UTF8Sanitizer's replacement rack.input never
reaches these values: `login` arrives UTF-8-tagged but not UTF-8-valid, and
sanitize_email -> Sanitize.fragment raises ArgumentError on it. That runs in
process_params, i.e. in Onetime::Logic::Base's constructor, which
Registration#request_reset_email invokes outside execute_with_error_handling
— so the raise happened before raise_concerns and therefore before the rate
limiter. No enumeration oracle and no mail dispatch (the request dies ahead
of the lookup), but unbounded 500s and Sentry noise, and the one submission
shape that never cost an attacker any budget.

process_params now scrubs invalid bytes first: a no-op for valid input, and
a garbage login flows through the limiter and fails the ordinary format
check (400/redirect) instead of crashing.

An earlier check of this claim wrongly refuted it — the probe string was an
ASCII-8BIT literal, in which those bytes are valid, so Sanitize never
raised. Reproducing through Rack::Utils.parse_nested_query, which returns a
UTF-8-tagged string with valid_encoding? false, shows the raise.

Covered both at the unit level (constructing with an invalid-UTF-8 login
does not raise, the scrubbed value reaches the limiter, the format check
then rejects it) and end to end through the real middleware stack with a
form-urlencoded body (no 500, and the per-IP counter is at 1). Removing the
scrub fails both.

[#3948] security: give unauthenticated audit writes their own retention domain

AdminAuditEvent's operator trail is capped by count with no TTL and evicts
oldest-first, so any writer an unauthenticated caller can drive competes with
purge/role-change/suspension/impersonation records for the same 10k budget.

The reset-request throttle bounded itself to one event per bucket per lockout
window and documented that as the control. The arithmetic does not support it:
at max_per_ip=10 / max_per_email=30, ten requests fill one masked-IP bucket
(one event) and three such buckets also fill one per-login bucket, so an
attacker mints ~1 event per 7.5 requests — ~75k requests to flush the trail,
which is cheap for a distributed source, for IPv6 prefix space, or for anyone
able to forge the resolved client IP behind an appending reverse proxy. A
documented frequency bound is not a boundary.

Split the storage instead:

- new `security_events` sorted set with its own count cap (1k) and, unlike the
  operator trail, an age bound trimmed by score on every write;
- `record_security` / `recent_security` / `security_count` / `trim_security!`;
- the throttle writes through `record_security`, so a flood evicts only other
  anonymous telemetry.

Frequency is still bounded at the call site, now for signal quality rather than
for the integrity of the operator trail. Tests pin both: no per-request event,
and zero writes into `events` under a sustained flood.

[#3948] colonel: merge both audit trails in the audit reader

Splitting security telemetry into its own capped collection is a storage
concern; the operator still wants one chronological feed. ListAuditEvents now
merges `events` and `security_events` newest-first on both the filtered and
unfiltered paths, so the throttle signal stays queryable at
GET /api/colonel/audit and the split costs no visibility.

The merge is bounded by MAX_COMBINED (both caps summed, i.e. the whole store),
the same ceiling the filtered path has always had.

Also carries the pre-commit RuboCop autocorrect of two pre-existing offenses in
this file (attr_reader line breaks, one nested conditional); both are
semantics-preserving.

[#3948] docs: point unauthenticated audit writers at record_security

AuditedFailure.authorization_rejection? is documented as the automatic half of
the operator-trail write invariant, but its guidance still described the
superseded rule: that a call site may write directly into `events` for an
unauthenticated event provided it bounds its own write rate per window. That
bar no longer exists — the boundary is now storage, not frequency, and any
unauthenticated-triggerable write must go to `security_events` via
record_security.

Left as-is, the next implementer reading the predicate that enforces this
invariant would be told the frequency-bound path is acceptable, which is
exactly the drift the split was meant to close. Comment only.

[#3948] test: pin that record_security applies BOTH bounds on the write path

The security trail's count cap and age bound are what keep the collection an
unauthenticated caller can drive from growing without limit. Nothing pinned
that record_security actually applies them: the tryout coverage calls
trim_security! explicitly after its writes, so deleting the trim call from
record_security left the whole suite green while turning security_events into
an unbounded sorted set — a worse failure than the eviction primitive the
split was introduced to close.

Adds the write-path equivalents of the existing MAX_EVENTS auto-trim example
(count cap, age bound), the best-effort rescue, and the operator-trail
isolation invariant, and extends the suite's cleanup to the second collection
so a security write cannot leak into a later example.

[#3948] security: add CreateAccountRateLimiter for unauthenticated signups

Audit 2026-07-30 finding #4: POST /auth/create-account had no limiter of
any kind, leaving unthrottled account creation reachable unauthenticated —
one Customer record (the hash carries no TTL) plus one welcome email per
distinct address, with subaddressing folding many addresses onto one
mailbox.

Single tier, keyed on the masked client IP, using the same atomic
check-and-record Lua shape as ResetRequestRateLimiter. The single tier is a
necessity rather than a preference: every request in the abuse pattern
carries a fresh address, so a per-address backstop would mint one bucket
per request and cap nothing. Nor does it key on anything account-derived —
this route's whole contract is that new and existing accounts respond
byte-identically.

The default cap is deliberately loose. The bucket is a whole masked /24,
and under the documented collapse condition it is the entire deployment,
where a lockout blocks signup for every new visitor rather than delaying a
recovery flow for an existing one.

Cap-hits write one AdminAuditEvent to the security trail, never the
operator trail, and only on the cap-reaching request. This is the second
unauthenticated writer into that store, and the MAX_EVENTS rationale on
AdminAuditEvent requires exactly those two properties of any such writer.

Registers create_account_ip in the ratelimit Registry, so bin/ots and the
colonel reset endpoint can clear a stuck lockout over the same keys.

Customer.create! in #process. An integration example asserts the absence of
the customer record directly, since datastore growth is the finding.

Malformed and disallowed-domain submissions still cost budget: they are
free to generate and equally good for flooding. A signed-in caller does
not, since that is a UI mistake rather than the abuse this bounds, and
charging them would drain a bucket shared across a masked network.

Disabled in spec/config.test.yaml so the many specs that sign accounts up
are not throttled — the cap is per masked IP and the whole suite shares

Reject billing overlay outside full auth mode

Billing rides on the full-mode auth stack: Stripe customer records live
in the auth database, which only exists when AUTHENTICATION_MODE=full.
Combining --overlay billing with simple/disabled lanes was silently
accepted but meaningless — the lane would run with BILLING_ENABLED=true
against a stack that has no billing surface, giving false confidence
that billing-flagged behavior was exercised.

tests/lanes/run now fails fast (exit 64, before service preflight) when
the loaded environment ends up with BILLING_ENABLED=true and any mode
other than full:

  $ tests/lanes/run simple --overlay billing
  error: billing requires AUTHENTICATION_MODE=full (lane 'simple' is 'simple')

The guard checks the resolved env rather than the overlay name, so any
future env source that flips BILLING_ENABLED (a new overlay, a lane env
edit) hits the same wall.

This encodes what ci.yml already practices — its billing on/off matrix
exists only on the ruby-integration-full job — so when matrix rows
become lane+overlay pairs, no valid combination is lost.

Also: billing.env header no longer claims the overlay works "for any
lane" (names the three full-* lanes instead), and the README matrix
note documents the restriction.

SessionSkip and HealthAccessControl matched the raw request path while
the Otto router dispatches on the normalized one (unescaped, single

both guards: GET /api/v2/status/ or /api/v2/%73tatus reached the status
handler but still minted a session per request (reopening the #3997

public IP bypassed the private-network gate to reach the advanced
health handler. Both matchers now canonicalize with

fix: remove hardcoded 30-day TTL clamp blocking configured longer TTLs (#4008)

V2's process_ttl applied `@ttl = 30.days if ttl >= 30.days` before the
real bounds check, silently overriding every configured ceiling — plan
secret_lifetime, ttl_options, the anonymous cap — so self-hosted
operators could not offer TTLs beyond 30 days no matter what they
configured. The frontend mirrored the same 30-day number in the
duration-dropdown filter and the ttl_options Zod schema, hiding or
rejecting longer durations before the backend ever saw them.

Remove the redundant clamp and raise both frontend mirrors to the
existing absolute bound, WithEntitlements::MAX_TTL (365 days). The
backend keeps a MAX_TTL safety clamp in its place because an unlimited
plan resolves limit_for('secret_lifetime') to Infinity and the bounds
ladder otherwise has no terminal bound. All real ceilings (plan limit,
anonymous 7-day cap, config ttl_options) are unchanged and still
enforced; V3 inherits the fix; V1 keeps its frozen 30-day contract.

Regression coverage: 90-day TTLs survive when the plan allows them,
exactly-30-day requests are preserved, unlimited plans clamp at
MAX_TTL, and the anonymous ceiling is proven unaffected.

[#4024] fix: drop the +1 depth remap that double-counted the peer

The YAML->otto translator mapped depth: N to otto trusted_proxy_depth
N + 1 (the otto#151 remap), reasoning that otto's chain is one hop
longer because it appends REMOTE_ADDR. But otto's index arithmetic
already accounts for that: the client sits at chain[-(N+1)], so otto
depth N means "N proxy hops counting the connecting peer as hop 1" --
exactly what the operator-facing depth: N documents ("1 = standard
single reverse proxy"). The +1 instead reproduced an internal
off-by-one of the deleted ClientIpHelpers walker.

Consequences of the remap, now fixed: every honest request in a
documented topology hit otto's short-chain fallback and resolved the
PROXY address as the client (rate limits, bans, and audit attribution
keyed on the proxy IP), and a client that smuggled one forged leftmost
X-Forwarded-For entry past the proxy got the forged value resolved as
its client IP. With the direct mapping the true client is selected on
honest chains and padding never wins (positions counted raw from the
right).

- middleware_stack.rb: trusted_proxy_depth = ots_depth (clamp 1..10
  unchanged); comments corrected.
- middleware_stack_spec.rb: remap specs now pin the direct mapping
  (depth 2 -> 2, clamp 50 -> 10, blank -> 1).
- ip_privacy_parity_spec.rb: depth fixtures corrected to the honest
  single-proxy topology; new padding-resistance spec pins that a forged
  leftmost XFF entry is never selected.
- detect_host_ip_privacy_stack_try.rb: depth case now uses the honest
  single-entry XFF (REMOTE_ADDR rewritten to the masked PUBLIC client,
  so the otto key stays the only trust signal); new case 7 pins padding
  resistance through the production stack. 7/7 pass locally.
- detect_host.rb: the "spoofable in the documented single-proxy setup"
  caveat is obsolete; replaced with the origin-lockdown note.

Operators who compensated by setting depth one lower than their real
hop count should correct it to the actual number of proxies (see
changelog fragment).

[#4023] fix(domain-validation): normalize tag=value DNS records before comparing

Sender DNS verification compared TXT records as raw substrings, causing
three defects:

- False negative: 'v=DMARC1; p=none;' failed against expected
  'v=DMARC1;p=none' despite parsing to the same tag list
- False positive: .any? over the full TXT record set let a duplicate
  _dmarc record pass, though RFC 7489 §6.6.3 treats >1 DMARC record as
  an error (and RFC 7208 makes duplicate SPF a permerror)
- Latent: global downcasing would case-fold DKIM base64 p= values,
  violating RFC 6376 §3.2 case sensitivity

Add Onetime::DomainValidation::RecordNormalizer implementing the
RFC 6376 §3.2 tag-list grammar (WSP-tolerant, optional trailing ';',
duplicate tag names invalidate the record, per-tag case policy with
case-sensitive base64). record_matches? now dispatches by discriminator:
DMARC/DKIM via tag-subset compare, SPF via the existing matcher, opaque

Address PR review (terminal-failure regression): migrating credentialed
rejection from the env-marker guard to Otto's terminal AuthFailure made the
failure halt the chain UNCONDITIONALLY, dropping the deliberate carve-out the
old NoAuthStrategy enforced (it refused only when the session was anonymous —
`if cust.nil?`). A logged-in browser whose request also carried a stale cached
Basic credential, or a reverse proxy forwarding its own htpasswd header, would
be 401'd mid-session on every basicauth,noauth route (including web-UI conceal).

same request already resolves a valid (non-stale) session identity, so Otto's
chain reaches the session-resolving NoAuthStrategy and the session wins. With
no such session it stays terminal and the chain fails closed (401), preserving
the audit fix (docs/security/audits/2026-07-29-api.md item 1). The decision now
travels on the AuthFailure itself — no env-marker coupling, no dependence on
strategy order.

- helpers.rb: credentialed_failure(reason, env=nil) + private
  valid_session_identity? (reuses load_user_from_session so the #3810
  credential-watermark staleness check applies — a stale session can't rescue
  a bad header).

get_canonical_domain resolved `default || site.host`, so setting
features.domains.default REPLACED site.host as the single classification
anchor. In a split deployment (app served at api.example.com, links
generated on secrets.example.com) requests to the app's own host fell
through every Chooserator branch and classified :invalid.

Both hosts now parse at boot into a canonical set: a request matching
either classifies :canonical, a subdomain of either :subdomain, with the
registered-custom-domain lookup unchanged and still last. The public
canonical_domain reader and the display_domain fallback keep resolving
`default || site.host`, and the dev-only implicit domain-context
override no longer treats a request to site.host as an override when a
distinct default is configured.

Also adds an advisory boot guard for config drift: #3841 blocks
registering a domain that overlaps the canonical set, but nothing
stopped an operator from later pointing features.domains.default at an
already-registered custom domain — a state where the domain's brand and
SigninConfig are silently ignored because :canonical wins before the
custom lookup ever runs. Boot now logs a loud error naming the shadowed
domain. Advisory only: the lookup is rescued so Redis unavailability at
middleware construction can neither fail boot nor change classification.

Coverage: multiple_canonical_try.rb grows 6 -> 28 cases pinning
split-deployment classification, default-unset parity with the old
single-host behavior, override consistency, and the drift guard
(logged when shadowed, silent when unregistered, fail-open on lookup
errors).

fix(domains): default_domain? covers the full canonical host set

CustomDomain.default_domain? compared input against site.host only,
while the DomainStrategy middleware treats features.domains.default as
canonical. In a split deployment a client passing
share_domain=<default link domain> was not filtered as "the default",
so redundant share_domain metadata got stored for the very domain
links default to.

Extract a canonical_hosts helper — the deduped [site.host,
features.domains.default] read straight from config, keeping the model
layer independent of the middleware — and share it with
overlaps_canonical_domain? (whose behavior is unchanged).
default_domain? now exact-matches the normalized input against each
host, port-stripped and downcased the same way overlaps derives
bare_host. It stays deliberately narrower than
overlaps_canonical_domain?: exact match only, no base-domain overlap.

Behavior delta worth naming: the configured host is now normalized
before comparison, so site.host values like localhost:3000 or
Example.com match where they previously (and silently) never did.

Coverage: 16 new examples in input_sanitization_spec.rb pinning both
hosts matching in a split deployment, exact-only rejection of
subdomains and shared base domains, port/casing/trailing-dot
normalization, and empty-default parity with unset.

fix(domains): DomainContext dropdown anchors on canonical_domain

The dropdown's canonical entry was derived from store.site_host in
useDomainContext's getConfig(). That single read feeds the dropdown
entries, the displayed label, and the value submitted as share_domain —
all three wrong whenever DEFAULT_DOMAIN differs from site.host.

The dropdown chooses which domain the generated share link uses, and
that is precisely what canonical_domain is: the server resolves it as
`features.domains.default || site.host` and it already ships in the
bootstrap contract. Read it with a site_host fallback for older
payloads where the schema default yields ''.

resetContext and getPreferredDomain flow through the same read, so
"reset to canonical" now also means the link domain — the intended
semantics on every surface. The guest custom-domain path is untouched:
SecretForm still overrides with display_domain when
domain_strategy === 'custom'.

Coverage: 3 new composable tests (canonical_domain preferred across
entry/label/availableDomains, site_host fallback, isCanonical judged
against canonical_domain); setup helper gains an optional
canonical_domain seed defaulting to '' so existing tests keep
exercising the fallback branch.

fix(domains): consolidate canonical-host set and fix custom-domain precedence

Address verified review findings on the canonical-set change:

- New Onetime::Utils::CanonicalHosts is the single derivation point for
  the canonical host set (primary first: features.domains.default per
  #3841, else site.host), normalized via DomainParser; DomainStrategy
  and CustomDomain.canonical_hosts both consume it.
- choose_strategy precedence is now exact canonical match > registered
  custom domain > peer/subdomain sweep, so custom domains under
  site.host's base domain keep :custom (branding/signin intact).
- Public DomainStrategy.canonical_host? predicate; OmniauthTenant and
  UpdateDomainContext use it instead of the singular canonical_domain,
  so auth agrees with the middleware in split deployments.
- Remove write-only @canonical_domain_parsed and its stale-state

- default_domain? rescues Onetime::Problem (dead PublicSuffix-only
  rescue); choose_strategy tolerates unparseable set elements
  per-element instead of poisoning the whole set.
- Move warn_if_default_shadows_custom_domain to the ConfigureDomains
  initializer (once per boot, index lookup without hydration) instead

On a split deployment (browser on site_host, canonical_domain = link

    validate.py matched before

feat(i18n): gate task writes with --strict and add tasks audit

Two blocking checks on the translation write path, which until now had none:
nothing between "agent writes the DB" and "content committed" could refuse a
bad write.

tasks update --strict (implies --validate)
  On a key-set mismatch, prints the same diagnostic and returns 1 *before*
  update_task(), the only writer. Without --strict the advisory path is
  unchanged: it still warns, still saves, still exits 0. That behaviour is
  documented and has callers, so it is preserved byte-for-byte.

tasks audit <locale> [--json] [--strict]
  Audits completed rows pre-export. Four checks, each a pure function over
  (source_map, translation_map) with no I/O or printing:
    key_set  (error)    - key sets must match; a blank translation that
                          export_locale would silently drop counts as missing,
                          via the same _exportable() predicate export uses
    tokens   (error)    - per-key multiset equality across {var} {{var}}
                          %{var} printf <tag>; Vue-i18n plural strings are
                          split on | and compared per form, otherwise every
                          locale whose plural-form count differs from English
                          reads as a violation (ja/ru: 7 findings -> 0)
    status   (error)    - in_progress rows are invisible to the pending==0
                          gate and to a completed-only audit, so a locale
                          could export half-translated and still pass both
    en_leak  (advisory) - reported, excluded from the --strict exit code

  en_leak is advisory by design. As a gate it fired on "Status", "TTL",
  "Amazon SES", "Canada" - the class of strings whose correct translation is
  the English string. No allowlist covers that, so the only way to pass would
  have been to write a wrong translation.

  --strict also fails when rows_checked == 0, matching the glossary handler:
  a locale with nothing to verify is unverified, not clean.

AuditFinding.to_dict() is the single serialization behind both --json and the
human renderer, and check_key_set shares diff_key_sets() with
validate_translations, so neither pair can drift.

feat(i18n): gate export-all.sh on audit, not just pending count

export-all.sh skipped a locale only when pending != 0. pending == 0 proves
neither currency nor cleanliness, which is exactly the gap
AGENT_TRANSLATION_PROTOCOL.md's audit stage describes in prose.

Per locale, before export: tasks audit <locale> --strict.
After a successful export: validate variables, plus the register lint when
the resolver is available.

Details that the naive version gets wrong:
  - validate variables exits 0 even when it finds mismatches, so the gate
    counts details entries rather than trusting $?. Metadata leaves
    (context/note/source_hash) are excluded - context is en-only authoring
    prose that tasks export structurally cannot write, so summing the
    summary marked every locale dirty after a byte-perfect export.
  - The register lint needs both .translation-rules/ and the derived
    generated/i18n/.resolved/<locale>.json. Both are absent unless
    derive-governance.sh has run; it skips with a notice and never fails.
  - A failing audit exits 1 by design, which set -e would turn into an abort;
    every gate is invoked so the loop survives and all locales get processed.
  - The shared db export is guarded so a failure there cannot discard the
    summary before exit.

Four reported outcomes: exported, failed audit, failed export, exported but
dirty. Any of the last three forces a non-zero exit. "Not drained" stays a
normal state and still exits 0.

Dry-run still runs the read-only audit so the preview reflects the real gate.

test(i18n): cover the write gates, and stop the suite reading the real DB

Extends test_i18n_cli.py rather than adding a file. 36 -> 62 tests.

tasks update: the most important case is the regression guard on advisory
mode - --validate without --strict must still save and still exit 0. Then

tasks audit: each check attributed correctly; the token check against a
dropped token, an added token, and a count change ({x} twice in source, once
in translation) across all five families; plural forms per Vue-i18n form;
in_progress rows caught by the status check; blank translations caught by
key_set. The en_leak cases that matter most are the negative ones - brand
names, empty source, no-letter strings - since a noisy advisory is one people
learn to ignore. --strict exit codes, including the zero-rows case, and
--json parity with the human output.

Harness fix, unrelated to the above but latent until now: setUp copied
os.environ and overrode only I18N_DB_DIR. config.py cascades DB_DIR -> DB_FILE
as a default, so an exported I18N_DB_FILE in a developer's shell outranked it
and pointed the whole suite at locales/db/tasks.db. setUp now drops every
ambient I18N_* var before adding its own. Verified: 62/62 with
I18N_DB_FILE=/tmp/bogus-does-not-exist.db.

docs(i18n): make the audit the documented definition of drained

AGENT_TRANSLATION_PROTOCOL.md
  Per-task cycle step 4 now uses --validate --strict, and step 5 states the
