fix(dev): stop test-mode env leaking into worktrees; write locales atomically

Two local-dev boot failures with one root cause each:

1. Worktree .envrc starts with source_up_if_exists, so a main checkout in
   TEST MODE (.test-mode) exports its .env.test into every worktree shell
   before the worktree's dev-mode .env loads. Keys .env does not define
   survive: PGPORT=2154 retargets a port-less AUTH_DATABASE_URL
   (...@authdb/...) at the test Postgres container, which has no ots_*
   roles ("password authentication failed for user ots_migrator").
   ENABLE_*, HMAC_SECRET, STDOUT_SYNC, OIDC_*, STRIPE_* leak the same way.

   The .envrc template (ENVRC_REV 2 -> 3) now unsets every key declared in
   .env.test (fallback: tracked .env.test.example) before dotenv_if_exists
   in dev mode, and watches .env.test.example. Stale worktree .envrc files
   regenerate on the next bin/setup.

2. `i18n content compile` wrote generated/locales/<loc>.json in place, so a
   compile killed mid-write (or racing a backend boot) leaves a torn file
   and puma dies in Load Locales with Familia::SerializerError. save_json_file
   now writes a sibling temp file and os.replace()s it into place.

Drop correct_passphrase from the frontend secret details schemas

The backend is removing details.correct_passphrase from the v1/v2 secret
responses: it reported whether a supplied passphrase was correct even on a
metadata-only request (continue=false), which made the endpoint a
non-destructive passphrase oracle. show_secret is the only reveal signal.

Remove the field from secretDetailsCanonical and the v2 wire shape outright
rather than marking it optional: the detail objects are plain (non-strict)
z.object chains, so a response from an older backend that still emits the
field parses and is stripped. A regression block in
secret-schema-contract.spec.ts pins both halves (absent shape parses;
legacy field is stripped, never surfaced). Fixtures and specs that named
the field drop it; boolean-coercion coverage moves to the remaining detail
booleans instead of being deleted.

Adds the Security changelog fragment for the fix.

Gate passphrase verification on continue; drop correct_passphrase from secret details

The v1 and v2 show, reveal, and burn logic evaluated secret.passphrase?
before consulting the continue param, and show/reveal returned the verdict
as details.correct_passphrase. A request with continue=false therefore
learned whether a guess was right without consuming the secret -- a
non-destructive passphrase oracle bounded only by the rate limiter. v2
reveal and both burn endpoints leaked the same verdict through the HTTP
status (wrong guess raised a form error; right guess with continue=false
returned 200 without acting).

Invariant now: secret.passphrase? runs only when continue=true.
correct_passphrase folds continue in, so it is false for every
metadata-only request, right guess or wrong; the failed-attempt/raise
branches and the rate-limit clear/record block are gated on continue
(a guess that was never checked is not an attempt); and
correct_passphrase is no longer serialized -- show_secret is the only
reveal signal. v2 reveal is normalised to the show form
(!has_passphrase? || passphrase?) so the three classes read identically.

Regression specs in apps/api/{v1,v2}/spec/logic/secrets and tryouts pin:
continue=false never calls passphrase?, returns byte-identical details
for right and wrong guesses, records no attempt, and raises nothing; the
continue=true paths (raise + record on wrong, reveal/burn + clear on
right) are unchanged.

Address review: scope changelog to v2, add rate-limit positive controls

The v1 controller forces continue='true' and renders its own JSON, never
success_data, so the v1 API was not exposed to the oracle; the v1 logic
change is parity hardening. Say so in the changelog instead of implying a
v1 wire change.

The v2 show/reveal specs asserted the passphrase:attempts key stays nil on
continue=false but never asserted it is written on a committed wrong guess,
so a key-format drift would have made them pass vacuously. Add the positive
control to each. Trim the success_data comments to one line (the #process
comment is the load-bearing one) and fix the "for the reveal path" drift in
the show classes. The v2 reveal/burn debug logs now record
passphrase_correct: nil when continue=false -- the guess was not checked,
which is different from wrong.

Align passphrase rate-limit ordering across show/reveal/burn

Two consistency fixes on the v2 secret logic, neither of which changes
what a caller can observe about a passphrase:

RevealSecret settled its rate-limit bookkeeping inside the reveal branch,
so the clear ran only after the atomic reveal claim. A caller that lost
the burn-after-reading race with a correct passphrase therefore ended up
in a different rate-limit state than the winner, even though both guessed
right. The clear and the failed-attempt record now both hang off the
passphrase verdict, before any claim -- the same ordering ShowSecret
already used. The predicates are unchanged, so the resulting Redis state
is identical for every non-race path.

BurnSecret placed its rate-limit gate inside #process, behind the
`return unless potential_secret` guard, while ShowSecret and RevealSecret
both gate in raise_concerns. The gate still fired before the passphrase
was evaluated, so there was no bypass, but the asymmetry meant a future
edit that moved that early return earlier would silently skip it. The
check now lives in raise_concerns alongside the others; the secret is
loaded once through a memoized reader that both methods share.

Specs: the burn rate-limit examples now run process_params ->
raise_concerns -> process (the controller's real order) instead of
process alone, plus a new example asserting the lockout is refused by
raise_concerns on its own. RevealSecret gains a losing-racer example
proving a correct guess clears the limit whether or not it won the claim.
fix(locales): use unique temporary files for writes

Correct the reveal rate-limit race narrative and make its spec distinguishing

Review of 27a9a1c1e6 showed the losing-racer spec passed against the
parent implementation: with viewable? stubbed true, the old code entered
the reveal branch and ran its clear before reveal!, so old and new
behaved identically in the window the spec constructed.

The real divergence is one window earlier. The old clear was gated on
the process-time show_secret verdict, not on winning the atomic claim:
a concurrent consumer claiming the secret after this request passed
raise_concerns but before process recomputed viewable? left a correct
passphrase verification without its corresponding rate-limit clear (and
without a failure record). The hoisted bookkeeping settles both on the
passphrase verdict alone, closing that gap.

The spec now mirrors production ordering -- process_params,
raise_concerns, concurrent claim, process -- with no viewable? stub, so
viewability is naturally false by the time show_secret is computed.
Verified red against the parent implementation and green against the
current one. Comments in both files reworded to match; the claim in
27a9a1c1e6's message that the clear ran "only after the atomic reveal
claim" was wrong in the same way and is corrected by this narrative.

fix(diagnostics): mount Sentry middleware from config intent, not SDK state

MiddlewareStack.configure gated the CaptureExceptions mount on
defined?(::Sentry::Rack::CaptureExceptions) && ::Sentry.initialized? —
two pieces of process-global runtime state flipped elsewhere (an earlier
spec, SetupDiagnostics) at some other time. That made the universal
stack's shape a function of boot/suite order instead of config, which is
exactly the drift the middleware manifest characterization spec exists
to catch — and it kept catching it: any earlier spec that left
d9s_enabled true and Sentry initialized grew the stack by one entry.

The guard also bought no safety. sentry-ruby 6.6.2's
CaptureExceptions#call opens with
`return @app.call(env) unless Sentry.initialized?`, so an uninitialized
SDK already no-ops per request. All the build-time check could do was
silently drop error capture from any app whose stack built before
SetupDiagnostics ran.

Now the mount is a pure function of config: inside with_diagnostics,
require sentry-ruby (idempotent; fails loudly if diagnostics is enabled
without the gem) and mount unconditionally. Runtime uncertainty stays at
request time, where the SDK handles it.

The manifest spec pins the one remaining global input, d9s_enabled, per
example (around-block save/restore) and characterizes both branches:
diagnostics off → the 21-entry base list, on → base plus
Sentry::Rack::CaptureExceptions before RetryAfterHeader. This closes the
blind spot where the Sentry line was only ever asserted absent, and
makes the spec immune to suite order.

Reject malformed multipart bodies with 400 before params are read (#4283)

Otto::Locale::Middleware reads req.params on every request, so a broken
multipart body was parsed for the first time inside gem middleware:
Rack::Multipart::EmptyContentError and BoundaryTooLongError surfaced as
500s blamed on the nearest in-app frame (EntitlementPreviewContext,
which never touches the body), and a boundary-less or zero-length
multipart body quietly fell back to urlencoded parsing, reaching V1
POST /share with no fields — the misleading "You did not provide
anything to share" response.

New Onetime::Middleware::ValidateMultipart, mounted after
NormalizeContentType and before Rack::Parser/session/locale:

- 400 for a multipart Content-Type without a usable boundary parameter
- 400 for a multipart request with Content-Length: 0
- 400 for a body Rack's multipart parser rejects (empty, truncated,
  boundary never found)
- eagerly parses valid multipart via Rack::Request#POST so the result
  is memoized for every downstream consumer, then rewinds rack.input

[#4212] Retire the Stripe Payment Link provisioning path

Payment Links were the pre-2026 purchase flow: Stripe redirected the buyer
to GET /welcome?checkout={CHECKOUT_SESSION_ID} and
Billing::Logic::Welcome::FromStripePaymentLink provisioned them from the
checkout session. Those links are no longer active, and nothing in the
codebase mints that URL any more — every current checkout success_url points
at /billing/welcome?session_id=, handled by ProcessCheckoutSession.

The retired class was the riskiest branch left in billing. Its
no-account path (welcome.rb:103) created a customer with verified = false
from an unauthenticated request, then provisioned a workspace for it — email
ownership proven by nothing but possession of a checkout URL. Hardening that
for a cohort that cannot reach it is the wrong trade; removing it is the
cleaner outcome.

Nothing here served existing customers. This endpoint only ever ran once,
at purchase time. Legacy identity-plan subscribers keep their subscriptions
through the webhook handlers and the customer portal, neither of which
touches this code.

The route stays as a reporting stub rather than a 404, because a stale link
can still sit in a bookmark or an old receipt. Every hit is now captured to
Sentry with the checkout session id when one is present. That signal matters:
the checkout.session.completed webhook is NOT a safety net for a Payment Link
subscription — it carries no customer_extid metadata, so CheckoutCompleted
skips it. If a link were somehow still live, the id in Sentry is what lets
support reconcile the payment by hand.

Also corrects two comments that had the two /welcome endpoints backwards:
billing/routes.txt called the current session_id endpoint the legacy Payment
Link one, and the core controller's header claimed GET /welcome redirects to
/billing/welcome, which it never did.

[#4212] Let a caller decline the federated-subscription claim

CreateDefaultWorkspace has always done two things at once: create the
workspace, and claim any PendingFederatedSubscription waiting for that
customer's email hash. Callers could DEFER the claim (require_verification:,
which resumes from after_verify_account) but not decline it.

The checkout-completion surfaces need to decline. They arrive holding a paid
LOCAL subscription that they apply to the workspace moments after creating
it, so claiming there consumes the customer's cross-region pending record —
destroying the only copy of it — to deliver a benefit they are about to
receive anyway, and leaves the org flagged federated for a subscription it
actually owns. Deferral is no help: a checkout completion has no second
chance to re-claim from.

claim_pending_federation: defaults to true, so all five existing callers keep
claiming exactly as before and none of them changed. The gate sits above the
verification gate because it is not a deferral, and it returns before any
lookup: the pending record is left untouched for the surface that can resolve
it properly — the next federated subscription webhook, which reads the plan
from subscription metadata.

The two gates now answer different questions ("not yet" vs "not by me") and
are pinned by separate specs. The new one is deliberately untagged so it runs
in the unit lane; create_default_workspace_federation_spec.rb is type:
:integration, which APPS_FAST_TAG_FILTERS excludes from spec:fast.

Refs #4212

[#4212] Give both checkout surfaces one workspace-creation policy

A completed checkout is handled twice: once by the checkout.session.completed
webhook and once by the browser redirect. Steps 1-3 of "which org does this
belong to" already lived in CheckoutTargetResolver so the two could not
disagree. Step 4 — what to create when nothing resolves — did not, and they
disagreed on both halves of it.

The webhook ran CreateDefaultWorkspace first and fell back to
create_billing_workspace; the redirect went straight to the fallback. Same
checkout, two outcomes: a workspace named "Default Workspace" or one named
"<email>'s Workspace", and a cross-region PendingFederatedSubscription either
claimed or left alone, decided by nothing but which surface got there first.

Step 4 now lives beside steps 1-3 as create_checkout_workspace, and both
surfaces call it. The canonical create runs first (orphan adoption,
is_default, the whole signup policy), with create_billing_workspace behind it
for the case the canonical create refuses: a customer whose only orgs are
archived, who has a paid subscription and nowhere live to put it.

The federation claim is now declined on BOTH surfaces rather than made on
both. Either would have unified them; declining is the correct half. A
completion path holds a paid local subscription that it applies to this
workspace moments later, so claiming the customer's pending cross-region
record there destroys the only copy of it to deliver a benefit they already
have, and marks the org federated for a subscription it owns.

create_canonical_workspace and adopt_email_reserved_workspace moved from the
webhook handler to the resolver unchanged apart from taking logger/label as
arguments instead of reading the handler's constants.

[#4212] Clear the federated marker when an org buys its own subscription

subscription_federated_at was set by mark_subscription_federated! and never
unset. clear_federated_status! existed for exactly this and was called from
nowhere in app code.

An org that federated a benefit from another region and LATER bought its own
subscription kept the marker forever. The predicates read correctly —
subscription_federated? is false once subscription_owner? is true, so no
federation notification was ever mis-shown — but the stored timestamp still
claimed the subscription arrived by federation. Anything reading the field
rather than the predicate (an export, an admin view, an audit trail) was told
the wrong story about where a paid subscription came from.

ApplySubscriptionToOrg#apply_owner_fields is the one place stripe_customer_id
is written on the owner path, so clearing the marker belongs beside it. That
also heals historical rows: the next subscription webhook fixes them without
a migration. The federated path is unchanged and now asserts it.

Scope each expected-outcome drop to what makes it expected

Review follow-up on the #4286 noise filter. The filter matched on outcome
alone — 404, aborted, network — which meant the same rule that suppressed a
consumed secret also suppressed a routing defect, a timed-out request, and an
unreachable API. Each rule now carries the condition that makes it expected.

- 404 only on identifier-addressed routes. `/secret/:id`, `/secret/:id/reveal`,
  `/receipt/:id`, `/receipt/:id/burn`, recognized by the identifier's shape
  (mirrors VERIFIABLE_ID_PATTERN) rather than a loose segment match, so
  `/secret/conceal` and `/secret/generate` stay reportable. A 404 from a
  mis-versioned or renamed endpoint is a regression, and those are exactly
  what the beforeSend layer was hiding.

- Timeouts separated from cancellations. Axios rejects both `xhr.ontimeout`
  and `xhr.onabort` with ECONNABORTED, so dropping 'aborted' would have taken
  every timed-out request with it during an API slowdown. Setting
  `transitional.clarifyTimeoutError` on the shared client makes timeouts
  arrive as ETIMEDOUT, leaving ECONNABORTED to mean abort and only abort.
  requestOutcome() gains a 'timeout' class that reports and groups on its own.
  Note the reviewer's suggested fix — removing ECONNABORTED from ABORT_MARKERS
  — would have regressed the navigate-away case it is there to catch: on the
  XHR adapter that code is the only signal an actual abort produces.

- Network errors follow connectivity. ERR_NETWORK is dropped only while
  `navigator.onLine` is false. `onLine` is trustworthy in the negative and not
  in the positive, which is the right way round here: a client-side blip goes
  quiet, while DNS, TLS, CORS, or an unreachable deployment — indistinguishable
  from offline on the wire, and ours to fix — keeps reporting.

Tests pin every drop rule from both sides. A filter like this fails silently:
over-dropping produces no error and no event to notice the absence of, so the
near-miss case matters as much as the case it must drop. Adds a createApi spec
for the timeout contract, since removing that flag would re-blind Sentry while
every other test still passed.

Onetime::Utils::RedirectPaths.safe_internal_path? (Ruby) and a hardened
isValidInternalPath (TS) enforce the identical ruleset: must start with /
(not // or /\), no backslashes, no ://, no control characters, and after
one percent-decode no backslash, control character, leading //, or ..
path segment. Query string and fragment ride along untouched. Parity was
verified case-for-case across both implementations.

Removes the dead validateRedirect/validatePathString/validateUrl subtree:
no non-spec consumers, and it was strictly weaker than the surviving
validator (accepted raw NUL/CRLF, %00, %0D%0A, and same-host absolute

[#4305] feat(auth): persist the signup redirect and replay it at verification

Customer gains pending_auth_redirect (24h TTL, sibling of
pending_plan_intent). after_create_account stores a validated ?redirect=
from the signup POST; after_verify_account returns it as
json_response[:redirect], single-use, deleted on read whether or not it
wins. Server resolves precedence and sends one destination: a valid plan
intent arrives as /billing/plans?product=X&interval=Y, else the stored
redirect, else no key. Persisting server-side (rather than in the email
link) is what makes the destination survive opening the verification
link in a fresh browser, and keeps resent links equivalent to originals.

Also fixes plan intent being destroyed before JSON clients ever saw it:
rodauth's json feature discards the redirect() argument, and
autologin_session never fires after_login, so deleting the intent inside
after_verify_account left the /auth/login billing fallback with nothing.
The intent now survives verification and is consumed by
add_billing_redirect_to_response at real login; failure paths still
delete. The non-JSON verify_account_redirect keeps working and now
consumes both session keys instead of short-circuiting on ||.

[#4305] feat(auth): carry the redirect from verify-account through every signin path

verifyAccount() was the primary drop point: it always pushed a bare
/signin, losing the destination before the user could authenticate. It
now takes the redirect from the verify-account response (falling back to
a validated ?redirect= query param), and pushes /signin?redirect=...
while preserving the verified-banner history state. VerifyAccount.vue
threads the param onto its escape links, and the auth-route guard
returns the raw string instead of { path } — vue-router's parseURL was
silently stripping query and hash from the object form.

The billing-first destination logic moves into a shared
usePostAuthRedirect composable, and the two passwordless epilogues that
hard-pushed '/' — magic-link verification and WebAuthn primary auth —
now resolve through it, so plan intent > redirect > default holds on
every way into a session. MFA already forwarded the redirect correctly
and is unchanged.

lib/onetime/utils/redirect_paths.rb and TypeScript in src/utils/redirect.ts.
Until now the two were held together by "change both or neither" comments and
two overlapping-but-independent spec suites, which is discipline, not a test.
A rule relaxed on one side only would ship: an open redirect in the worst case,
a silently-dropped signup journey in the best.

tests/fixtures/redirect_path_cases.json is now the single accept/reject table,
87 cases wide — the union of what the two suites previously asserted
separately. Both suites read it and generate one example per case, named by the
case id, so a disagreement names the offending input on whichever side lags.

Modeled on tests/fixtures/email_redaction_corpus.json, the existing
cross-language fixture. Scope is JSON strings only; the type-level cases stay
language-local (Ruby keeps nil/Integer/Array/Hash and the force-encoded
invalid-UTF-8 String, TS keeps undefined/null/number/object/array), as do the
examples asserting more than a boolean.

Both suites also pin the #4305 acceptance-criteria ids and the two length
boundaries, and assert the case count is non-zero. Erosion is the one failure
mode a fixture-driven suite cannot otherwise detect: empty the fixture and it
would pass vacuously.

All 87 cases agree across both validators as written — no parity bug found.

[#4305] test(redirect): restore the ruleset taxonomy the fixture flattened

Generating one example per case bought enforced parity but cost the reading
the hand-written contexts gave: `with percent-encoded escapes`, `absolute URLs
and any embedded ://`, `with backslash variants`. No input was lost — every
one of the 42 Ruby and 60 TypeScript inputs the old suites asserted is in the
fixture — but 87 flat examples do not tell you WHY any of them is there, and
that reason was the useful half of those blocks.

Each case now carries a `group`, and both suites nest their generated examples
under it. The taxonomy is back in the test output, stated once in the fixture
instead of restated in two languages, and finer than before: what was a single
`with percent-encoded escapes` context is now split into escapes that decode
harmlessly (accepted), structure smuggled through encoding, control characters
smuggled through encoding, and malformed encoding.

87 cases in 14 groups. Both suites also assert every case is filed, so a new
case cannot land unlabeled.

[#4305] ci: add a digest-pinned Mailpit service to compose.test.yml

The test-service file had no SMTP sink, so any suite that needs to read a
real delivered email had to be pointed at the shared dev Mailpit — or, more
often, simply had no lane at all. Add one on the file's own 21xx scheme.

Mailpit's two canonical ports (1025 SMTP, 8025 HTTP) both end in 25, so the
plain "21 + last two digits" rule collides them onto 2125. The HTTP one takes
the runner-only control-plane form the RabbitMQ management API already
established — "1" prefixed to the service's primary test port — giving 12125.
The port a test SENDS to keeps the 21xx form; the port a test READS state
from is the 121xx variant.

Distinct from docker/compose/docker-compose.mailpit.yml, which is the DEV
sidecar and keeps the canonical 1025/8025. Same separation as every other
service here: a leaked dev config can never reach the test instance, and a
test run can never read dev mail.

The healthcheck restates the probe the image already ships (its ENTRYPOINT
is /mailpit, which carries a `readyz` subcommand; there is no shell in the
image to write a curl probe with) on a tighter interval, so `up --wait`
returns in seconds rather than the image's 15s cadence.

[#4305] ci: give the signup-redirect journey a CI lane

e2e/auth/signup-redirect-preservation.spec.ts is the strongest guard for the
redirect fix — it is the only test that opens the verification link in a
browser that has never seen the signup tab — and until now nothing ran it.
Container E2E cannot: it boots with AUTH_AUTOVERIFY=true and
EMAILER_MODE=logger, so no verification email is ever generated there, and
the whole "signup → email → verify → signin" half of the auth surface has no
browser coverage at all.

The new lane boots the app on the runner (bin/setup, pnpm run build,
bin/ots server — visual.yml's shape, not the baked OCI image) with the four
conditions the spec's header names, each of which fails silently rather than
loudly when wrong:

  AUTHENTICATION_MODE=full   Rodauth is mounted; /verify-account exists.
  AUTH_AUTOVERIFY=false      an autoverified account sends no email, so the
                             lane would pass while testing nothing.
  RACK_ENV=production        auth.defaults.yaml force-disables the
                             verify_account feature whenever RACK_ENV=test.
  EMAILER_MODE=smtp          the email is really sent, and read back over
                             Mailpit's HTTP API by the spec.

Mail travels the production path: JOBS_ENABLED=true publishes onto RabbitMQ
and a scoped `bin/ots worker --queues=email.message.send` delivers it. The
`--check` run before the server boots is not just fail-fast — Publisher sends
to the default exchange with the queue name as routing key, so a message
published before that queue exists is dropped silently by the broker, and
--check runs the same QueueDeclarator.declare_all the worker does.

CREATE_ACCOUNT_RATE_LIMIT_ENABLED=false is the knob
etc/defaults/config.defaults.yaml already wires. The spec creates four
accounts per run against a cap of ten per masked client IP per hour with a
one-hour lockout, and CI Playwright retries twice; on a runner every request
resolves to the same masked network, so without this the cap is per-run.

The invocation is scoped to two specs rather than the e2e/auth/ directory:
the two SSO specs are dormant behind E2E_SSO_UI, and pending-plan-intent
needs billing and a populated plans API, has never run in CI, and would make
an unrelated red the default outcome of this lane. Widen the list as specs
are proven against this stack, not before.

Failure forensics cover the three indistinguishable causes of "the email
never arrived": server log (never enqueued), worker log (never consumed or
SMTP failed), and the Mailpit mailbox plus RabbitMQ queue depths.

[#4305] fix(config): SSL=false must mean non-Secure session cookies

First real run of the e2e-full-auth lane failed with a CSRF 403 on
every POST /auth/create-account. The chain, straight from the server
log: session.secure is absent from the rendered config when SSL is not
'true', boot.rb's ssl_enabled? fallback then defaults it to TRUE under
RACK_ENV=production, Session refuses to write a Secure cookie over a
request it sees as plain HTTP, so no session ever persists and the
CSRF token has nowhere to live. bin/visual already documents SSL=false
as 'pins http:// links/cookies' — true for links, silently false for
cookies; that lane never POSTs, so it never noticed.

Emit secure: false only for the exact string SSL=false. Unset stays
absent, preserving the production fallback to Secure; SSL=true is
unchanged. A plain-HTTP deployment gains nothing from a Secure cookie
that is never written, and a TLS-proxied deployment sets SSL=true
anyway because it needs https:// links.

ASSUME_HTTPS=true was the tempting alternative and is wrong here: it
upgrades the scheme for redirects and HSTS on a server with no TLS
listener.

[#4305] test(redirect): define the length cap in code points, pin fixture triples

Review follow-ups on the parity fixture.

The 2048 cap was measured in each host language's own .length — code
points in Ruby, UTF-16 units in JS — and the fixture pinned the boundary
only in ASCII, where the two are identical by construction. An astral
input near the cap ('/x' + '😀' * 1024) was Ruby-accepted and
TS-rejected: the server stored a redirect the SPA silently dropped. The
cap is now defined in Unicode code points; isValidInternalPath counts
them explicitly (UTF-16 length as a cheap lower bound, then code-point
stepping with early exit), and the fixture pins the boundary with
astral-length-at-cap / astral-length-over-cap, which both suites measure
in code points.

The anti-erosion guards also pinned bare case ids, so retargeting a
pinned case's input while flipping `expected` kept both suites green
with the rejection gone from coverage. The six #4305 acceptance-criteria
cases are now pinned as (id, input, expected) triples; the four length
cases stay pinned by id plus constructed length and expected.

[#4305] Follow-ups: shared redirect-parity fixture + full-auth E2E CI lane (#4308)

Pass the capture hint so beforeSend rules see the original error

`Client.captureException` does not build a hint the way
`Scope.captureException` does — it forwards the one it is given. This
facade gave it `undefined`, so `hint.originalException` was absent for
every capture the app makes, and both beforeSend rules that read it were
inert in production: the expected-transport-outcome drop (#4286) dropped
nothing and the api-error grouping (#4287) fingerprinted nothing, so
axios failures fragmented into a fresh issue per call site per deploy.

Prettier reflow of three untouched signatures rides along; it is a
byproduct of formatting the edited file, not a separate sweep.

Skip the after_login hook for Rodauth internal requests

`Auth::Config.valid_login_and_password?` (account destroy, change email,
change password, /auth/link-sso) runs the real login route to check a
credential and throws the result away. Its session is a bare Hash, so
`session.id` raised NoMethodError — one Sentry issue per confirmation
endpoint — and a password confirmation was recording login_success in
the auth audit stream, attempting the deferred SSO bind, and could fire
the new-sign-in security alert.

/auth/link-sso is unaffected: it verifies with the internal request but
establishes its session with its own `rodauth.login('password')` on the
actual route.

Reject session cookies whose bytes are not valid UTF-8

A cookie value is client-controlled bytes, and `String#match?` raises
ArgumentError on invalid UTF-8 — a request carrying a binary session
cookie 500s before any handler runs. An unmatchable byte sequence is by
definition not a valid sid.

Group v1 form errors by endpoint instead of message

v1 is unauthenticated and under constant bot traffic, and the default
grouping key for a message event IS the message — so every distinct
validation string anonymous input could provoke minted its own issue at
error level. Changing how malformed bodies fail (#4283 multipart
rejection) then read as a new escalating defect when it was the same
bots failing one step earlier.

The message stays the event text, so the backend scrubbers still see it
and the title still says what failed; only the fingerprint changes.
Level drops to warning: rejected input is the validator working.

Accept a boolean vhost keep_host from the proxy API

The vhost blob is Approximated's response stored verbatim and they
document keep_host as a boolean, but older stored blobs carry it as a
string. Declaring it string-only rejected the whole
CustomDomainListResponse on every dashboard load for any domain that
carries the flag. This field is not ours to normalize.

Add in-app browser bridge errors to the third-party ignore list

Observed on secret-link views as `xbrowser`/`swbrowser is not defined`
when the host app's injected object never loaded. The prefix identifies
the app, so the list grows one app at a time rather than matching a bare
`browser is not defined` that would also swallow our own.

Two defects shared one cause: pending_plan_intent was deleted the
moment a login response was built. An MFA-gated login therefore burned
the intent at the primary factor (the completion response then had
nothing to replay), and any client failure between sign-in and the
plans page lost the selection permanently.

The auth hooks now only peek: after_login surfaces billing_redirect
solely when no second factor is pending (reusing the same mfa_decision
branch condition), after_two_factor_authentication surfaces it on the
completion response, and neither deletes. Consumption moves to the one
authenticated plans-flow entry point every billing route converges on,

[#4306] fix(auth): keep the plan intent on the webauthn factor and encode its query

Two review findings on the post-auth redirect, both in the same path.

The webauthn second factor discarded its /auth/webauthn-auth completion body,
so the billing_redirect the backend replays there (#4306) never reached

guaranteed to survive the MFA hop. useWebAuthn now keeps that body in
mfaVerifyResponse, mirroring useMfa.verifyResponse, and MfaChallenge feeds the
completing factor's own body into completeChallenge.

The billing routes were built by interpolating product and interval into a raw

[#4305] fix(auth): keep accepted redirects out of the auth log

The accept branches of the capture and surface hooks logged the redirect
VALUE. Accepted redirects here are routinely bearer credentials in their
own right: /invite/<token> and /secret/<key> are both canonical accepted
shapes, and both grant access to whoever replays them. Auth::Logging
obscures only :email, so the whole string reached the log stream --
:auth_redirect_surfaced at :info, which is on in production.

Note the asymmetry this removes: the reject branches next door already
logged value_length only, "because the value is attacker-supplied". The
accept branches are the ones that by construction carry a working return
path, so they needed the same discipline more, not less.

loggable_path keeps the leading path segment -- the part with diagnostic
value ("they came back for an invite") and none of the secret. Two
details it gets right and a naive slice does not:

  - It slices the DECODED form. /secret%2f<key> is one raw segment but
    two real ones, so a raw slice carries the first 22 characters of the
    key into the log.
  - It caps the segment. No route puts a credential in the first segment
    today (the only top-level dynamic routes are 404 catch-alls), but a
    future one would be truncated rather than logged whole.

Callers log value_length alongside, so nothing diagnostic is lost.

[#4305] fix(diagnostics): scrub invitation and confirmation tokens

An invite_token is a bearer credential -- a valid one is accepted as
proof of email ownership -- and it reached Sentry in the clear. Two
independent holes, one on each side of the mirror:

  - The backend had no /invite/ arm in either path pattern. The token is
    SecureRandom.urlsafe_base64(32): 43 mixed-case characters, so it
    matches neither IDENTIFIER_PATH_PATTERN's lowercase-base36 shape nor
    IDENTIFIER_TEXT_PATTERN's 62/31-char shapes. Nothing caught it.

  - The frontend had an /invite/ arm but its value class was
    [a-zA-Z0-9]+, which stops at the first '-' or '_' that base64url
    emits. /invite/ab-cdef scrubbed to /invite/[REDACTED]-cdef: a partial
    credential that READS as redacted. That is worse than an obvious
    miss, because it survives a glance at the payload.

Reachable because signup (#4305) threads the return destination through
the browser URL as ?redirect=<path>, so an invited user's /invite/<token>
rides inside a query value. Both halves apply their path patterns to the
whole URL string and their value classes stop at '?' and '#', which is
what makes a query-embedded path scrubbable at all.

confirm gets the same treatment and for the same reason. The backend was
pinned to /account/email/confirm/ while the frontend has always matched
the bare /confirm/ segment, so a confirmation token under any other
prefix was scrubbed in the browser and passed through on the server. The
bare arm subsumes the prefixed one -- output is unchanged for the path
that already worked.

The (?!:) guard is new in both halves and pays for the widened class:
Sentry transaction names are route TEMPLATES, and /secret/:secretKey
names a group rather than an instance of one. The old alphanumeric class
excluded ':' incidentally; without the guard every parameterized
transaction would collapse into /secret/[REDACTED]. Redacting a template
that carries no data is pure signal loss, so the corpus pins it from the
other direction with `preserved` rows.

tests/fixtures/sensitive_path_corpus.json is the shared specification,
read by both halves the way email_redaction_corpus.json already is. It
carries no expected output: the two scrubbers reach the same contract
through different pattern sets (the backend discriminates identifier
paths by length, the frontend leans on generated route metadata), so
pinning one output string would pin an implementation detail instead of
the security property. Rows scoped `ruby` name the reason the browser
never sees that shape.

Verified non-vacuous: reverting the backend arms fails 4 rows including
the query-embedded one, and reverting the frontend class fails on the
token TAIL -- the exact bytes it used to leak.

Fingerprint v1 form errors on the route template

The endpoint grouping added earlier keyed on req.path. On the wildcard v1
routes -- /secret/:key, /receipt/:key, /receipt/:key/burn and the
/private/ and /metadata/ aliases -- that path is the concrete secret or
receipt key, so the change inverted its own goal there (one issue per
key) and put a bearer credential in the payload: before_send reaches
request.url, transaction and contexts.request.url, never tags and never
the fingerprint.

Otto stamps the matched route on the env during dispatch, and its
declared path ('/secret/:key') is the endpoint identity we wanted all
along -- it structurally cannot carry request data. The fallback, for
harnesses that invoke a controller without Otto's dispatch, scrubs the
raw path rather than trusting it and fails closed to 'unknown'.

The endpoint tag had the same defect one line away and now shares the
helper.

Scrub identifiers from fingerprints and the context path

Two spots in an outbound event that no scrubbing pass reached.

event.fingerprint is serialized verbatim and tags are not scrubbed
either, so a call site that groups on a request path leaks whatever that
path carries. The v1 grouping key is a route template now, but this is
the backstop that makes a repeat impossible rather than merely unlikely.
Static components -- 'v1-form-error', '/secret/:key', Sentry's
'{{ default }}' -- match none of the patterns and pass through
byte-identical, so grouping is unchanged for every well-behaved caller.

contexts.request.path is the live one. ErrorHandler.safe_request_context
deliberately drops the query string and keeps the bare path, and on
/secret/<id> the path alone is the credential; nothing downstream looked
at that key, so every capture_error call site -- v1 and web core alike
-- was shipping it.

Guard the internal-request check in the after-login hook

internal_request? is only defined when Rodauth's :internal_request
feature is enabled. config/base.rb enables it unconditionally today, so
this changes nothing now; it keeps a future conditional enablement from
turning every real login into a NoMethodError. Same shape as
hooks/create_account.rb, including the include_all argument that
respond_to? needs for a private method.

Correct what the captureMessage hint actually does

originalException is the half that matters -- it is what the beforeSend
rules read. syntheticException is not: eventFromMessage consults it only
under attachStacktrace, which this app never sets, so the comment
promised the message path a stack it cannot produce. Keep passing it so
both capture paths hand the client the same shape, and say why.

Pin that an absent vhost keep_host still parses

The union is nullable and not optional, which reads like a stored blob
predating the field would be rejected. It is not -- both shapes end in
.partial() -- but that is two files away from the field, so assert it
rather than leave the next reader to re-derive it.

The context scrub added a commit ago read contexts['request']['path'] and
so matched nothing in production. Sentry::Scope#set_context merges the
caller's Hash verbatim -- no key normalization anywhere in the path --
and every producer in this repo writes SYMBOL inner keys under a STRING

shipping from v1 capture_error and from the web error middleware, which
is the public secret-reveal surface.

third-party Ruby API, which is where the string-key convention makes its

fix(billing): require org owner for Stripe invoice URLs

The list_invoices endpoint returned Stripe invoice_pdf and
hosted_invoice_url bearer links to any organization member, because
load_organization was called without require_owner: true (the default
is false). Its four sibling endpoints (checkout, change-plan,

Add require_owner: true so only owners can fetch invoice URLs, and add
a regression spec asserting a non-owner member is denied (403).

fix(config): never ship a non-Secure session cookie in production

Restore the pre-regression fail-closed behavior for the session cookie
Secure flag.

The session-cookie config emitted `secure: false` for any SSL=false, so a
production deployment with SSL=false (the shipped quick-start default) got a
session cookie without the Secure attribute. Previously a non-'true' SSL
value omitted the key and boot.rb's ssl_enabled? fallback forced Secure on
in production.

Guard the escape hatch on environment: emit `secure: false` only when
SSL=false AND not production. In production (RACK_ENV=production, or unset,
which boot.rb treats as production) the key is left absent so ssl_enabled?
forces secure: true. Development keeps the plain-HTTP escape hatch.

Set SSL=true in .env.example: both shipped compose stacks terminate TLS at
the edge. The former SSL=false guidance becomes a comment scoping it to
bare-metal plain-HTTP development.

fix(secrets): rate-limit anonymous secret creation

The secret-creation path had no rate limiter on the modern API surface.
A single anonymous client sustained ~113 req/s at ~18 KiB of Redis per
secret, writing ~1 GiB of Redis in ~8.6 minutes. Because Redis also holds
sessions, this is a full-outage DoS reachable by any unauthenticated
client (finding F-02).

Add a registry-managed `create_secret` limiter (single-tier, per masked
client IP) and enforce it on every anonymous creation entry point:

- V2/V3 API conceal and generate via the shared
  V2::Logic::Secrets::BaseSecretAction#raise_concerns (raises
  LimitExceeded, rendered as a 429 by otto_hooks)
- V1 API share/generate/create at the controller, using V1's own
  return-based error idiom over the same masked-IP subject

Charged only to guests; authenticated callers are accountable and are
the legitimate high-volume creators. Default 500/window (1h), configurable
via site.secret_options.create_rate_limit / SECRET_CREATE_RATE_LIMIT_*.
Disabled in the test config so the suite is not throttled.

fix(auth): allowlist host in auth email links to prevent reset-link poisoning

Rodauth's base_url roots every auth email link (password-reset, magic-link,
verify-account, verify-login-change, unlock) and the SSO redirect_uri. The
host was taken from env['onetime.display_domain'] / Rack::DetectHost without
requiring positive evidence that it is a served tenant host, and the canonical
fallback read Rack::Request#host — which Rack 3.2 resolves from a
client-settable X-Forwarded-Host/Forwarded. Either path let a genuine service
email carry a link to an attacker origin (account takeover, cross-tenant).

- Auth::PublicHost.resolve now accepts a candidate only when it names a
  registered CustomDomain (from_display_domain), failing closed on a datastore
  error. Independent of the fragile :custom classification, so a real customer
  domain still builds links on itself even when Chooserator degrades to :invalid.
- The base_url / public_display_domain overrides fall back to the canonical
  host from site config, never request.host.
- New StripForwardedHost middleware deletes X-Forwarded-Host / Forwarded after
  Rack::DetectHost has consumed them, so no later request.host read can carry a
  client-supplied authority (defense in depth).
- WebAuthn rp_id/origin route host derivation through the same resolver (G-16).
- Updated the public_base_url / omniauth_full_host unit specs and the middleware
  manifest; added regression cases for unregistered and forwarded attacker hosts.

fix(colonel): stop exposing live session-cookie values in session APIs

The per-customer colonel session view serialized SessionMetadata via
safe_dump with :session_id in the allow-list. That field is the plain
session id, which is byte-identical to the onetime.session cookie value
and the session:<sid> Redis blob key. A privileged operator listing a
user's sessions therefore received a replayable session cookie for any
user, enabling silent, unattributable impersonation past MFA (F-01).

Replace :session_id in the allow-list with :session_handle, a
non-reversible truncated HMAC-SHA256 of the sid keyed with the global
secret. The colonel list and revoke round-trip on this handle; the raw
sid never crosses the API. The single-session revoke adapter resolves
the handle back to a sid by matching it over the target customer's own
active_sessions set, so the untrusted handle can only ever name one of
that customer's sessions. The revoke operation stays keyed by the raw
sid internally (unchanged), so its audited invalidation semantics are
preserved.

The end-user /auth/active-sessions route is unaffected: it joins on the
Rodauth active_session_id HMAC and reads only display fields from the
sidecar, never the raw sid. The global session console is a separate
scan/decrypt path and is out of scope for this finding.

fix(auth): stop doubling the port when the canonical host carries one

The full-auth E2E lane went red on b55ecede: every verification email
carried `http://localhost:7143:7143/verify-account?key=...`, which
`new URL()` rejects, so all four signup-redirect specs died in
rebaseOnto with `TypeError: Invalid URL`.

`origin_for` takes the port from the request and interpolates the host
as-is, which is right for the tenant tier — `resolve` only ever yields a
bare custom-domain hostname. The canonical-request tier added in
b55ecede breaks that assumption: `site.host` is configured as an
AUTHORITY (`localhost:7143` in this lane, `secrets.internal:8443` on an
on-prem install), `DomainStrategy#call` copies it verbatim into
`display_domain` whenever domains are disabled, and `canonical_host?`
admits it PORT-INSENSITIVELY — so `canonical_request_host` legitimately
hands back a ported host on every ordinary request to such a deployment,
and the request port was then appended to it a second time.

Normalize the host through `Onetime::Utils::DomainParser.extract_hostname`
before building the authority: the same port-stripping normalizer
`canonical_host?` admits the candidate with, so the hostname emitted is
exactly the one that passed admission. It cannot widen the allowlist —
`origin_for` is only ever reached with an already-allowlisted host, and
stripping a port cannot turn a rejected host into an accepted one.
IPv6 literals come back bare from that normalizer, so re-bracket them per
RFC 3986 3.2.2 rather than emitting `http://::1:7143`.

Not lane-only: this shipped a dead link in every verification, reset,
magic-link and unlock email on any deployment whose site.host names a
port — the exact artifact this PR exists to protect.

Regression coverage in public_base_url_spec.rb pins the lane's own
topology (site.host with a port, http, domains disabled) end-to-end
through the Rodauth override, plus the default-port and IPv6 cases on
`.canonical_request_base_url`. All four fail on the parent commit with
the CI symptom (`http://localhost:7143:7143`) and pass here.

feat(audit): external sink, export, and tamper-resistant retention (#4334)

Retention was a hard 10k count trim with no sink, no export, and a public
`trim!(0)` that wiped the trail in one call. Three changes, in that order of
importance.

THE SINK (the load-bearing one). Every event — both trails — is now emitted
as a structured log line on its own `ColonelAudit` SemanticLogger category
BEFORE the datastore write. Ordering is the guarantee: a Valkey outage, an
eviction or a trim can no longer lose the record, because the line has
already left the process. The two destinations are independent in both
directions — a sink failure is caught and logged and never costs the Redis
write or the caller (nor, for a fail-closed verb, aborts the operation over
a broken appender), and a datastore failure never un-emits the line, which
is what makes #4333's fail-closed posture survivable. The model header now
says plainly which half is the durability story and which is the queryable
cache. `setup_loggers` gains an OPTIONAL syslog appender behind
`audit.syslog` (default off, filtered to the audit category, one boot
warning instead of a failed start if it cannot be built). The sink level is
pinned in code rather than read from the logging config: the audit stream
must not go quiet because the global level was raised. `syslog` joins the
Gemfile's stdlib section — Ruby 3.4 made it a bundled gem, so without it
Bundler blocks the appender the moment an operator enables it; the local
`syslog://` path needs no third-party gem (the level map is passed
explicitly to avoid autoloading a formatter that requires `syslog_protocol`).

EXPORT. `GET /api/colonel/audit/export?format=csv|ndjson` downloads the
whole retained trail under the current filters, with Export CSV / NDJSON
links on the admin screen and `bin/ots audit list` for the shell. The merge,
the filter semantics and the FIELD ALLOWLIST move into
Onetime::ColonelAuditReader (in lib/, so the CLI reaches it without an app
autoloader) so the three readers cannot drift on what an operator may see.
The export is the one colonel route that is not `response=json`: Otto's
Logic-class handler never sees the Rack response and its JSON handler
re-encodes every body, so it uses the `Klass.method` form Otto documents for
that case (repo precedent: Internal::ACME::AskHandler.call). A non-JSON body
has no Zod shape, documented where the shape would have gone.

TAMPER RESISTANCE. `trim!` and `trim_security!` clamp in the widening
direction — a cap below the constant is raised to it, and a positive
security max_age below SECURITY_EVENT_RETENTION is raised to it (the age
bound was the second door into the same wipe). `trim!(0)` is now a no-op;
narrowing retention is a change to the constants, under review. Stated
honestly in the docs: this bounds the audit API, not the Familia collection
behind it — `events.clear` still exists and is what test setup uses.

feat(audit): budgeted sensitive-read audit stream (#4335)

CONTRACT 4 used to read "audit is for mutations; reads never audit." That
protected the operator trail from read-volume eviction — a real and still
necessary property — but it also meant the console could disclose a customer's
email, decrypt their live session, or export a year of usage with no record of
who looked. The two goals were never in tension; they only looked that way
while there was one collection. The contract now reads:

  Reads never write the OPERATOR trail. Curated sensitive reads write their
  own budgeted stream.

ColonelAuditEvent gains a third class_sorted_set, `access_events`, with
`record_access` / `recent_access` / `access_count` / `trim_access!` mirroring
the security trio. Own budget: MAX_ACCESS_EVENTS = 5_000 (half the operator
cap — "who looked" is supporting context for "who changed") plus a 30-day age
bound, longer than the security trail's 7 days because an observation is an
attributed operator action worth reviewing weeks later, still bounded because
an indefinite record of everything an operator ever looked at is itself
surveillance data. Both trim arguments clamp in the widening direction, like
the other two (#4334). Fail-open always, with no fail_closed keyword: an
observation mutated nothing, so failing closed could only break the console
over a broken audit write.

CURATED CALL SITES — recorded when a read exposes customer material or is a
bulk extraction; the other ~25 colonel reads stay unaudited, and the trends
endpoint's "no event on either trail" test pins that the curation is real:

  secret.receipt_view          owner's full email
  customer.diagnostics_view    auth-log tail + sessions + lockout, one person
  session.inspect              decrypts one live session
  session.list_for_customer    where one named person is signed in
  session.list                 every row carries email/IP/UA; search is a
                               free-text index over customer addresses — MORE
                               customer material than the per-customer view,
                               so auditing only the narrower one would have
                               been backwards
  audit.list / audit.export    all three readers, incl. the CLI
  usage.export                 365 days, SCANs 10k secrets + every customer

raw sid: a live session id is the cookie itself (F-01), and audit events are
emitted to the log sink and leave the process immediately, so recording it
would put a replayable credential into the log stream.

The audit-read verbs are single-sourced on ColonelAuditReader rather than the
model — a multi-emitter verb belongs on whatever its emitters already share,
and the model knows nothing about reading surfaces.

feat(audit): record dry-run previews and no-change attempts (#4337)

Two families of operator action changed nothing and therefore recorded
nothing. Both now record, and they go to DIFFERENT trails — which is the
distinction the change is actually about.

DRY-RUN PREVIEWS -> the observation trail (#4335's access_events).
A preview mutates nothing, but it enumerates exactly what a destructive run
would touch: the message count a purge would delete, the members and domains
an org delete would take with it, the addresses a replay would re-fire. That
is reconnaissance, and several of these ops default to dry_run: true, so the
preview is the step an operator always takes first — the one that left no
trace at all. Each records one event with the op's OWN verb and target, so a
preview and the apply that followed read as one sequence when filtered by
verb, plus result: 'preview' and dry_run: true in the detail. Volume lands on
the budgeted stream by design, never on the operator trail. Failure paths
already disambiguate via `dry_run` in AuditedFailure detail and are untouched.

The survey's list of dry-run ops was incomplete. Verified by grep, the set is
15, not 11: it also includes memberships/entitlement_override (which defaults
to dry_run: true), email/send_test, email/sync_provider_feedback (whose real
run this branch made audited in #4336), and customers/reconcile_role_index.
That last one is gated on a known actor, matching its own audit_repair gate:
its report-only path is reachable with actor: nil from the doctor tooling, and
an observation attributed to nobody is noise, not accountability (ADR-023).
Two more ops have a dry_run — auth/backfill_tenant_issuer and
auth/bulk_sso_migration — but they write NO audit events at all today, so
auditing them is an unaudited-mutation question (#4336's shape), not this one.

NO-CHANGE ATTEMPTS -> the operator trail.
Suspending an already-suspended account, setting a role to the role it already
holds, re-applying the current plan: these returned :no_change and skipped the
audit write under an "only audit an actual change" rule. That rule read the
trail as a log of EFFECTS; it is a log of what operators DID. Reaching for
`colonel` on an account that already holds it is the same reach for the same
privilege, and a trail that goes quiet for it can show nothing while an
operator repeatedly probes a privileged account. These now record under the
op's normal verb with detail: { outcome: 'no_change', ... } — not fail_closed,
since nothing was destroyed or revoked, and turning an idempotent no-op into a
500 would be a regression.

Six sites: customers/set_suspension, set_role, set_plan, set_verification,
memberships/set_role, org/set_plan. set_verification was not in the survey but
is a direct peer in the same directory with the same skip.

Ops that REFUSE on no-change rather than skipping are already audited through
their refusal path and are deliberately left alone.

Tests: a new spec pins both halves and, importantly, that they do not cross
(a preview never reaches `record`; a no-change never reaches `record_access`).
Four incumbent tests asserted the old "no-change audits nothing" behaviour and
are updated to assert the new event rather than deleted.

feat(audit): optional operator-supplied reason on destructive verbs (#4338)

The operator trail said who did what to whom and how it went, and never
WHY. "ur_colonel purged ur_alice" cannot be told apart from a GDPR erasure,
a mistake, or an insider clearing their tracks without leaving the system to
find the ticket — and for a purge the account it names is gone, so there is
nothing left to inspect. Every destructive verb now takes an OPTIONAL
`reason:` and puts it in its audit `detail`.

Onetime::AuditReason (lib/) owns both rules once, so twelve ops cannot drift.
BLANK IS ABSENT: stripped, and an empty or whitespace-only reason is nil,
never "" — an empty string in the trail reads as "they gave a reason" when
they did not. ABSENT MEANS UNCHANGED: with no reason the detail hash is
byte-for-byte its pre-#4338 self, with no `reason: nil` key, which is what
lets this ship without touching one incumbent expectation. MAX_LENGTH is 255,
one UNDER the model's per-value truncation, so what an operator types is what
a reviewer reads back; `reason` is deliberately not a sensitive key.

It rides INSIDE `detail`, not as a new wire field: ColonelAuditReader::FIELDS,
the Zod shape and the CSV header are one linked contract, and `detail` is
already rendered and exported verbatim.

Scope is exactly the set commit 1 declared destructive enough to fail closed —
customer.purge/.set_role/.suspend/.unsuspend, organization.delete,
session.delete/.revoke/.revoke_all, secret.delete, queue.dlq.purge,
domain.remove, membership.remove/.set_role — plus their #4337 peers: a
no-change attempt and a dry-run preview each carry the reason too, because an
attempted-but-no-op action and a reconnaissance pass each have a why.

Three surfaces. AdminConfirmDialog grows `requestReason` (default FALSE, so
every incumbent call site is untouched and still emits `confirm` with no
payload); it never gates the button, because requiring a reason is the second
step of this rollout, not this one. Twelve colonel adapters read the param
through ONE ColonelAPI::Logic::Base#operator_reason_param — POST to the body,
DELETE to the query string, since DELETE bodies are not reliably parsed here.
Nine CLI peers gain --reason, joining `customers suspend`, which has had one
since before this issue and is the precedent the rest follow.

Two deliberate exclusions, both because `reason` is already taken and one key
cannot mean two things. The membership REFUSAL events use it for the refusal
STATUS; a refusal mutated nothing, so what a reviewer needs there is why the
system said no. The email suppression ops use it for the suppression
classification. The customer-facing org delete sends none either: an owner
deleting their own workspace is not an operator explaining an action on
someone else's data.

feat(audit): record failed colonel sign-in attempts (#4339)

A successful colonel.signin has been audited at both auth modes' session
sites since the trail gained a signal for operator presence. A FAILED one
recorded nothing at all, and both emitters carried the same rationale: the
operator trail is capped by COUNT with no TTL, so an event an
unauthenticated caller can trigger is a log-eviction primitive against it.

That argument was correct, and still is for `events` — which is why both
success writes stay `.record`. It stopped being a reason to record NOTHING
once the store grew a second budget (#4335's split). So the highest-signal
security event the trail could hold, somebody working through passwords
against a real admin account, was the one event it did not hold: a
brute-force against a colonel was invisible.

Both emitters now write `colonel.signin_failed` to `security_events` via
.record_security — full mode from the Rodauth after_login_failure hook,
simple mode from its credential-rejection funnel — through one shared
guard, Onetime::ColonelSigninFailure, so the two modes cannot drift on the
lookup, the role gate, the obscured target or the fail-open rescue.

Shape and bounds:

- Only attempts against an account that EXISTS and holds the colonel role
  record anything. An event per submitted address would let anyone mint
  rows for invented strings; the curated signal is "a real admin account is
  being targeted".
- Target is the OBSCURED email, as on every other event in this stream —
  never the raw address, never an extid (nobody has proven they are that
  account), never an objid. Events ship to the external ColonelAudit sink
  at write time, so the payload must be safe to leave the process. Detail
  is auth_mode + a coarse failure_reason ('invalid_credentials', the
  vocabulary the sites' own failure logs already use). No client IP: this
  is a detection signal and the origin is in the log line each site
  already writes, matching the three record_security precedents.
- No throttle. Budget separation is the control (WRITE-FREQUENCY
  INVARIANT): a flood evicts only other anonymous telemetry, and the login
  rate limiter already gates the surrounding path. At most one event per
  failed attempt — simple mode's two rejection branches are mutually
  exclusive, and full mode emits once outside its log branch.
- VERB_COLONEL_SIGNIN_FAILED is spelled with an underscore, not as
  `colonel.signin.failed`, because ColonelAuditReader matches a verb
  exactly or as a DOTTED CATEGORY PREFIX: the dotted spelling would
  silently widen the existing `colonel.signin` filter from "who signed in"
  to "who tried". As siblings each stays separately filterable and
  `colonel` still rolls both up — which matters here because the two live
  in different collections with different retention.

The obsolete "failures deliberately record nothing" rationale is
superseded honestly at both sites rather than deleted. The Rodauth SQL
audit log (account_authentication_audit_logs) is out of scope and
untouched.

feat(colonel): add a step-up (sudo) window for destructive colonel actions (#4327)

No sudo mode, no password re-entry, no session-age check existed anywhere in the
colonel ops, so a leaked colonel cookie was standing destructive capability.

Adds a 10-minute elevation window recorded on the session as the registered
sidecar field `elevated_until` and checked server-side by
ColonelAPI::Logic::DestructiveAction in the tier-1 logic classes — not the router
— so it composes with #4326's confirmation.

The stored value is {extid, exp}, not a bare epoch, and elevated? ignores a
record naming a different account. That matters because one onetime.session can
outlive an identity change: simple-mode login (authentication.rb:96-120) neither
clears nor renews the session, and full-mode :renew carries the hash to a new
sid. Both login paths now also drop the field outright.

Two factors. `password` re-verification branches on
Onetime.auth_config.full_enabled? BEFORE naming Auth::Config (apps/web/auth is
not loaded in simple mode). `recent_auth` elevates without a credential inside a
post-sign-in grace, but ONLY for accounts that cannot satisfy the password factor
and ONLY when an operator sets a non-zero grace — the default is 0. Handing that
grace to password holders (the first draft) would have made step-up a no-op for
the first five minutes after every colonel sign-in, which is the exact condition
this issue exists to remove. SSO-only fleets set the grace or disable elevation;
MFA as a step-up factor is a follow-up.

POST /api/colonel/elevation brings its own throttle (the Rodauth internal-request
password check bypasses lockout) and its own audit events: .record on success
carrying the factor, .record_security on failure, and nothing at all on an
ElevationRequired refusal, which a cookie holder can drive on demand against a
count-capped trail.

The console fetches GET /api/colonel/elevation on mount, after an elevate/drop
and on a 403, and counts down client-side. It deliberately does NOT poll:
TrackMetadata advances last_activity_at on every authenticated request, so a
polling banner would make #4331's idle timeout unreachable while a tab is open.
A 403 elevation_required opens an in-place sudo prompt that always requires an
operator gesture, then retries once.

Residual risk, stated in the config comment and the operator guide: while a
window is live, a stolen cookie is as capable as before. The window bounds and
audits the capability; binding it to a value the cookie does not carry is the
follow-up.

SetUserRole had no self-target guard (unlike PurgeUser), no peer-colonel guard and
no last-colonel count: a colonel could demote every colonel including themselves,
and recovery was CLI-only. DeleteSession had the same gap for the acting session.
UnverifyUser had it too, and worse: has_system_role? refuses elevated roles to
unverified accounts, so unverifying the last colonel is a demotion by another
name — and it was reachable in one un-gated POST, straight past any last-colonel
check on the role endpoint.

predicate (Operations::Customers::RoleSupport), refusals as op Result statuses
routed through a single `build` exit point so the :failure audit cannot be
skipped, and adapter-level 422s that name the remediation. Living in the ops
means `bin/ots customers role demote` is interlocked too, with a CLI spec.

The roster deliberately does NOT use Customer.colonel_count: the role index drifts
upward (add-only partial writes; TTL-expired customer hashes leave members behind
forever), so counting it would make the guard fail open. active_colonels
re-validates exists? && role == 'colonel' && verified? on every member.

Interlocks run AFTER elevation and confirmation (the guard-order contract in
colonel/logic/base.rb), so their 422s cannot be used as a free "who is the last
colonel" / "is this session mine" oracle by someone holding only the cookie.

Revoke-all against your OWN account is deliberately NOT refused: it is the first
containment step for a leaked colonel cookie. It routes to
RevokeAllForCustomerExceptCurrent and keeps the session you are working in.

was stripping '@' and '.' out of email identifiers), extracts the acting
colonel's own session handle into a shared CurrentSession mixin, and makes
revoke-all resolve its target instead of silently returning zero counts.

The bounds scope to the API SURFACE (/api/colonel), not to the session object and
not to the /colonel SPA shell. Expiring the session itself would log a colonel out
of the tenant app too, and on a self-hosted install the colonel is often the only
customer; 401ing the shell would return a bare JSON error on an HTML navigation
with no way to render the expired banner, which lives inside the SPA. The shell
loads, the first API call 401s, the banner explains. This gets the security
property with no tenant-side regression; splitting the admin surface onto its own
cookie remains the fuller fix.

The idle bound reads the best-effort SessionMetadata sidecar and SKIPS itself
when no record exists — a lapsed 30-day sidecar or a pre-feature session must not
log anyone out. It also depends on the admin console making no periodic requests,
since TrackMetadata advances last_activity_at on every authenticated commit; the
#4327 elevation UI is built without a poll for exactly this reason and an
integration test pins it. Both bounds are configurable; 0 disables either.

One addition the design did not spell out: a REFUSED request is not activity.
The strategy stamps onetime.admin_session_expired into the Rack env and
TrackMetadata skips its upsert when it sees it. Without that, the very request
the idle bound rejected would advance last_activity_at on its way out and the
next one would sail through — the bound would cost an attacker exactly one 401.
Verified by removing the gate and watching the integration example fail.

fix(colonel): close the last-colonel check-then-act race with post-write re-validation (#4328)

The last-colonel / last-verified-colonel interlocks in SetRole and
SetVerification were check-then-act: the pre-check reads the roster, passes,
then the op writes with no atomicity. Two concurrent demotions (or unverifies)
of the two distinct last colonels can each pass the pre-check (each still sees
the other) and both write, leaving the install with zero colonels — CLI-only
recovery, the exact outcome #4328 exists to prevent.

Both ops now re-run the active-colonel check AFTER the write. If this write
emptied the roster, the change is rolled back (role restored / re-verified) and
the same :last_colonel refusal is returned through the single build() exit, so
the :failure event still audits. Over-preserving on a concurrent double-rollback
is the safe direction. The post-write check is guarded so only a demotion FROM
colonel / an unverify OF a colonel triggers it — an unrelated change is never
rolled back because the roster is empty for another reason.

Op specs simulate the roster dropping to zero between the pre-check and the
post-check (find_all_by_role returns non-empty then empty) and assert the write
is reverted and a :last_colonel failure is returned and audited.

Out of scope for this epic: the analogous sole-owner interlock in
Memberships::Remove / Memberships::SetRole has the same theoretical race, but
(1) #4328 is scoped to the colonel roster / admin lockout, and (2) rolling back
Memberships::Remove means resurrecting a destroyed through-model plus its four
materialized-entitlement sub-keys, which is not a safe field-restore and needs
its own design rather than a copied post-write check.

fix(colonel): confirm-header byte cap and + handling for multibyte tokens (#4326)

The X-OTS-Confirm cap was measured on the percent-ENCODED value and applied by
truncation (raw[0, 512]). encodeURIComponent expands a UTF-8 token up to 12 bytes
per 4-byte codepoint, so an org display_name (up to 100 chars, ~900 bytes encoded)
was severed mid-escape and decoded to nil/prefix — a permanent 403 on delete,
transfer, entitlements and add-membership for that org, with no operator
workaround since the token IS the name.

Reject an over-long header whole instead of truncating (a sliced multibyte token
would 403 anyway), raise MAX_CONFIRM_BYTES to 4096 (clears the largest legitimate
token; the real limit stays MAX_CONFIRM_LENGTH, post-decode, in the logic layer),
and decode with URI.decode_uri_component to match the console's encodeURIComponent
exactly — it does not map '+' to space, so a plus-addressed email sent raw by a
non-browser client survives. Specs cover the multibyte token, the + preservation,
and reject-not-truncate.

fix(auth): validate simple-mode login against the attempted identity only

Logic::Base seeds @cust with strategy_result.user — the session-carried
customer. process_params only overwrote it on a passphrase match, so a
login POST arriving with a session could re-authenticate as the CARRIED
customer whenever the submitted password matched that customer, silently
ignoring the account the login param named — and skipping the failure
funnel, so the attempt was never rate-limit-counted or audited. The
'Login failed' log line likewise reported the carried identity.

Not privilege escalation (whoever got authenticated had their own
password presented), and unreachable through the stock controller
(StrategyResult#authenticated? is !user.nil?, so authenticated sessions
are turned away before the logic runs) — but the logic class is the
authentication boundary and now enforces this itself:

- process_params overwrites @cust unconditionally: the attempted account
  on a passphrase match, nil otherwise. raise_concerns becomes the
  single failure funnel for every rejected credential, carried session
  or not.
- success? is nil-safe and fails closed unless @cust is the very object
  the login param resolved to.
- The failure log attributes to @potential_customer, matching the
  colonel.signin_failed attribution fixed in #4361 (6ab5303c) and full
  mode's after_login_failure, which logs the submitted login.

in this app), so full mode resolves the account from the submitted login,
verifies the password against that account alone, and switches the
session on success. Simple mode now agrees; the identity-switch success
path is pinned in the spec so this fix cannot regress it.

refactor(account): dispatch notification-preference fields through an explicit table

UpdateNotificationPreference read and wrote the customer with
`cust.send(field)` on a request param. The send was gated by the
VALID_FIELDS allowlist, so it was safe — but the allowlist and the
reflection were two things that had to agree, and a scanner cannot see

name reaches nothing on the customer.

preference (objid) reads nothing, is refused, and writes nothing; and
VALID_FIELDS cannot drift from the table it is derived from.

fix(rack): pin Rack::Request.forwarded_priority to the X-Forwarded-* family

Rack 3.2 defaults forwarded_priority to [:forwarded, :x_forwarded], so an
RFC 7239 Forwarded header from any client outranks the X-Forwarded-* family
the proxy actually manages. Caddy overwrites X-Forwarded-Host/For/Proto but
passes an unmanaged Forwarded header through untouched, which left
request.host (and everything built from it) resolvable to a client-chosen
authority whenever a Forwarded header reached the app.

Add Onetime::Initializers::ConfigureRack, which pins the priority to

[#4121] test(admin-gate): Forwarded is no longer a host source

The admin gate derives its forwarded-host provenance keys from
Rack::DetectHost::FORWARDED_HEADERS, which no longer lists the RFC 7239
Forwarded header. The stale case fabricated a detected host that
DetectHost can no longer produce from a Forwarded header alone and
expected the gate to refuse it on provenance.

Replace it with the new contract: a Forwarded host parameter never
enters the decision. The Host-derived detected host is judged on the
allowlist as usual, a stray Forwarded value cannot evict a good request,
and the provenance key list is pinned to the three headers DetectHost
still honors.

[#4121] fix(admin-gate): refuse a disagreeing RFC 7239 Forwarded host from an untrusted peer

Review of #4383 found that removing Forwarded from DetectHost's header set
turned a fail-closed denial into an admission. An edge that rewrites Host to
the origin's own canonical name and carries the public host only in
`Forwarded: host=` used to 404 both admin surfaces (the detected host came
from Forwarded and disagreed with Host). After the removal the detected host
is the Host-derived, allowlisted one, and rules (b)/(c) admit it — so the
admin console is served on every tenant-domain request in that topology.

Presence in FORWARDED_HOST_ENV_KEYS would not close this: rule (c) compares
the detected host to the Host-derived host, and they are now equal. The gate
therefore judges Forwarded by VALUE (rule d): the first host= parameter,
parsed by Rack::Utils.forwarded_values and normalized like the detected host,
is refused from an untrusted peer when it names a host other than what Host
alone produced. An agreeing host=, a Forwarded with no host=, or one Rack
rejects as malformed is no claim and is admitted as an ordinary Host request.
A trusted peer (otto.via_trusted_proxy == true) is admitted as before.

FORWARDED_HOST_ENV_KEYS stays derived from DetectHost's contract; Forwarded
gets its own RFC7239_FORWARDED_ENV_KEY constant so the presence set and the
value-judged header cannot be confused.
