Drop the development-only /auth/admin/stats stub

It computed authdb aggregates behind no role check and was reachable only
when Onetime.development? held. The standalone Rodauth Admin serves the
same numbers behind real authentication, and the rodauth-admin charter
lists deleting this stub as one of the three sanctioned integration
seams. The specs that tolerated any status on the path now pin the
router's JSON 404 in every environment.

Add RODAUTH_ADMIN_URL and the Onetime::RodauthAdmin link builder

The colonel console's only relationship with the standalone Rodauth Admin
is outbound links (rodauth-admin charter, section 4): no shared session,
no cross-service call, no credential. The base URL is therefore optional
everywhere, including production, and unset means callers render plain
text. Both builders are gated on full auth mode because simple mode has
no accounts table to link to, so a configured URL is ignored rather than
producing a link that cannot resolve.

The account link targets the admin's inbound lookup route
(/account?q=<external_id>), which redirects to the canonical numeric
account page; the admin keys account pages by Rodauth id, so there is no
/accounts/<extid> to link to directly.

Deep-link the colonel customer page to its Rodauth Admin account

The read-only use of the accounts.external_id == Customer.extid join. The
server decides whether a link exists (full auth mode and RODAUTH_ADMIN_URL
both set) and the page only renders what it is handed, so the admin's
internal hostname never reaches a public bootstrap payload. The Show
operation carries the same link for the CLI. The locale key is added
without a content hash; the rehash script owns those.

Say the colonel session views are non-authoritative in full auth mode

Both the sessions console and the per-customer sessions panel read the
Redis session store, which is the authority only in simple mode. In full
mode Rodauth's account_active_session_keys table is authoritative and
Rodauth-authenticated users may have no Redis session at all, so the
views were presenting a partial list as complete.

The charter rules out growing SQL awareness here (section 4, seam 2):
the listings now carry a session_authority block and the views render a
notice that links to Rodauth Admin when RODAUTH_ADMIN_URL is set. The
block is optional in the schemas so a backend predating it still parses,
and the notice renders nothing in simple mode. Locale keys are added
without content hashes; the rehash script owns those.

Point docs/specs/rodauth-admin at the standalone codebase

The two specs scoped Rodauth Admin as a graft inside the colonel console;
that plan was reversed and the documents live on verbatim in the
rodauth-admin repository's inherited specs. What stays here is a table
of the three integration seams and the config that drives them, plus
the changelog fragment for the series.

Link every customer and session row to its Rodauth Admin account

The customer detail page already handed over by extid; the customers list
drawer, the sessions console rows and the session drawer now carry the
same server-built link, so the non-authoritative banner's hand-over is
per-session rather than per-console. Same rule everywhere: the server
builds the URL (full auth mode and RODAUTH_ADMIN_URL both set) or sends
null, and the views render plain text for null or an absent field. No
new seam; the same outbound link on more rows. The locale key is added
without a content hash.

Enforce Rodauth's active-session table on every full-mode request

In full mode a signed-in browser holds two records: the Redis session
blob that every per-request gate reads, and a row in Rodauth's
account_active_session_keys that only the /auth/active-sessions routes
consulted. Deleting the row — a user revoking another device, "sign out
everywhere", or an operator in Rodauth Admin — therefore ended nothing;
the blob kept answering authenticated until it expired.

Onetime::ActiveSessionGate joins the blob to the row on the digest the
active_sessions feature already stamps into the session at login, one
primary-key SELECT per authenticated request, memoized in the Rack env
so the Otto strategy and the controller helpers share the verdict. Both
now refuse a session whose row is gone.

Three things are deliberately not enforced. A blob without the stamp
(signed in before it existed) is skipped rather than mass-logged-out on
deploy. An unreachable authdb fails open with an error log: a blip must
not sign out every user, and logins already fail during one. The
inactivity and lifetime deadlines stay on the sessions page; the gate
only refreshes last_use, throttled to once per five minutes, because
that page's sweep now actually ends sessions and a stale last_use would
sign out an active user.

Fail closed when the active-session row cannot be checked

The gate shipped failing open: an unreachable authdb logged an error and
let the request through on the Redis session alone, on the argument
that a database blip must not sign out every full-mode user at once.
That was an availability argument dressed as a security one. The
Rodauth row is the revocation authority in full mode, and a check whose
security property holds only while its store is reachable fails
insecure. Logins already need the same database, so the site is
degraded during an outage either way; failing open merely kept revoked
sessions alive through it.

ActiveSessionGate.revoked? now refuses on both :revoked and
:unavailable. The verdicts stay distinct so the strategy can refuse
under its own marker, [SESSION_UNVERIFIED], and the error log names the
posture, so an outage reads as an outage in the logs and never as a
revocation nobody performed. The Redis session is left intact and is
honoured again once the database returns.

Name the two records behind a full-mode session

Prose around the gate used "session" for both the per-request HTTP
session in Redis and Rodauth's authentication record in the authdb,
which made the fail-closed decision hard to state precisely. The
distinction is now vocabulary, recorded in
docs/architecture/terminology.md and in the gate's module doc:

  Rack session        env['rack.session'], cookie-bound, stored by
                      Onetime::Session as an encrypted blob in Redis
  active-session row  a row in Rodauth's account_active_session_keys
                      table in the authdb; full mode only
  join key            active_session_id_hmac, stamped into the Rack
                      session at login, equal to the row's session_id

  revoke   remove an active-session row (Rodauth's verb)
  destroy  delete a Rack session's blob from Redis (logout)
  refuse   401 / authenticated? == false while the Rack session stays
           in Redis; the only thing the gate does

The colonel console's per-customer "revoke" predates the distinction
and is a destroy; the table records it as the exception.

Applied throughout the gate, its two callers, the failure markers, the

The gate's module doc also regains its structure: the failure-posture

Decide the last_use refresh in the database's clock

The gate compared Ruby's Time.now with the row's last_use, a naive
timestamp Rodauth writes with SQL CURRENT_TIMESTAMP. On any host whose
process TZ differs from the database session's the comparison is off by
the offset: west of the database the throttle never fires, last_use
stays at the login timestamp and the inactivity sweep signs out an
active user a day later; east of it every request writes.

The existence SELECT now also asks the database whether the refresh is
due (CASE on last_use < CURRENT_TIMESTAMP - TOUCH_INTERVAL, via the
date_arithmetic extension Auth::Database already loads, as an integer
because SQLite has no boolean type) and the UPDATE writes
CURRENT_TIMESTAMP. Ruby's clock is no longer consulted; the steady
state stays one read-only SELECT per request.

A failed refresh now logs at warn rather than debug, naming the
consequence: last_use feeds the inactivity sweep, so a write that keeps
failing ends in a live session being revoked, and that sign-out must be
traceable to its cause.

Share the gate's env memo with controllers that spell the request `req`

SessionHelpers looked for the Rack env only through `request`, but the
core and billing controllers expose it as `req`, so on those surfaces
`authenticated?` never found the env memo and paid for a second
active-session SELECT the strategy had already made. Both spellings
are now tried.

Run the admin session bound before the active-session gate

The gate refreshes the active-session row's last_use, and it ran ahead
of the admin-surface lifetime bound, so an admin session the bound had
declared expired kept registering activity on its row on every 401 and
never aged out of Rodauth's inactivity sweep. The bound now runs first:
a request it refuses touches neither the sidecar (EXPIRED_ENV_KEY) nor
the row. Both refusals precede any authdb round trip.

Enforce the active-session gate on the /auth surface and at login

The gate was wired into the Otto strategies and SessionHelpers only.
The Roda auth app authenticates on rodauth.logged_in?, which reads the
Rack session alone, so a browser whose active-session row an operator
had just revoked was refused on /api/* yet could still GET
/auth/account, unlink identities, remove passkeys, change the password
and revoke every OTHER row through remove-all-active-sessions.

The router now consults the gate ahead of r.rodauth. A :revoked Rack
session is destroyed and refused with the session_expired key, the
handling this surface already gives an orphaned session; login
continues so a stale cookie can sign in again, and logout is answered
with success (Rodauth's global-logout branch dereferences the account
and must not run on a revoked browser). An :unavailable verdict refuses
with SessionUnverified, keeping the Rack session for when the authdb
returns, except logout, which grants nothing and is answered directly.

The join-key stamp at login was best-effort, and a failed stamp minted
a Rack session the gate would skip forever. It now refuses the login:
the Rack session is cleared and the error propagates; Rodauth's login
transaction rolls the row back. The pre-stamp exemption therefore
covers only sessions that already exist.

The orphaned-session logout spec asserted the audit_logging override's
skip; the gate now reaches an orphaned session first, so the spec pins
that order instead.

  possibly-different pooled connection and could false-negative a valid
  exact hit (greptile P1).
- Domains::List: split SCAN_COUNT so the un-MATCHed owners walk keeps a
  100-COUNT (ceiling ~100k pairs), not the 1k the MATCH-filtered index
  scan needs; MATCH is what makes the large COUNT safe (claude review).
- FilterBar + org-picker/add-member modals: disable the search input while
  a request is in flight so the visible term cannot diverge from the
  results that land (greptile P1 stale-results). AddMemberModal: allow a
  same-term resubmit after an errored search so a transient failure is no
  longer a permanent no-op.

Mint the invite-signup session through a real Rodauth login-session

Invite acceptance created the account via Rodauth's internal_request and
then hand-wrote the auth fields into the Rack session. No login path ran,
so nothing stamped the active_session_id_hmac join key and nothing
inserted the account_active_session_keys row: every invite-minted session
was exempt from the active-session gate forever, invisible to the sessions
page, "sign out everywhere" and Rodauth Admin.

setup_session now runs login_session inside internal_request_eval with the
account pre-loaded, so the same update_session chain a browser login uses
inserts the row and stamps the join key, and merges the resulting Rodauth
session hash (keys stringified) into the Rack session.

Enforce the session deadlines in the gate and let revoked cookies present any credential

The gate refreshed last_use on every request but applied neither of
Rodauth's deadlines, and check_active_session has no call site, so a
session never expired by inactivity or lifetime: the sessions-page sweep
only ever saw fresh rows. The deadlines now live in the gate's own SELECT,
computed in the database clock alongside the touch throttle. A row past
either deadline is removed, as the sweep would remove it, and the Rack
session refused as :revoked, before last_use is touched, so the request
that finds an expired row never revives it. The two values are owned by
the gate and fed to Rodauth's configuration from there, so the gate and
the sweep cannot drift apart.

On the /auth surface only the login route escaped the 401 a revoked Rack
session gets on its first request. The other routes Rodauth serves without
a login (sign-up, verification, password reset, magic link, passkey
login, unlock, and the OmniAuth request and callback routes) now continue
as the anonymous request the destroyed session leaves behind. The 401
self-healed on retry everywhere except the OmniAuth callback, whose
authorization code is spent on the first attempt.

Log every branch of the active-session gate with its outcome and in-flight state

The router's :revoked event now carries how the request was answered
(logout answered, continued anonymously, refused) and what the Rack
session was carrying when it was cleared: the OmniAuth keys parked in the
session blob, which the clear drops, and the sidecar hand-off fields bound
to its sid, which the clear leaves to expire on their TTL. When either
list is non-empty a separate warn event names them and the consequence,
so a row revoked between an SSO flow's request phase and its callback,
the one case the credential-route exemption cannot save, can be tied to
the SSO failure the user then sees. The :unavailable branch, which had no
router-side line, gets one per refused request and per answered logout.

The gate's own lines now name the join they refused or could not check,
account_id and a join-key prefix, including a new info line for the plain
revoked case, which was the only verdict logged nowhere.

fix(domains): drop the exists? rechecks after index-backed loads

Domains::List rechecked `exists?` on every exact-identifier hit and on the
resolved org of an org filter. Familia `load` / `find_by_extid` already run
with check_exists and return nil for a missing record, so the recheck could
only confirm what the load had just established. For the org it was worse
than wasted: Organization inherits Familia's `exists?`, which can false-
negative on a different pooled connection and silently empty the filter
(the same hazard PR #4392 review flagged in the organizations list).

fix(colonel): tier the organizations search so an index hit skips the window

Every non-exact search paid for the contact index, the customer-index walk
AND a 5,000-row window hydration, even when the contact-email index had
already answered. The sources are now tiered, narrowest first:

- exact objid / extid still answers alone;
- the contact_email index runs for every term;
- the owner-email walk over Customer.email_index runs only for an
  address-shaped term (contains '@'). A default workspace is created with
  the owner's address as its contact_email, so a plain term is already
  covered by the contact index;
- the window is read for every plain term (display_name has no index and
  skipping it would silently drop company-name matches), and for an
  address-shaped term only when neither index answered.

`capped` is now raised only by a tier that actually ran, so an
index-settled email search reports a floor only when that scan stopped
short, not because the fleet is larger than a window it never read.

fix(colonel): read the subscription index for status and sync-status filters

A filter-only read walked the newest 5,000 organizations by save time and
nothing else. potentially_stale means the planid drifted because NOTHING
wrote the record, so those organizations sit at the old end of the
instances set, exactly where a newest-first window cannot reach, and the
sync-health screen could not find the rows it exists for (PR #4392 review).

Status and sync-status reads now union every organization in
stripe_subscription_id_index with the window. subscription_status and both
informative sync states need billing data, so the subscription index is
the population those filters are about, and it holds only subscribed
organizations, so the un-MATCHed walk is a handful of round-trips (it stops
on BILLING_INDEX_LIMIT ids, not on the round cap). The window still raises
`capped` when it truncates: fast writes cannot maintain class-level
indexes (ADR-0002), so nothing certifies completeness for the rest.

The capped caveat copy no longer prescribes "narrow the filters", which
only shrinks the same window; it says what the filters cover.

fix(admin): return focus to a search box after its busy cycle disabled it

Disabling the search input while a request is in flight (the fix for the
stale-results review finding) blurs it, and re-enabling does not give focus
back. The org picker and add-member dialog have no other submit control, so
after every search the operator's next keystrokes went to <body> until they
clicked back in. useRefocusAfterBusy remembers whether the input had focus
when it went busy and restores it on the tick after busy clears.

refactor(utils): share the case-insensitive Redis glob helper

The organizations list carried a private helper that escapes glob
metacharacters and widens every ASCII letter to a [aA] class so a Redis
MATCH is case-insensitive. The customers and domains lists each carried a
plain escape-and-downcase instead. Move the helper to OT::Utils so every
index scan builds its pattern the same way; the domains scan adopts it as
well (display domains are stored lowercase, so that one is defensive).

fix(customers): match the email index case-insensitively and try the exact address

An exact, all-lowercase address could return nothing for a customer who
plainly has an account. The search lowercased the term and passed it to
HSCAN MATCH, which is case-sensitive, while the customer:email_index keys
are not guaranteed lowercase: only Customer.create! normalizes, so migrated
legacy customers and pre-normalization writers left keys like
Bob@Example.com in place (the customers doctor downcases both sides when
it compares them, which is the admission). The exact lookups only tried
extid and objid, never the address itself.

The scan now uses the shared case-insensitive glob, and an address-shaped
term also gets an O(1) find_by_email on its normalized form so a pasted
address resolves even when the scan is capped or runs out of rounds.

fix(customers): consult the auth database for an address the Redis index cannot resolve

In full auth mode the accounts row, not the Redis email index, decides
whether a person can log in. A drifted index entry (a half-completed email
change, a legacy key never rewritten, a lost HSET) or an accounts row with
no Customer at all left a real account invisible to the admin search, which
then read as "no such account, check the other regions".

For an address-shaped term the search now also asks the accounts table for
the one row whose email equals the normalized term. A row that links to a
customer the Redis arms missed is appended and the drift logged by extid; a
row that links to nothing is reported in a new orphaned_accounts field
(never counted in total_count). The query is restricted to live statuses
because the only index on accounts.email is partial on those, so that
predicate is the difference between an index probe and a full table scan
on every miss. Simple mode has no connection and skips; a raising query is
contained and the Redis results stand on their own.

The customers list now renders the search response's orphaned_accounts as
a notice above the table, one row per account with its status and Rodauth
id, each linked to the customer detail route by address. That route 404s
on the record fetch for an orphan, so the account diagnostics section is
mounted under its not-found panel: the diagnostics endpoint answers for an
orphan by email, and without it the link would dead-end on the one page
that can explain the state.

refactor(audit): consolidate the #4337 attempt/preview envelope behind a mixin

The two #4337 row families were hand-rolled per op: every emitter re-typed the
same five kwargs, and the correctness of the whole feature rested on ~28
hand-written kwarg lists agreeing with one another.

Add Onetime::Operations::AuditAttempt and convert all 13 cohort ops to it. The
point is not DRY -- the kwarg lines are dwarfed by the per-op security comments
above them, and those comments stay exactly where they are. The point is that
three marker fields were enforced only by convention, and each is now
structural:

  * `result:` is no longer a kwarg a call site types. It is decided by which
    method you call: record_no_change_attempt writes the operator trail
    (ColonelAuditEvent.record, result: :success), record_preview_observation
    writes the observation trail (record_access, result: 'preview').

  * `outcome: 'no_change'` and `dry_run: true` are merged into the detail LAST,
    so a call site cannot displace the marker every verb-filter query needs.

  * There is no `fail_closed` parameter at all, so a no-change row cannot be
    fail-closed by construction. A no-change destroyed nothing, so there is no
    irrecoverable fact for a hard failure to protect; all it could do is fail an
    operation that had already succeeded by doing nothing (#4333).

AuditAttempt is a SIBLING of Onetime::AuditReason rather than part of it.
Reason policy has per-op variance the envelope does not: set_suspension keeps
`reason:` present unconditionally on SUSPEND but omit-when-absent on UNSUSPEND,
so a module that auto-merged the reason would break that shape. The two compose
at the call site -- record_no_change_attempt(with_reason(purged: 0)).

Three hooks carry the per-op parts: audit_actor (defaults to @actor), audit_verb
(defaults to the class's AUDIT_VERB) and audit_target (no default; it raises
rather than let an op record a row against nil). Both entitlement_override ops
already defined audit_verb under exactly that name, so they satisfy the hook
untouched, and set_suspension overrides it for the suspend/unsuspend direction.

Also fix the divergence hand-rolling had already produced. ChangeEmail did not
include Onetime::AuditReason and stored @reason raw. AuditReason::MAX_LENGTH is
255 specifically so a reason is never silently clipped by ColonelAuditEvent's
256-char per-value bound; the colonel HTTP adapter sanitizes, but the CLI passes
--reason straight through, so a long reason on the highest-value verb in the
trail landed truncated. It now includes the module, normalizes both @reason and
@ticket, and shares one with_provenance helper between its no-change and
applied events. This is the one intentional behaviour change here.

Extend the cross-op contract spec from 8 to all 13 cohort ops, and add two
sections the per-op examples cannot cover: the envelope's own invariants (the
markers cannot be displaced, there is no fail_closed parameter, the target hook
has no default) and a cohort-membership walk, so a fourteenth op that
hand-rolls the envelope fails CI rather than review.

Every existing spec and tryout passes unedited, verified against a pre-change
baseline on the same tree: rspec 5588 examples / 1 pre-existing unrelated
failure (mailer_spec, identical before and after); tryouts identical failure set
before and after; dlq_try 29/29 and all 28 try/integration/api/colonel files
green. Every fail_closed: true call site is byte-identical apart from
line-number shifts, no emitter switched trails, and the per-op rescue/logger
wrappers are preserved verbatim.

The 9 pre-#4337 preview-only emitters are deliberately left hand-rolled and are

Give router fallback responses per-request headers

Otto returns the static `router.not_found` / `router.server_error`
triples by reference, and every application builds those triples once in

Annotate config keys with the release that introduced them

Adds Caddy-style "Since vX.Y.Z" markers to .env.reference and
etc/defaults/*.yaml so a self-hoster can tell, from the config file alone,
whether a setting exists in the version they run. 416 markers: 251 env vars
and 165 YAML settings.

Markers are inline, at the end of the key's own line, so a single copied line
carries its own version. Keys introduced before v0.24.0 carry no marker; each
file's header explains that absence. Precision is full patch, not minor,
because this project ships config keys in patch releases — rounding
"v0.26.3" down to "v0.26" would promise a key to someone on v0.26.1 that
does not exist until v0.26.3.

Versions are derived by scanning the tree of every stable release tag and
taking the earliest release beginning an unbroken run through HEAD, rather
than by pickaxing for an introducing commit. Four independent failure modes
made the commit-based approach unusable: 17 of 85 stable tags are not
ancestors of HEAD, so containment filtered by --merged HEAD skipped them;
prose dated keys from documentation rather than code, including a vendored
third-party reference doc; a Ruby-only ENV[] pattern missed frontend
process.env reads; and taking the first match ever dated a removed-then-
reintroduced key to its abandoned first attempt. Scanning release trees is
also two orders of magnitude faster, since the cost is per-tag not per-key.

Adds three scripts and a CI ratchet:

  config-yaml-version-map.py    resolves YAML settings, inheriting the version
                                of the ENV var each one reads so git history is
                                queried once rather than per file
  annotate-config-versions.py   applies the markers; idempotent, refuses to
                                re-date an existing marker without --force
  resolve-unreleased-versions.sh  rewrites "# Since unreleased" to the version
                                being cut, run before tagging
  check-config-versions.sh      requires a marker on every new key and freezes
                                markers that already shipped

The ratchet compares against the merge-base with the PR's base branch, not a
hardcoded origin/main: feature PRs here target develop, and comparing a
develop-based branch against main would report long-settled keys as new.

Also removes a duplicate QA_VISUAL_SEED block in .env.reference. The variable
was documented twice in the same section with two different explanations,
which left no unambiguous line to annotate.

Close four holes the ratchet and the annotator left open

All four surfaced in review. Each is reproduced by a test in the commit
message rather than in code, because the guard has no harness yet.

1. A sequence written at its parent key's indentation swallowed the sibling
   key that followed it. extract_yaml_sites() skipped everything at
   `ind >= entry indent`, but YAML allows `links:` and its `- text: ...`
   entries at the same column, which config.defaults.yaml uses. Adding
   `max_items: 5` after that sequence produced a brand-new unmarked config
   key that the guard passed (site count unchanged at 894 — the key was
   invisible, so rule 1 could not demand a marker and rule 2 could not
   protect one). The sequence now ends at the first line at that indentation
   that is not an entry; the injected key is reported as
   site.interface.ui.workspace_links.max_items.

2. Rule 2 could not see a marker stripped from one of several lines
   declaring the same YAML path. It asks whether a key/version PAIR still
   exists somewhere in the file, so deleting `# Since v0.24.0` from one of
   the three site.session.secure ERB branches left the other two answering
   for it and the guard passed — while a line that shipped in v0.24.0 began
   claiming it predates the baseline. New rule 4 compares the declarations
   against each other and needs no base ref. .env.reference is excluded: it
   declares five keys twice by design, and only the active line is marked.

3. `--force` would re-date any marker, not just an `unreleased` one. The
   documented invariant is that it exists for the release step alone, so a
   stale map plus `--force` could silently rewrite a shipped version — the
   exact edit immutability exists to prevent. It is now scoped to
   `unreleased` -> a release; the sanctioned transition still works.

4. Two well-formed markers on one line read as valid. MARKER_RE is anchored
   only on the right, so `KEY=x  # Since v0.24.0  # Since v0.25.0` matched
   via the last one and `--check` passed a line CI already rejects, while
   with_marker() would have stripped only that last one.

Also makes a failed git command fatal in the map generator instead of an
empty answer. Every caller reads absence as meaning something specific — no
such commit, no such tag, key absent at that release — so a command that
fails and returns "" yields a wrong answer, and the ratchet then freezes it.
A nonzero exit from the delegated archaeology script is fatal for the same
reason: its partial output is indistinguishable from keys that have no
answer, so the map is emitted short and the annotator reports success having
marked a subset. A shallow clone triggers exactly that.

The emitted map is unchanged: 220 rows, byte-identical. Site and marker
counts are unchanged at 894/529, and all four guards pass.

Date the 74 YAML settings that were claiming to predate v0.24.0

Three defects from review, the first of which was shipping wrong content
rather than risking it later.

A dropped row is not silence. The defaults-file headers and the contract both
define a line with no marker as the positive claim "this predates v0.24.0",
but config-yaml-version-map.py dropped every row it could not prove — "Silence
is correct here", said its own docstring. Silence is only correct where absence
means nothing. Here it means something specific and, for a setting that shipped
in v0.25.0, false. 75 settings were affected, in three ways: the key was newer
than the env var it reads (site.interface.ui.header.logo.show_name reads
LOGO_SHOW_NAME, dated v0.25.0, but the key itself only appears at v0.26.0);
the key was OLDER than the env var and the proof rejected it for that
(email_providers.ses.region, absent at v0.24.9, present at v0.25.0); or the
leaf name repeats so often that a pickaxe could not be aimed at it.

All three are answered by asking the release trees about the dotted path
directly, which is the method the env archaeology already uses and is strictly
better than either cheap path — it reads the shipped file instead of inferring
from an env var or a diff. It is the fallback only because it is the expensive
one, and the cost is bounded by tags x files rather than by keys, since
TagIndex caches per (file, tag) and the proof pass has already read most of
them. Adding it emits 295 YAML rows instead of 220.

Nothing is re-dated: a proved row is a two-point sample of this same scan, so
the two agree by construction, and only candidates with no row at all reach
the fallback. The annotator confirms it — 74 added, 0 rewritten, 528 already
correct — and re-running is a no-op. Spot-checked against the tagged trees:
show_name absent at v0.25.12 and present at v0.26.0; region absent at v0.24.9
and present at v0.25.0; ttl_max_anonymous absent at v0.26.2 and present at
v0.26.3 (its inherited answer was v0.23.3, from the older of the two env vars
it reads).

Rule 1 also failed a correctly marked new env var. It required EVERY
declaration of a new key to carry a marker, but .env.reference documents five
vars twice on purpose — an active default plus a commented override in the
DEVELOPMENT ONLY block — and the annotator deliberately marks only the active
line. Adding `FOO=bar  # Since unreleased` together with `#FOO=debug`, the
exact shape the file already uses for DEFAULT_LOG_LEVEL, failed CI asking for
a marker no tool in this family will ever write. It now fails only when NO
declaration of the key is marked; rule 4 keeps YAML strict, where the
declarations of one path must agree.

And the release step could report success having rewritten nothing.
`sed -i -E` is GNU-only: BSD sed takes `-E` as the backup suffix, compiles the
script as a BRE where `(` and `+` are literal, matches nothing and leaves a
stray `.env.reference-E`. The count printed afterwards came from a grep taken
BEFORE the substitution, so the release would be tagged with `# Since
unreleased` in the shipped tree while the script said PASS. macOS is a
supported host — CI runs a bash 3.2 parity gate. Now a temp file plus `cat`
back over the original, which behaves the same everywhere and keeps the file
mode, and the result is re-checked rather than trusted. Also replaces `[ \t]`
with `[[:blank:]]`: in a bracket expression that was space, backslash and `t`,
never a tab, so a tab-form marker — valid per the recognizer — was neither
counted nor resolved and would have shipped as `unreleased` forever. Verified
on both marker forms.

Spell the pickaxe boundary in POSIX ERE, not GNU

yaml_key_first_release built its pattern as `\bleaf:`, two functions below an
ere_escape whose own docstring says this is "git's pickaxe, which is POSIX ERE
— not Python's dialect". `\b` is a GNU extension, not POSIX ERE, so the file
was already inconsistent with its own stated reasoning.

git compiles a -G pattern with regcomp(REG_EXTENDED). On a BSD regcomp —
macOS, which this repo supports and gates for with the bash 3.2 parity job —
`\bttl:` degrades to the literal `bttl:`. Confirmed here: searching for
`bttl:` matches nothing, so every pickaxe would have returned "no commit adds
a definition site" and every key would have routed to the rescue pass.

The failure would have been invisible. verify_row proves every emitted row
against the release-tree scan regardless of how it was proposed, so the map
would be byte-identical and only the provenance would differ — which is the
unobservability this file's header already warns about, arriving exactly where
it warned.

`(^|[^A-Za-z0-9_])` is what `\b` means here, in POSIX ERE. Verified three
ways: it agrees with `\b` on every leaf tried, including that neither matches
`ttl:` inside `default_ttl:` since `_` is a word character in both spellings;
the regenerated map is byte-identical at 295 rows; and the pickaxe still
returns real commits (secure -> v0.24.0 @ 9f12a6d11, enabled -> v0.24.0 @
9c612ca1d) rather than the degraded "no commit adds a definition site", so the
cheap path is demonstrably live rather than merely producing the right answer
by way of the rescue pass.

so a checkout made with core.autocrlf=true — the Windows default — puts CRLF
in the working tree. annotate.py handles that deliberately: read_lines()
splits the CR off each body before the recognizer runs and join_lines() puts
it back, so a rewrite is a byte no-op. The ratchet's recognizers all anchor on
[[:blank:]]*$, and CR is not blank.

So the two tools disagreed about the same bytes. Reproduced by converting the
four annotated files in place:

    bin/envref check    FAIL: 305 config key(s) added without a version marker
                        FAIL: 605 malformed version marker(s)
    bin/envref annotate PASS: all 295 mapped site(s) carry the correct marker

telling the author to write the form they had just written. CI is Linux and
the committed files are LF, so nothing was red — the trigger is a
contributor's checkout, which is the worst place for a guard to be wrong,
because the person seeing it has no reason to doubt it.

the base ref would compare unequal to an LF worktree on every line and rule 2
would report every shipped marker as lost.

this removes. That is the same trap as the pickaxe boundary two commits ago.

Proof is a frozen payload stored on the Rack session under :recent_reauth:

  { account_id:, at:, surface:, methods: }

The four bindings the ticket names all live in one place: account_id is
compared with Integer equality; at is a UTC unix second and the gate
refuses anything older than the caller-supplied max_age (also anything

with its own store.

(federated). Everything else — 'password', 'webauthn' primary, with or
without a completed second factor — is what may record. The gate itself
does not read methods; it is diagnostic only, so support can distinguish
password+otp from webauthn-primary in an audit.

mismatched account_id, expired at, corrupted payload — every unanswered
question returns false, which is what a caller about to mint a Connect

[#4414] Add Onetime::ReauthPolicy for surface-aware re-authentication offer

The pure seam behind #4414 (epic #4408). No callers yet — this commit is
the module the tenant re-authentication UI and the future re-auth POST
endpoint will both consult to answer the one question that must be
consistent between render-time and accept-time: which credential paths
may THIS request's surface offer?

The floor for tenant safety already holds by construction: WebAuthn
`rp_id`/origin route through Auth::PublicHost, so a passkey registered
on the canonical host cryptographically cannot verify on a custom
domain, and the restrict_to gate already refuses `webauthn` on tenant
surfaces (SigninConfig#restriction_available_for_custom_domain?). But
the floor is not enough: a UI that OFFERS the button then fails the
ceremony is a dead-end that the user reads as "no valid path". So the
policy refuses to offer WebAuthn on a surface a credential cannot
verify against — on the same evidence the server would use to accept
the ceremony.

Three positive evidence rules, each a POSITIVE test with no widening
default:

  - a credential explicitly scoped to :platform matches the :canonical
    surface (the default and today the only stored scope, so a
    platform credential is offerable on canonical and nowhere else);
  - a credential explicitly scoped to :tenant with a matching
    CustomDomain identifier matches that :custom surface (per-surface
    credential storage is the future wiring in the sibling thread);
  - a caller-supplied `related_origins` set — surface descriptors the
    RP has declared this origin is part of — accepts a credential
    registered on one of the OTHER declared surfaces, and only when
    the CURRENT surface is itself a declared member. An empty set is
    the safe default.

A nil surface (:invalid or unresolved :custom) reads as "no path
here" — [] rather than "offer password anyway", because the
alternative is a login redirect, not a fail-anyway button. The single
gate `eligible_methods(surface, password_enabled:, webauthn_credentials:,
related_origins:)` is the ONE function every consumer will call; no
bespoke checks anywhere else.

The MFA-completion side of #4414's acceptance criteria — "required MFA
completion feeds the shared recent-full-reauthentication state only
after the complete ceremony succeeds" — is already satisfied by the
existing after_two_factor_authentication hook (#4410), which records
`RecentReauth` only when the primary was a local credential and the
second factor has just completed.

[#4414] Add related_origins field on CustomDomain::SigninConfig

The tenant-side declaration behind ReauthPolicy's related_origins:
argument (#4414). Stored as a JSON array of absolute origin URLs on a
sibling `related_origins_json` field; read tolerates any historical
shape (nil, blank, parse error) as "nothing declared"; write validates

query, userinfo, or fragment, normalizes to lowercase scheme+host with
default ports elided, and deduplicates.

`related_origin_surfaces` is the resolver ReauthPolicy actually
consumes: one {SessionSurface}-shaped descriptor per declared origin
that resolves to a served host (canonical-set match first, then
verified CustomDomain lookup), silently dropping origins the deployment
does not know. An operator can list an origin the database has never
heard of (a fresh tenant not yet added, a canonical host from a peer
install) without breaking the policy — the offer just does not extend
to it. Fails closed to [] on any StandardError from the lookup.

FIELD_SPECS declares `related_origins` as a `:string_array` for the
colonel writer, keyed by the validating setter, so the registry stays
the one place model fields are named and typed. The value must agree
with what the deployment actually serves at /.well-known/webauthn — we

[#4414] Add Auth::Operations::ReauthOffer to assemble the policy inputs

The single seam every re-auth surface will consult (#4414). Loads the
four inputs {Onetime::ReauthPolicy.eligible_methods} needs — surface,
password capability, WebAuthn credentials with per-surface scope,
tenant-declared related-origin surfaces — and returns the offer
callers act on:

    {
      surface:              <SessionSurface descriptor or nil>,
      methods:              ['webauthn', 'password'] (ordered subset),
      webauthn_credentials: the ReadWebauthnCredentials projection
                            (safe to render, no verification material),
      related_origins:      resolved surface descriptors ([] on
                            canonical or on a tenant with no declared set),
    }

No caller may re-derive `methods` from the other keys; the policy is
the only place that decides which paths may be offered, and reproducing
that logic caller-side is the drift {ReauthPolicy} exists to eliminate.
Every consumer (future GET /auth/reauth-offer, POST /auth/reauth,
diagnostic surfaces) reads exactly what this returns.

FAIL-CLOSED at every input:
  - unresolved surface (:invalid, missing) → methods: []
  - nil account_id → methods: [], password refused too (an offer whose
    owner is unknown must not claim ANY path works — password would
    otherwise fire from the install-level capability alone)
  - {ReadWebauthnCredentials} raise → credentials: [], no webauthn
  - {SigninEnabled} raise (any StandardError, including
    SigninPolicyUnavailable) → password: false
  - {SigninConfig.find_by_domain_id} raise → related_origins: []

The surface descriptor is still reported when known so a caller can
render a "wrong host" notice even when methods is empty. The payload
and the credentials array are both frozen so a caller cannot mutate
what the policy just decided.

[#4414] Add GET /auth/reauth-offer endpoint

The read half of the tenant-surface-compatible re-authentication API
(#4414). Thin JSON wrapper around Auth::Operations::ReauthOffer — the
UI polls this before rendering, and the offer's methods list is the
only thing it may present as a button. The write half (POST
/auth/reauth) needs WebAuthn challenge/verify plumbing and is a
separate commit.

WIRE:

    GET /auth/reauth-offer
    → 200 {
        "surface": { "kind": "canonical" }
                 | { "kind": "subdomain", "host": ... }
                 | { "kind": "custom", "id": ... }
                 | null,
        "methods": [...],  # ordered subset of ['webauthn', 'password']
        "webauthn_credentials": [
          { "scope": "platform" },
          { "scope": "tenant", "id": "..." }
        ],
        "related_origins": [ <surface descriptors> ]
      }
    → 401 unauthenticated
    → 500 { "error": "Failed to build reauth offer" }

SECURITY:
  - Authentication required — the offer is per-account state
    (returning it anonymously leaks whether an account has WebAuthn
    credentials, and how many).
  - Scoped strictly to `rodauth.session_value`; a caller cannot query
    another account's offer.
  - The credentials projection carries ONLY the shape ReauthPolicy
    consumes (`{scope:}` / `{scope:, id:}`) — no public keys, no sign
    counters, no credential ids.
  - Cache-Control: no-store + Pragma: no-cache — the offer depends on
    session, request host, and account state, so intermediaries must
    not launder one account's offer to another viewer.

The endpoint delegates entirely to ReauthOffer for logic; this file
is wire framing plus the auth gate. Tests exercise: 401 anonymous,
exact response shape, Cache-Control, serialization of each surface
kind and each credential-scope shape, and the 500 failure path.

Router: include and mount alongside handle_webauthn_credentials_routes.

[#4414] Persist session surface descriptors as string-keyed hashes

The SessionSurface, ReauthPolicy, and SigninConfig descriptors are
carried through the encrypted JSON session codec, which round-trips
keys and symbol values as strings. Symbol-keyed hashes silently became
string-keyed after decode, breaking every downstream match. Emit
strings from the source; keep read paths symbol-tolerant so a caller
holding a live descriptor still resolves.

re-authentication challenge is single-use, session-id-bound, and
atomically consumed before verification. Absent slot always refuses,
which is what the completion endpoint relies on.

RecentReauth now stores the proof under a string key with string
fields so the JSON codec round trip preserves the payload. The
recording gate flips from a denylist of non-local primaries to a
positive LOCAL_PRIMARIES allowlist — remember-me restoration never
runs after_login, so primary_auth can be nil there and a denylist
laundered "remember + OTP" into a false full-reauth proof. The gate
now refuses unless the first completed method is password or webauthn.

column onto the policy descriptor, and ReauthPolicy refuses a
related-origins widening unless the credential carries a stored RP
so a rotated related_origins declaration cannot retroactively grant
platform credentials to a tenant surface.

[#4414] Route WebAuthn RP ID and origin through a dedicated resolver

Auth-link generation and WebAuthn ceremonies have different threat
models: an auth-link redirects a visitor to a host, so it must decline
on any doubt; a WebAuthn ceremony merely tries to match browser origin
against server RP, so a mismatch fails the ceremony rather than leaking
anywhere. Split the two callers so the WebAuthn resolver may trust a
classification (canonical, subdomain, or a :custom whose CustomDomain
was already stashed by middleware) that auth-link generation deliberately
does not.

Related-origin members now carry the exact browser origin (scheme, host,
non-default port), not just a surface descriptor. ReauthPolicy takes the
current origin and only offers a credential registered elsewhere when
its stored RP ID identifies one of the OTHER declared members and the
current origin is itself a declared member; scheme or port drift alone
refuses. Credentials registered on a platform subdomain retain that
exact host as their own scope rather than collapsing to canonical.

SigninConfig#related_origin_members carries origin plus surface for
each declared entry, resolves subdomains through DomainStrategy
classification, and reuses the current request's stashed CustomDomain
instead of a second datastore read. Reauthenticate passes each stored
row's rp_id into ReauthPolicy.webauthn_offerable? so ineligible rows are
discarded before challenge generation. The offer endpoint serializes
related_origins as a bare list of origin strings for the client.

The recent full-re-authentication proof used to live in the Rack session
blob. Move it to the encrypted SessionSidecar under an explicit-use key
whose gate atomically consumes it, so one completed ceremony authorizes
exactly one sensitive admission and cannot be replayed sequentially or
concurrently. Record fails closed when persistence raises or when the
session has no usable public id; the gate fails closed on any datastore
failure and on any malformed row it consumes.

Reauthenticate uses the record return value to refuse the ceremony with
invalid_surface when the proof cannot be persisted.

[#4440] Add receipt-backed bulk audit suppression for nested operations

A bulk orchestration that calls the membership, session-revocation and
org-delete operations per record emits one audit event per nested call,
which buries the single action an operator actually took. Suppression has
to be unforgeable: the context carries a receipt bound to actor, verb,
target and scope, and each operation re-verifies it against its own
arguments before skipping its event. A context that does not verify audits
as usual, so the failure mode is a duplicate event, never a missing one.

[#4440] Classify default-workspace collisions and latch the failure on the account

Provisioning used to adopt any org holding the contact email as long as it
had no members, or fall through to a second, unaddressable workspace. Both
outcomes are wrong when the address is held by someone else's live org or
by retained data: one hands over a stranger's workspace, the other leaves
the customer permanently unable to reach theirs.

WorkspaceCollision classifies the holder instead, and the contact-email
index is probed tolerantly because it is keyed verbatim while callers look
the address up normalized. An unresolvable collision is recorded on the
Customer as bounded, non-sensitive state, so every later request answers
with one registered AccountProvisioningFailed (409, stable code and
classification) rather than retrying the same collision and leaking
OrganizationExists out of whichever endpoint happened to run first.

[#4440] Diagnose and repair contact-email collisions from the doctor

Diagnose now reports the collision classification and any persisted
provisioning failure, so an operator can tell an ownerless index entry
from a live foreign workspace before touching anything. Doctor repairs
only the ownerless case, and does it compare-and-set against the entry it
classified — a blind delete would drop an entry that another request
legitimately reclaimed between the diagnosis and the fix.

[#4440] Gate every account purge behind a fail-closed organization preflight

Account deletion reached teardown without ever asking what the account
still owned, so a purge could strand domains, live members or retained
data, and an operator saw only success or a bare system error.

PurgePreflight plans the whole deletion first and refuses on any blocker:
custom domains, billing state, retained data, members other than the
owner, stale membership rows, or index drift. Eligible empty default
workspaces are deleted through Org::Delete rather than a second teardown
path — the operation takes a self-revalidating capability that waives only
is_default and last_org, so the domain and subscription guardrails still
apply and the plan is re-checked immediately before it mutates. Non-owner
memberships go out through the membership operation so materialized
entitlement subkeys leave with them.

Every deletion entry point runs the same preflight: Colonel, CLI,
self-service, and Rodauth's close-account, which needs both hooks —
before_close_account to refuse while the SQL account is still open, and
after_close_account to apply the plan. Purge reports success, refused,
partial or not_found instead of a boolean, because the Redis and SQL
stores cannot be committed together: once the Rodauth account is closed, a
failed Redis stage is reported as partial rather than raised, which would
roll the SQL transaction back and reopen an account whose data is already
half gone.

[#4440] Report purge refusals and bulk audit summaries in the customers CLI

The purge commands printed a boolean outcome, which cannot express a

structured result and the planned actions, and the bulk command wraps its
run in one audit context so a sweep writes bounded start and completion
records instead of an event per nested operation. Diagnose and doctor
surface the collision classification and provisioning-failure state.

the one call site that builds it. Also coerce the membership evidence flag
to a real boolean and drop a debug warn left in the spec.

The shallow path a request takes must not read the global registries, and
content that is destroyed with the organization — receipts, outstanding
invitations, a description — is action evidence rather than a reason to
refuse. Only drift, foreign members, domains, billing and an in-flight
migration block. Pins the global sweep to the deep operator path.

Older organizations store the owner's custid in owner_id. Compared raw
against member objids it never matches, so the preflight reported
owner_missing and refused a purge that is in fact clean.

[#4440] Stub membership lookups in the preflight spec defaults

Default the target to no default workspace and neutralize the membership
finders in the shared setup, so each example states the rows it wants
rather than inheriting a lookup that resolves by accident.

[#4440] Stop refusing a purge over a dangling default-workspace pointer

The customer's default_org_id is used for discovery, so a pointer to an
organization that is already gone finds nothing and strands nothing. It
also dangles by design between the cleanup and teardown stages of a purge,
which made the residual revalidation refuse the very state it had just
created.

[#4440] Pin the preflight depth the reason specs expect

Operator surfaces ask for the deep registry sweep and the self-service
path does not, so the expectations name the depth rather than matching any
preflight construction.

[#4440] Annotate the preflight and teardown metrics exemptions

Both are decision tables rather than tangles: the preflight's branches are
the blocker taxonomy, and teardown's are the cross-store outcome matrix
over an ordering that cannot be reordered. Splitting either scatters rules
that must be read together, so the cops are disabled with the reason
stated, matching the neighbouring customer operations.

[#4440] Document discovery depth and what a purge does not refuse over

Records why the contact-email index must be probed tolerantly, which entry
points pay for the global registry sweep and which stay shallow, and the
line between retained data belonging to another party and content that is
deleted with the sole-owner workspace. Also states the two self-service
differences: actor attribution, and the security trail, which a caller who
can retry at will must not be able to trim.

Blockers, planned cleanup, completed cleanup and completed stages were
four copies of the same block differing only in i18n key and argument
name. One renderer covers all four and takes the failure-message builder
back under the statement limit.

Erasure must not become unavailable to an ordinary account because its own
workspace carries its own description. The refusal example now uses an
in-flight migration, which owns rows outside the workspace and does still
block, and a companion example asserts the ordinary case commits. Also
pins the self_service attribution the simple-mode endpoint passes.

original design.

  and FAILS CLOSED: fetch_claim no longer swallows errors, so an auth hash

  'claim_unreadable' hold instead of minting a verified Customer.

- The customers doctor's :sso_customer_unverified check reports a held
  record at MEDIUM with reason: <hold> and repairable: false, and never
  auto-repairs it, even under --repair. Without the hold the repair would

Operators upgrading past 0.26.5 (#3973) had only a changelog line telling

Recovered from branch claude/inspiring-darwin-62961z (715ce0831c,

[#4440] Let a caller decline the untracked-session keyspace walk

RevokeAllForCustomer follows its guaranteed tracked kill with a bounded
SCAN of the whole session keyspace, decrypting each key, to catch
pre-sidecar blobs. Every call pays for the whole walk, so a bulk purge
that revokes per account repeats the fleet scan once per candidate.

`sweep_untracked: false` skips that step only; the tracked revocation,
sidecar tidy and Rodauth row purge still run. The audit detail records
`untracked_sweep: skipped` so a zero count cannot read as a completed
sweep. TeardownAccount threads it through as
`sweep_untracked_sessions:`.

[#4440] Keep collecting contact-email claims past an exact hit on request

find_contact_email_claims returned on the first exact key, so a second
spelling of the same address held by a different organization was never
reported and the preflight's ambiguity refusal could not fire when an
exact key existed. `exhaustive: true` runs the bounded scan after an
exact hit and merges; the default keeps provisioning on a single HGET.

[#4440] Capture the membership registry once per bulk purge run

Shallow preflight discovery derives an organization's membership rows
from the organization's own members set, so a live row whose customer
fell out of that set was invisible and a shared workspace could read as
sole-owned. Deep discovery sees it but sweeps the registry once per
preflight, and a purge runs several per candidate.

MembershipSnapshot reads the registry once for the whole run, grouped by
organization by parsing the composite objid with no per-row load, and
every candidate's shallow preflight unions those rows with the members
set. Rows are re-loaded when used, so one removed by an earlier
candidate is skipped rather than reported as drift. The bulk command
also declines the per-account untracked-session sweep, and the preflight
now asks the contact-email finder for every spelling so two holders are
refused as ambiguous.

[#4440] Correct what a purge does with receipts and record the bulk-run costs

Receipts were described as deleted with the organization. No purge path
destroys Receipt or Secret records: the organization and customer
receipt indexes are dropped and the records expire on their own TTL.
Also aligns the organization-deletion table with the note-not-blocker
policy, states the accepted shallow-discovery residual on the
self-service path, and records the two per-account costs the bulk sweep
pays once per run.

[#4440] Authorize a bulk candidate before its first refusal so refusals stay off the operator trail

Purge#call refused a candidate before authorize_bulk_audit ran, so every
refused bulk candidate wrote its own customer.purge failure event to the
capped operator trail. One maintenance run with thousands of refusals could
evict the entire pre-existing audit history. The receipt-backed authorization
now precedes both refusal returns; the bulk completion receipt already carries
the refused count, and the CLI now logs each refused or partial candidate's
identifier and blocker codes (never the email) since that is the only place
the codes persist.

[#4440] Keep the colonel purge on shallow discovery

The colonel endpoint passed deep: true, which PurgePreflight's own contract
reserves for operator sweeps: three whole-registry scans per preflight, run
twice per purge, synchronously inside a web worker where a client timeout does
not stop the mutation. Request paths use the reverse indexes and the
contact-email claim; the deep global sweep is purge-one's job. A spec pins the
colonel call so the contract cannot be violated again.
[#4440] Document discovery depth per purge path and the bulk audit receipt pair

[#4440] Latch provisioning only on a classified collision and serialize default-workspace creation

Two ways into the 409 latch were not real collisions. A transient error during
classification (:unreadable) marked the account failed, and since the request
path refuses to run EnsureDefaultWorkspace once the flag is set, nothing ever
released it. And lazy creation had no serialization: two requests for the same
org-less customer could delete each other's live index reservation and
provision a second workspace, or latch an account that had just received one.

Unreadable now raises Onetime::AccountProvisioningUnavailable (503 with
retry_after) without persisting anything. Creation takes the same Familia::Lock
key CreateOrganization already uses, re-checks under the lock, and a contender
waits briefly for the holder's workspace or fails retryably; it never classifies
a collision that may be its own in-flight org. A real-datastore tryout races two
callers and asserts exactly one workspace.

[#4440] Give the provisioning latch an evidence-backed doctor release

The doctor only released a latch through a repairable index claim, so a stale
latch beside a healthy workspace, or one whose collision had since resolved,
had no operator path out. check_provisioning_failure now re-classifies and,
under --repair, converges through EnsureDefaultWorkspace when the customer has
a workspace or the classification is clear; unreadable stays report-only as
transient, and a retryable error during repair is deferred rather than
re-latched as provisioning_error.
[#4440] Runbooks: retryable provisioning error, creation lock, and doctor latch release

[#4440] Let the racer tryout accept a loser that converges before the lock

The concurrency assertion counted outcomes by testing the return value
for nil, so it only recognised two of the three legal outcomes. A
contender that arrives after the winner has finished never reaches the
lock: #call's up-front workspace_already_exists? sends it straight to
converge_on_existing_workspace, which returns nil by design. On CI the
two threads serialized that way and the outcome count came back 1.

Record each thread's outcome with a tag (:returned / :failed) instead,
so converging counts as an outcome, and keep the invariants: exactly two
outcomes, every returned workspace is the one workspace, every failure
is retryable.

[#4440] Assert the redaction on the log text, not with an unanchored regex

CodeQL flags /example\.com/ as a missing-anchor alert: read as a URL
pattern it matches any host that merely contains the string. The
assertion here is the opposite of anchored — it checks the address never
appears anywhere in a log line — so anchoring would defeat it.

Capture the OT.info messages and assert on the substring directly. Same
guarantee, no pattern for CodeQL to misread.

Accept numeric subscription period ends in Colonel schemas

Colonel emitters pass Organization#subscription_period_end through
untouched. Familia JSON-serializes field values, so a record written
with an Integer comes back as a JSON number while the zod schemas only
allowed a string, and one such record failed validation for the whole
organization list, detail, investigate and user-billing responses.

Widen every site to number | string | null rather than coerce on the
server: legacy string rows are not migrated and both forms must stay
readable.

Store subscription period ends as integer epoch seconds

Stripe hands back current_period_end as an Integer; the three writers
each applied .to_s before assignment while other paths did not, so the
field held two types depending on which code wrote it. Keep the value
numeric on the way in. Existing string rows are left as they are and
remain readable through the compatibility boundaries.

Pin billing overview period_end to a string and parse it as a date

The overview endpoint is the one wire boundary that declares period_end
as a string, so the controller now guarantees it regardless of the type
the model holds. The two consumers parse it through parseDateValue
instead of multiplying by 1000: an absent value used to render
1 Jan 1970 and a non-numeric one rendered an invalid date. Zero, empty,
null and malformed values now render no date at all.
Add changelog fragment for the subscription period-end fix

Changes
Updated apps/web/auth/config/hooks/account.rb
A nonblank external_id is now authoritative.
If lookup by external_id fails, resolution returns nil and account deletion is refused.
Email fallback occurs only when external_id is blank.
Added apps/web/auth/spec/config/hooks/account_customer_resolution_spec.rb
Resolves valid external IDs without consulting email.
Rejects a missing nonblank external ID even when another customer matches the email.
Preserves email fallback for accounts without an external ID.

[#4440] Treat a workspace without a contact email as clean, not as index drift

contact_index_blockers refused every discovered organization whose
contact_email was blank, and it runs for member-only organizations too. A
blank address is the normal shape of a workspace created through the
product UI: the modal submits display_name and description only,
Organization.create! persists nil and reserves nothing in
contact_email_index, and delete! skips the index for it. So any account
that was ever invited to a UI-created workspace could not delete itself:
before_close_account refused with account_deletion_refused, and the
Colonel and CLI purge paths refused the same account for the same reason,
with no remedy available to a non-owner.

Only an address the organization actually carries can disagree with the
index. A blank one contributes no blocker; the spec pins a member of a
contact-less workspace planning an ordinary membership removal.

[#4440] Remove SQL credential rows on self-service close-account again

after_close_account built Purge with authentication_closed: true, and
TeardownAccount read that flag as "skip close_auth_account". That was the
only production call to RemoveAuthenticationData on this route, so a
user-requested deletion left account_identities, account_otp_keys,
account_recovery_codes, account_webauthn_keys, account_remember_keys,
account_jwt_refresh_keys and account_active_session_keys in place under a
closed account. On main the same hook ran the default teardown and removed
them. A surviving (provider, issuer, uid) identity also resolves the closed
account on the next SSO sign-in and blocks a fresh JIT create on the
unique index.

The flag's premise was wrong: Rodauth's close_account only flips the
status column and deletes the password hash. Everything else is
contributed by feature-level after_close_account methods (omniauth,
two_factor_base, active_sessions, remember, jwt_refresh), and the hook
block overrode that chain without calling super.

The flag is gone. TeardownAccount runs the SQL credential removal on every
path, with retain_account so it composes with Rodauth's own status
transition inside the same transaction, and the hook calls super() first
so the feature chain runs as well. The integration spec seeds an SSO
identity and a remember key before closing and asserts they are gone
along with the active-session rows; the partial-purge example now selects
the post-teardown scan by stage rather than by call count, since the
authentication_closure gate adds a revalidation on this path.

[#4440] Resolve the closing account by external_id alone when one is present

Implementation half of b122c89e9e, whose spec landed without this hunk.
A present external_id is authoritative for account closure; falling back
to email after that lookup misses could select a different Customer that
has since claimed the same address. Email resolution remains only for
accounts with no external_id.

[#4440] Fixed the collision-evidence email leak.

- Centralized report redaction in `WorkspaceCollision.reportable_evidence`.
- Masks `:normalized_email`, `:index_key`, and `:contact_email`.
- `WorkspaceCollision::Result#to_h` now masks its top-level `:email` and evidence, securing Diagnose

Added regression coverage

organization_evidence called CustomDomain.instances and loaded every record

healthy :current_valid_workspace path. That runs on the colonel customer-detail
request (GetAccountDiagnostics), once per customer scanned by customers doctor,
and on the signup/login collision branch.

Use the bounded pair purge_preflight already uses: the listed domain ids
existence-checked, plus org.unlisted_owned_domains (one HGETALL over the owners

directions.

[#4440] Find contact-email claimants through the index, not a registry walk

Organization already carries `unique_index :contact_email, :contact_email_index`,

walk caught and the index cannot — an organization carrying the address with no

Add Apple, Auth0, Zoom and DigitalOcean SSO providers

Extends Onetime::SsoProvider::Registry with four platform providers. Each is
one definition file plus a registry line; the strategy gems are required
lazily, per provider, in configure_provider, so a deployment that configures
none of them never loads them. Verified: the registry loads all eight
definitions under `ruby --disable-gems`.

Issuer classification

  apple         issuer-capable, static  https://appleid.apple.com
  auth0         issuer-capable, pinned from AUTH0_DOMAIN
  zoom          issuerless, platform-only
  digitalocean  issuerless, platform-only

All four are absent from SsoConfig::PROVIDER_ROUTE_MAP, so none is reachable
on the tenant surface.

Apple exposes its verified `iss` as extra.raw_info.id_info[:iss] — nested,
symbol-keyed, and not a shape resolve_issuer's token-issuer branch reads. The
definition declares the issuer as a strategy option instead, which
resolve_issuer returns at precedence #1. The value is the same constant
omniauth-apple's verify_iss! enforces, so a row can only exist if Apple
asserted it.

Auth0's issuer is pinned from AUTH0_DOMAIN rather than read from the token,
because the gem's claim validation never runs: the gate reads
session_authorize_params[:scope], but that hash is built as `params.to_hash`
on a Hashie::Mash and carries string keys, so the symbol lookup is always
nil. Confirmed empirically against omniauth-auth0 3.2.0. The id_token
signature IS still verified against the tenant JWKS, so the uid stays
attested; only the claim checks are skipped. Pinning is the stronger
arrangement here — nothing in the token can move the issuer — and the pinned
value carries Auth0's trailing slash, so validation would start working
unchanged if the gem is fixed.

AUTH0_DOMAIN must include the scheme. AuthConfig#origin_from_url rejects a
schemeless value, so Auth0's own bare-hostname convention would authenticate
while contributing no CSP form-action origin — a break visible only in a
browser. Auth0.issuer_value raises at boot instead, naming the variable.

Apple requires site.session.same_site: none with secure: true. Its callback
is a cross-site POST (response_mode=form_post, confirmed against the gem), and
a SameSite=Lax cookie is withheld on it, taking the OmniAuth state and nonce
with it. Documented as an operator prerequisite rather than changed globally.

Note: omniauth-auth0 requires `jwt ~> 2`, which pins jwt to 2.10.3 where the
lockfile previously resolved 3.2.0. Every other consumer floors at >= 2.9.2,
so the bundle still resolves, but this is a repo-wide pin rather than an
SSO-local one. Integrating Auth0 through the existing OIDC strategy instead
would avoid it.

Verified locally: registry shape invariants replicated and passing, scope and
response_mode probed against all four real strategies, `bin/envref check`
passes (23 new keys), frontend suite passes (209 tests).

Fix Apple form_post callback 403 and bound the Auth0 boot failure

Both defects were raised by the automated review on this PR. I verified each
against the code before fixing.

1. Sign in with Apple could never complete.

Rack::Protection::HttpOrigin guards the auth app (authenticated_web profile),
and Apple's response_mode=form_post callback is a cross-site POST carrying
Origin: https://appleid.apple.com. Walking accepts?: not a safe method, Origin
present, Origin != base_url, and the existing allow_if only ever matches
https://<display_domain> — so it denies with 403 before OmniAuth runs, with no
failure redirect. Every provider before Apple had a GET callback, which safe?
short-circuits, so nothing had exercised this path. The documented SameSite
prerequisite was necessary but not sufficient.

HttpOriginOptions now allows a POST to an OmniAuth CALLBACK path when the
Origin is one of the IdP origins this deployment has configured. This is
parity rather than a new hole: a GET callback bypasses HttpOrigin entirely
today via safe?, from any origin, and this grants a POST callback strictly
less than that. The request phase is deliberately excluded — it mints the
account-bound Connect intent nonce and keeps full Origin protection.

The origin set is AuthConfig#sso_idp_origins, split out of
sso_form_action_origins so a per-request caller does not emit that method's
split-endpoint warning on every request. Reusing it keeps one answer to
"which IdPs does this deployment trust": the origins allowed to receive the
redirect are exactly those allowed to post the callback back.

2. A schemeless AUTH0_DOMAIN took down the whole install.

Auth0.issuer_value raises, and configure_provider runs inside Rodauth
configuration, so the exception failed the entire auth app — password, MFA and
magic links included — over one optional SSO provider. A bare hostname is
Auth0's own documented format, so this was reachable from a plausible typo.
configure_provider now rescues a raising strategy_options, logs an error
naming the provider and reason, and skips that provider, matching how every
other misconfiguration here degrades. The diagnosis stays loud; the blast
radius is bounded.

request phase, nested paths, non-SSO paths, unconfigured deployments and

failures. RuboCop clean, full pre-commit hygiene lane passes.

Guard tenant SSO against constant-issuer providers

Follow-up to the automated review's non-blocking observation, which is
correct and worth a test rather than prose.

Tenant isolation rests on each tenant resolving a DISTINCT issuer, but
:issuer_capable does not express that. Two different things hide behind it
now. The issuerless providers resolve to the '' sentinel and are refused on
the tenant surface by refuse_issuerless_on_tenant?. Apple and Auth0 are
issuer-capable yet carry a DEPLOYMENT CONSTANT — Apple's is the single global
appleid.apple.com, Auth0's is pinned from one env var — and a non-empty
resolved issuer is precisely what disables that refusal. They are held off the
tenant surface only by their absence from PROVIDER_ROUTE_MAP.

That makes the map's contents a security boundary rather than a convenience,
enforced until now by nothing. Adding a route for a constant-issuer provider
would let every tenant's callback resolve the same (provider, issuer, uid)
key and silently inherit the platform's identity rows.

The new guard sits with the existing lockstep checks in the SsoConfig spec and
fails on exactly that edit. Verified by temporarily adding an 'apple' entry to
PROVIDER_ROUTE_MAP: the example fails and names the provider, why it is
unsafe, and what has to be true before it belongs there.

[#4440] Route self-service close-account audit off the operator trail

Threads self_service: through Purge -> TeardownAccount ->
RevokeAllForCustomer and Purge -> Org::Delete / Memberships::Remove. On
the self-service path each nested op writes its success event through

account-close hook already logs partial teardowns through its own path.

Before this, a user-triggered close-account produced at least two

docs(adr): let ADR-046 ordering rules pass logout, expiry, and key loss

Code review of the ADR found that its acceptance rules rejected the state
changes the periodic /bootstrap/me check exists to detect, and left three
server-side behaviours undefined.

Client acceptance
- Request generation now decides staleness. A response on the current
  generation is classified instead of being rejected outright.
- A new epoch on an ordinary refresh is a session replacement (logout or
  login in another tab renews the sid via delete_session). The client runs
  the logout store teardown, accepts the snapshot as a new stream, and
  retires the old epoch. Previously it was ignored as a successful 200, so
  failureCount never advanced and the tab stayed "signed in".
- Retired epochs are remembered for the page lifetime and always rejected.
- An equal or lower version on the current generation is a version
  discontinuity: one immediate retry, then a forced full page load. The
  client no longer freezes on rejected state with no recovery path.
- authenticated: false is never a reason to reject a snapshot.

Server allocation
- The counter is seeded from Redis TIME (microseconds) when the key is
  absent, then ordered by INCR. Expiry and revocation keep the sid (same
  epoch) but purge or expire the key; a counter restarting at 1 would sit
  below the accepted version. The seed also covers a live session whose
  counter expires because only bootstrap requests refresh its TTL.
- TTL is the authoritative expire_after, not the blob's remaining TTL.
- Allocation failure is defined per path: /bootstrap/me returns a retryable
  503; HTML hydration still renders, omits the ordering fields, and the
  client starts unordered until the first ordered snapshot. The schema
  validates the three fields as a unit.
- The counter gets a new `counter: true` registry policy. It is a bare
  integer, not an envelope, so the generic write/read/consume API raises
  for it. The claim that it preserves the storage model is corrected.

docs(adr): ground ADR-046 recovery paths in verified code and platform rules

Session replacement
- An ordinary refresh that returns a new epoch no longer applies the

  stream. In-place acceptance depended on logout's teardown resetting every
  session-scoped store. Checked: authStore.logout() resets the auth store,
  bootstrapStore user state, the diagnostics actor context and

  paths in useAuth rely on navigation. A login as another customer in a

Forced page load
- New section replacing the unqualified "full page load". It follows the

Finding 3, version orders allocation rather than observed state:
- Allocation now happens after session load and before any state the
  snapshot reports is read. The version is a start stamp: a snapshot
  reflects every write committed before its allocation.
- The reviewer's proposal to allocate after the read is recorded as a
  rejected alternative. An end stamp only guarantees that a snapshot
  omits later writes, which says nothing about how stale it is.
- State resolved ahead of the controller must not be serialized as-is.
  The auth strategy resolves the customer, the organization context
  (plan, entitlements, limits, role) and the authenticated decision, so
  the implementation allocates ahead of the strategy or re-runs that
  resolution after allocation.
- Neither placement orders overlapping server requests. The ADR says so,
  and the coordinator rule is tightened so that every complete-snapshot
  request takes a request generation, which is what keeps that case from
  reaching acceptance in one tab.
- The total-order claim is narrowed to the order of allocations.

- The downgrade guard covers only epoch and version.
- The schema validates epoch and version as a unit; the generation
  timestamp is an optional string.
