Exempt remembered active-session rows from the inactivity deadline

Migration 011 adds a nullable remember_until to account_active_session_keys.
ActiveSessionGate skips the 72h inactivity deadline for a row with
remember_until set and refuses it once remember_until has passed; the 30-day
lifetime deadline still applies. Same single SELECT, same closed failure
posture. Rodauth's sessions-page sweep now deletes on the gate's condition
(inactive_session_cond), so an idle remembered row is not removed when the
account opens its sessions page from another device.

Give remembered sessions a fixed 14-day blob and cookie lifetime

Onetime::RememberMe holds the rule: a Rack session stamped with an integer
remember_until gets the time left to it as the blob TTL and as the cookie's
Expires and Max-Age, on activity and passive requests alike, capped at 14
days. A missing, past or non-integer stamp falls back to the default 24h
rolling behaviour. Simple mode's login stamps it when the remember-me
parameter is truthy; the session store alone carries it there.

Honour the remember-me login parameter in full mode

after_login reads remember-me strictly (true, 'true', '1', 'on') and stamps
remember_until on the active-session row (database clock) and in the Rack
session. A login that still owes a second factor holds the choice in
remember_me_pending and after_two_factor_authentication applies it. Autologins
are never remembered. Rodauth's :remember feature is no longer enabled: its
per-account key could not be revoked per device and nothing consumed it.
AUTH_REMEMBER_ME_ENABLED=false still turns the behaviour off.

Report remember_enabled on the sessions list

The flag is true while the row's remember_until is in the future, asked of
the database in its own clock. Adds the full-mode remember-me integration
spec covering login stamping, cookie and TTL, the gate, the sweep and the
list.
Add changelog fragment for remember-me sessions

Confine the remember-me row stamp to a savepoint

The remember_until UPDATE runs inside Rodauth's login transaction. On
PostgreSQL a failed statement aborts that transaction, so rescuing it did
not give the documented fallback: the next statement (the audit insert)
raised InFailedSqlTransaction and the login returned 500. A savepoint
confines the failure to the stamp and the login completes as a default
session.

Make the remember-me switch govern existing and simple-mode sessions

RememberMe.enabled? read AuthConfig#remember_me_enabled?, which like every
Rodauth feature toggle is false outside full mode. In simple mode the
checkbox therefore did nothing in production; the specs passed only because
MockAuthConfig answers true in any mode. AuthConfig gains
remember_me_sessions_enabled?, the same AUTH_REMEMBER_ME_ENABLED switch
without the full-mode gate.

Switching it off now also ends remembered lifetimes already stamped: the
session store stops honouring remember_until (next write gets the default
blob TTL and cookie), the gate and Rodauth's sweep hold every row to the
inactivity deadline, and the sessions list reports remember_enabled false.

Drop the remember deadline from a revoked Rack session

Revocation refuses the Rack session but leaves its blob in Redis. With
remember_until the blob and cookie lived on for up to 14 days, and a
config change that takes the gate out of play (simple mode, active
sessions off) would have brought the revoked session back for that long.
The gate now drops the stamp on a :revoked verdict, so that request's
write returns the blob to the default TTL. :unavailable keeps it.

Correct the remember-me changelog on migrations and the switch

SKIP_AUTH_MIGRATIONS is documented in the migrations README but nothing
reads it; the web process always applies auth migrations at boot.

Enforce the session blob's absolute deadlines at read time

A remembered session's deadline was only a TTL choice made in
write_session: a stamp in the past read as "not remembered", and the
request that found it handed the blob a fresh rolling 24-hour TTL. In
simple mode, where no active-session row backs the blob, a request that
loaded the session just before its 14-day deadline and committed just
after it turned it back into a rolling session for good.

find_session now ends a session whose integer remember_until has passed
before anything reads it: the blob, sidecar and metadata go the same way
delete_session takes them, and the request continues under a fresh
empty session, as a missing key does. The same check gives every
session carrying an integer authenticated_at the 30-day lifetime bound
the full-mode row already has, so simple mode has an absolute bound
too. write_session clamps the blob to the time left to the nearer
deadline, and a write that straddled it gets a one-second blob instead
of a rolling one. A malformed stamp keeps the default rolling lifetime,
as before.

The simple-mode spec that expected a past stamp to fall back to the
default lifetime now expects the session to be gone and the old cookie
to stay refused; new cases cover the 30-day bound on either side and the
full-mode read.

Refuse a lapsed remember_until row whether or not the switch is on

Turning AUTH_REMEMBER_ME_ENABLED off used to make the gate ignore
remember_until entirely, so a row past its remember deadline was only
subject to the inactivity deadline again. A deadline that has passed is
a deadline that has passed: remember_lapsed_condition no longer consults
the switch, matching the blob's read-time check. The switch still
decides whether the login parameter is honoured and whether a row's
stamp exempts it from the inactivity deadline. Comments in the gate, the
feature and migration 011 say so.

Guard the active-sessions sweep override against a Rodauth rename

Features::ActiveSessions overrides Rodauth's private
inactive_session_cond so the sessions-page sweep deletes on the gate's
rule. A Rodauth upgrade that renamed the method would silently restore
Rodauth's rule and sweep idle remembered rows. The spec pins that
remove_inactive_sessions still calls inactive_session_cond, that the
override returns the gate's condition, and that the sweep keeps a
remembered idle row Rodauth's own rule would delete.

End the session cookie with the blob at an absolute deadline

When the absolute deadline bounded the blob's TTL, the cookie still
advertised the default rolling lifetime: on a write that straddled the
deadline the blob lived one second and the cookie claimed 24 hours. The
cookie now ends where the blob does whenever a fixed end is in sight,
the remember deadline or the nearer absolute one, with Expires and
Max-Age both set. A session with no fixed end keeps the default cookie.

Make the absolute session lifetime configurable

The 30 days a session may live from sign-in, however active, was a
constant on the active-session gate, fed to Rodauth's row deadline and,

next to expire_after, read through ActiveSessionGate.lifetime_deadline
so the row and the blob keep answering to one value. 0 disables the
bound, as the colonel's absolute_timeout does; a negative or malformed
value falls back to the default the same way that knob does. The
constant remains as the default.

than the rolling expire_after, and reported expires_at as sign-in plus
a day. Both predate the lifetime model: the rolling lifetime is an
inactivity bound the blob TTL enforces, not an age bound, and the
absolute deadlines (remember-me stamp, lifetime after sign-in) are
decided by Onetime::Session on the read, before this middleware runs.
Nothing consumed the refusal (the env flags have no readers, #3810),
so this changes what the metadata says, not who is authenticated.

Extract Onetime::Session.absolute_deadline as the one definition of

Return no records when a CNAME chain loops back on itself

The walk in DnsStubResolver#records was bounded by the answer-section
size, so a loop ended on whichever name the record count happened to
land on. A malformed reply that also listed TXT or A data under that
name (q -> t -> q with an even record count, or q -> q) had that data
read as the answer. Track the names already walked instead and return
nothing when a CNAME leads back to one of them: a loop is a broken zone
whichever name it lands on.

Say that never_confirmed? applies to the strategy's own errors on purpose

The rescue in CaddyOnDemandStrategy#txt_check described its result as
not being evidence about the customer's DNS, while never_confirmed?
turns that same result into a definitive false for a verified domain
with no confirmation on record. Both comments now say that this is
intended: the rule is no hold without proof on record, whatever made
the result indeterminate, and restricting it to results carrying :data
would let an internal error keep such a domain ready? and the ACME ask
endpoint open.

Date the certificate observation separately from the DNS check in the Caddy vhost blob

When the probe knows the name resolves but could not check port 443,
the blob carries the stored certificate claim and refreshes
last_monitored_unix, so a certificate seen days ago looked freshly
confirmed. The probe now writes ssl_checked_unix with has_ssl and the
carry keeps it, so last_monitored_unix dates the is_resolving
observation and ssl_checked_unix dates the certificate. A blob whose
probe did not learn has_ssl carries ssl_inconclusive: true, whether or
not it carries a certificate, so the domain pages can say "active,
last confirmed X ago" instead of presenting the carry as a fresh
result.

[#4517] Add the shared allowlisted host chain to Auth::PublicHost

Rodauth's base_url override and OmniAuth's full_host resolver both
need the same answer to "which origin may an auth URL for this request
carry", but until now each composed its own tiers. Auth::PublicHost
gains allowlisted_base_url and allowlisted_host, which fix the order
every consumer must share: the TXT-verified tenant host the request
resolved to, then the request's own host when it is in the canonical
set, then the configured site.host. The raw request authority is never
a tier, so a client-settable forwarded header or a doubled Host header
cannot reach a URL through either consumer.

The header documents why the chain exists, how local development is
served by the canonical tier, and the one known limit: the port comes
from the request authority, so a doubled Host on a non-default-port
site.host yields the host without its port.

Tier tests cover each rung, the unconfigured-site.host decline, and
the doubled-Host case Rack echoes verbatim.

The override composed the same three tiers inline. It now reads

super() only as the last resort behind an unconfigured site.host. No
behavior change: same tiers, same order. The point is that the chain
now has one home, so the OmniAuth resolver can read the identical
value and an SSO redirect_uri and an email link for one request can
never disagree about the host.

base_url, which is the Host header verbatim. Since StripForwardedHost
(#4319) removes X-Forwarded-Host at the stack edge, a proxy that sends
a doubled "Host: a, a" reached Rack unchanged and platform SSO on the
canonical host produced redirect_uri "https://a, a/auth/sso/...",
which the IdP rejected (#4517, reported in #4499).

full_host now reads Auth::PublicHost.allowlisted_base_url, the same
chain Rodauth's base_url override reads: verified tenant host, then
the request's own canonical host, then the configured site.host. Rack
remains only behind an unconfigured site.host, the misconfiguration
Rodauth's super() covers. There is no localhost exception: one would
widen the set of hosts a reset or verify link may carry. A dev browser
on a host other than site.host gets its SSO URLs on site.host, as its
email links already did.

redirect_uri, and the tenant SAML ACS URL and SP entity ID. The
unit spec stubs the canonical tiers and covers the doubled Host, an

canonical), the middleware-did-not-run case, and the Rack fallback

Tenant registration and the availability ladder never consult the

configured still gets the tenant's credentials injected. Every

DNS reply classifier (dns_stub_resolver.rb): ensure_usable! rejected every
NOERROR/NXDOMAIN reply with ra=0 and aa=0 as a non-recursive referral. ra
reports whether recursion is on offer, not whether the answer is good: a
nameserver that recurses for nobody can still answer from its cache, and
such a reply carried real A/AAAA/TXT data that the resolver threw away,
leaving the domain indeterminate on every check through that server. The
rejection now applies only when the answer section holds no data record
(empty, or CNAMEs only). Restricting it to empty answers alone, as the
review suggested, would be too loose: this resolver never re-queries a
CNAME target, so a CNAME plus an upward referral for the target would be
read as a definitive "no records" and demote the domain. Two TXT specs and
one address spec cover the accepted cached answer and the CNAME referral.

Loopback DNS server (spec/support): the 0926 merge from main kept this
branch's bind_both with 5 attempts over main's bind_pair with 20. UDP and
TCP ports are separate namespaces, so parallel specs can repeatedly draw a
UDP port already held by a TCP listener; the lower allowance failed
unrelated resolver specs with EADDRINUSE. Restore main's bind_pair verbatim
so the stack converges with main.

Only alias an A-label to its Unicode form when it round-trips

Unicode string to the display-domain lookup as an alias, so the ACME
ask endpoint answered 200 for a DNS name that was never registered.

Pin what registering a crafted A-label does after the round-trip guard

Before the guard, create! aliased a non-round-tripping A-label onto the
Unicode record's key and refused it as a duplicate. It is a different
DNS name, so it now registers as its own record with its own canonical
claim, unverified, and the existing record's verification does not
cover it. Cover that in the IDN lookup tryout so the change is explicit.

Cover the IDN round-trip guard with negative and pessimistic cases

The guard added in 4370c9aac3 decides whether the Unicode form of an
A-label may be used as a lookup alias. Every key it emits is treated as
the same DNS name as the input by the ACME ask endpoint, Host-header
classification and the auth hooks, so the rule needs more than the two
regression cases that landed with the fix.

How the guard works, for one name

    typed             A-label                 decoded + NFC        re-encoded
    ------------      ---------------------   ------------------   ---------------------
    bücher.example -> xn--bcher-kva.example -> bücher.example    -> xn--bcher-kva.example  == A-label: alias OK
                      xn--bucher-xyd.example-> bücher.example    -> xn--bcher-kva.example  != A-label: no alias
                      xn--secrets-.example  -> secrets.example   -> secrets.example        != A-label: no alias
                      xn--bcher-2pa.example -> bÜcher.example    -> xn--bcher-kva.example  != A-label: no alias

NFC picks one byte sequence per canonical-equivalence class, so the
U-label <-> A-label mapping is one-to-one for a legitimate name and the
re-encoded A-label equals the input. A crafted label decodes into
another name's equivalence class (or to plain ASCII, or to an A-label)
and cannot encode back to itself, so it gets only its own key.

Behavior change this pins, with no design authority behind it

Before the guard, create!("xn--bucher-xyd.com") was refused as
"Domain already registered": the preflight lookup aliased it onto the
bücher.com record. Now it registers as a separate, unverified record
with its own canonical claim, and the bücher.com record's verification
does not cover it. That outcome follows from the wire-name reading
(verification proves control of exactly one hostname as sent on the
wire), but no ADR, README or spec states that reading. It is the
author's interpretation made while working on this branch and PR, not
a documented project stance. Refusing non-round-tripping xn-- labels at
parse time, since IDNA2008 requires an A-label to encode an NFC U-label
and a registry will never delegate one, is a separate change and is not
made here.

Fall back to the canonical index when no exact-form key matches

display_domain_lookup_keys only derives the NFC Unicode and A-label
forms of a name. A domain registered with a decomposed spelling
(bücher) is stored under those exact bytes, so the ACME ask
endpoint and the Host header, which both carry the A-label, missed it
and the verified domain never got a certificate.

record created through the atomic gate, so consult it last. Exact keys
still win, so legacy duplicate registrations keep resolving to their
own record, and a crafted A-label for a name that was never created
still misses.

Switch Renovate automerge from branch to PR

automergeType has been 'branch' since the config was introduced
(76521423f, 2025-04-28). The commit gave no specific reason. The only
recorded rationale was a comment added in c75230849 ("Merge without
waiting for PR to be created in UI") and dropped by 5bfc074f1.

In #4472 the branch mode was kept on the understanding that pins and
lockfile maintenance would merge silently, with Renovate opening a PR
as a fallback when checks fail or stay pending too long. The repo
history does not bear that out:

- No update has landed on main by branch automerge since 2025-04-28.
  Every Renovate change on main's first-parent history arrived through
  a PR.
- The fallback PR is not appearing. deps/postgres-17 and
  deps/golang-1-26-bookworm were created on 2026-09-18, after #4472
  merged, and still have no PR. The ruby digest branch (2026-09-13) and
  both rabbitmq digest branches (2026-07-30) have none either.
- The silent set is wider than pins and lockfile maintenance. There is
  no `digest` override, so digest updates inherit the top-level
  `automerge: true`. Six of the seven PR-less Renovate branches are
  digest updates.

The likely reason branch automerge cannot land is that main does not
accept direct pushes from Renovate. That is inferred from the history
above, not read from the branch protection settings.

With 'pr', the updates that automerge (pin, lockFileMaintenance,
digest) get a PR. ci.yml runs on PRs to main, so they get real checks,
and Renovate merges them once those pass. If main requires an
approving review they wait like any other Renovate PR, which is still
visible, unlike a branch nobody sees. The 14-day minimumReleaseAge and
the patch/minor/major automerge settings are unchanged.

Own duplicate 401s while the reconciliation is in flight

`noteApiRejection` returned `throttled` (not owned) for every 401 inside
REJECTION_MIN_INTERVAL, so each duplicate produced its own toast. The
comment's rationale, that the coordinator will not run again for the
rejection, only holds once the reconciliation has settled. While it is
still in flight, the snapshot it is about to apply answers every 401
that arrived meanwhile, and the per-call toast duplicates the once-only
transition announcement.

Split the throttled case on the coordinator's existing in-flight record:

- flight up: `{ ownedByCoordinator: true, reason: 'reconciling-duplicate' }`.
  A newer flight that superseded the rejection's own request counts the
  same way; its snapshot is the coordinator's next verdict

A cookie planted from a sibling host carries a parent Domain= attribute,
and rack-protection's clear on the 403 is host-scoped (domain = request
host, one per path prefix), so the planted cookie stayed and the browser
kept getting 403 until it expired. Onetime::Middleware::CookieTossing

host with at least two labels, for the same path prefixes. One refused
request clears both the planted cookie and the legitimate one; the next
request starts a fresh session and the user signs in again. Not
public-suffix aware on purpose: browsers ignore a Set-Cookie whose

host clear only. Nothing is widened: cookies are cleared only on a
response that already refuses the request.

Pay one fallback notice when an owned batch gets no transition

Owning a rejection suppresses the caller's toast on the promise that the
coordinator will speak. A flight can settle without a transition: it
applies a snapshot that still reports `authenticated`, returns `failed`
or `allocation-unavailable`, or is dropped as stale. The first
`reconciling` rejection already lost its feedback there; owning
duplicates widened that from one call to the whole batch.

The store now keeps a store-level batch (count and the first caller's
message) for every owned rejection, and when the flight settles:

- `refused`, or `applied` to any status but `authenticated`: the UI
  change is the answer, nothing owed;
- `applied` still `authenticated`, `failed`, `allocation-unavailable`:
  one `rejectionNotice` (serial, count, message) is published. The retry
  after a failure starts with nothing owed, so it cannot repeat it;
- `superseded`: pays nothing; the replacement flight pays the batch when
  it settles (ADR-046#commit-generation-ownership). A local sign-out
  discards it.

The store stays UI-free. App.vue, which already announces parked session
transitions, watches `rejectionNotice` and shows it through the
notifications store, substituting the generic error text for a null
message as useAsyncHandler does. The interceptor passes the message the
caller would have shown (the classified message when of human interest,
else null) with each reported 401; its spec now builds real AxiosError
instances so the classifier recognises them.

Follows up #4461 under epic #4451.

cannot become a silent green.

[#4579] Refuse tenant SSO on a domain awaiting verification

A custom domain whose tenant SSO is set up and permitted but whose
ownership is not verified used to log the generic
omniauth_tenant_sso_not_enabled rung and fall through to
handle_missing_tenant_config, so it could be signed in through
platform credentials, or fail with a misleading error. Every absolute
URL a tenant flow hands an IdP is built on strategy.full_host, and
Auth::PublicHost roots that on a verified tenant host only, so a flow
started there could never complete.

The omniauth tenant hook now refuses such a host on every phase it
runs on (request, callback, SAML /metadata), before the env cache, the
session markers or any credential injection, and never offers platform
fallback. The new HELPERS.refuse_unverified_tenant_domain follows
refuse_unusable_tenant_config: it logs a dedicated
omniauth_tenant_domain_unverified event at warn, clears the whole
pending tenant context so a flow started before verification lapsed
cannot complete, and redirects to
/signin?auth_error=sso_domain_unverified.

The refusal keys on SigninConfig.tenant_sso_awaiting_verification?
(the :domain_unverified rung AND sso_permitted_for?). The same
predicate drives the restrict_to pin, so a domain whose sign-in
settings withhold SSO keeps the generic path, exactly as it would once
verified. The predicate now accepts the caller's loaded records, so
the hook pays one extra SigninConfig read, and only on this rung.

[#4579] Fold the verification refusal into one hook helper

The omniauth setup hook checked "reason is :domain_unverified and the
domain awaits verification" inline, which raised configure's
PerceivedComplexity from 24 to 26 and ran the availability ladder a
second time inside SigninConfig.tenant_sso_awaiting_verification?,
although the hook had just computed the same reason.

The hook now makes one call, HELPERS.refuse_if_awaiting_verification,
which returns for every other rung and otherwise hands off to the
unchanged refuse_unverified_tenant_domain. The predicate accepts a
precomputed reason: and skips the ladder when one is given; a private
sentinel is the default because nil is a real ladder answer. The rule
itself, :domain_unverified plus sso_permitted_for?, stays defined only
in SigninConfig, and callers that pass no reason behave as before.
configure is back to 24/20, the same as main.

Part of #4579.

[#4579] Drop the pending tenant flow when restrict_to 404s an SSO route

The tenant hook's refusals clear the whole pending tenant context,
but the restrict_to rejection answers first on an SSO-only custom
domain, and it left the context in place. When such a domain loses
verification mid-flow, its 'sso' pin keeps SSO off the method list,
so the callback GET got the 404 while the tenant markers and the OIDC
state/PKCE or SAML request binding stayed in the session. After
re-verification, that leftover binding could complete a flow the
platform had already refused.

Both restrict_to rejection branches (omniauth_setup and the backup
check in before_omniauth_callback_route) now go through
HELPERS.reject_restricted_sso. It clears the pending tenant context
when markers are pending, logs the same event plus
pending_tenant_flow_dropped, and halts with the same 404. The session
cookie is host-only, so pending markers always belong to a flow on
this host; a platform binding without markers is never touched.

A SAML response POSTed after the lapse still cannot reach the session
(SamlCallbackTransport strips its cookies), so that path is tracked in
#4610.

[#4579] Document the SAML POST-after-lapse gap in the unverified-domain section

The section said a sign-in started while the domain was verified cannot
complete after verification lapses. That holds only while the lapse
lasts: the SAML response POSTed after the lapse gets a cookie-less 404,
so it cannot drop the pending tenant context, and a still-valid response
resubmitted after the domain verifies again can complete. Say so and
point at #4610, which tracks the fix.

[#4579] Run the tenant Connect E2E when the sign-in config serializer changes

The unverified-domain companion check asserts /signin shows no SSO
button, which ConfigSerializer#build_sso_config decides. Without the

[#4579] Refuse an unverified domain even when the hook loaded no SSO record

omniauth_setup loads the domain's SsoConfig, then hands it to the
availability ladder, which reads the record again when handed nil. A
record created between the two reads lets the ladder reach
:domain_unverified while the hook's copy is still nil, and the refusal
then raised NoMethodError on sso_config.provider_type: a 500 instead of
the redirect, with the pending tenant context left in place. The record
only names the provider type in the log, so read it with &. and refuse
as usual.

[#4579] Say SSO is off until verification instead of that verification activates it

The SSO form's unverified-domain notice also shows for a connection that
is switched off, or that the domain's sign-in settings withhold. Telling
those admins that SSO activates after verification is false: verifying
changes neither setting. The notice now says SSO is off on the domain
until it is verified, which holds in every case, the same line the sign-in
settings badge already takes. The docs and the 0.26.14 CHANGELOG entry
use the same wording.

[#4450] Route SQLite authdb URLs through the shared redactor in ots status

The sqlite early return in sanitize_db_url printed a configured URL
verbatim, query string included, so sqlite://path?password=... escaped
the policy every other adapter follows. Every URL now goes through
OT::Utils.redact_uri_userinfo; a bare SQLite path is unchanged and any
query is masked.

[#4450] Refuse undecodable SAML callbacks and derive the body bound from the value bound

A SAMLResponse of whitespace or padding alone matched the base64
alphabet pattern and was staged, spending admission quota on a value
that can never decode. Stage now requires at least one data character.

MAX_BODY_BYTES was a fixed 200,000 unrelated to the 128,000-byte value
limit. It is now 3 x MAX_RESPONSE_BYTES + 4,096: URL-encoding a base64
character at most triples it, and the remainder covers parameter names
and RelayState, so no value Stage would accept can be refused 413 first.
A spec stages a maximal worst-case-encoded value to hold the invariant.

[#4450] Cap SAML_CALLBACK_*_LIMIT at 1,000,000

The Lua admission script compares counters as doubles, so an
astronomically large configured limit turned imprecise or infinite and
stopped acting as a cap. Well before that, a limit this large is no
longer a storage bound. Values above MAX_LIMIT now log a warning and
fall back to the default like any other invalid value.
[#4450] Note the SQLite URL masking in ots status in the changelog

[#4450] Keep SQLite paths whole in the shared URI redactor

A SQLite URL has no userinfo, but the shared redactor read a ":" or "@"
in the file path as credentials: sqlite:///tmp/auth:archive@backup.db
printed as sqlite:///tmp/auth:***@backup.db, and a "?" before an "@"
collapsed the whole URL to sqlite://***. The boot banner also showed
sqlite::memory: as "****" because it has no "scheme://".

OnetimeUriRedaction now masks only the query string of a sqlite: URL.
The rule lives in the shared primitive, so ots status, the health
endpoint, the boot banner, the migrator, Auth::DatabaseConnection and
the log scrubber all agree. A sqlite: span with a second "://" in it
(another URI glued on in free text) still gets the general policy.
